p.seg: 1.1 Mencius went to see King Huì of Liáng.
The king said,
"Sir,
you have come here from a great distance,
and surely you have some plan to profit my state?"
Mencius replied,
"O King, why must you speak of profit?
There is only benevolence and righteousness—that is all.
If the king says,
'How can I profit my state?'
the grandees will say,
'How can I profit my family?'
and the officers and common people will say,
'How can I profit myself?'
Superiors and inferiors will vie with each other for profit,
and the state will be in peril.
In a state of ten-thousand chariots,
the one who assassinates its ruler
will certainly be a family of a thousand chariots;
in a state of a thousand chariots,
the one who assassinates its ruler
will certainly be a family of a hundred chariots.
To take a thousand from ten thousand,
to take a hundred from a thousand—
these are not small gains.
If righteousness is put last and profit first,
they will not be satisfied until they have seized everything.
There is never a benevolent person who abandons his parents,
nor a righteous person who puts his ruler last.
Let the king speak only of benevolence and righteousness—
why must he speak of profit?"
1.2 Mencius went to see King Huì of Liáng.
The king was standing by a pond,
looking at the wild geese and deer,
and said,
"Does the wise man also delight in these?"
Mencius replied,
"Only the wise man can delight in such things;
the unwise man, though he possesses them, cannot find delight.
The Book of Odes says:
'He planned the Ling Terrace,
he measured and built it;
the common people worked on it,
and in no time it was finished.
He planned it without haste,
but the people came as if they were his children.
The king was in the Ling Park,
where does were lying;
the does were sleek,
and the white birds were shining.
The king was at the Ling Pond,
and the fish were leaping in abundance.'
King Wen used the strength of the people to build his terrace and pond,
yet the people rejoiced and delighted in it;
they called his terrace the Ling Terrace,
and his pond the Ling Pond,
and they delighted that he possessed deer, fish, and turtles.
The ancients shared their pleasures with the people—
that is why they could truly delight.
The 'Speech of Tang' says:
'O sun, when will you perish?
Let us die together with you!'
When the people wished to perish together with him,
even if he had towers, ponds, birds, and animals,
how could he enjoy them alone?"
1.3 King Huì of Liáng said,
"In governing my state,
I have done my utmost.
If Hénéi suffers famine,
I move its people to Hédōng
and move grain to Hénéi.
When Hédōng suffers famine,
I do the same.
When I examine the governance of neighboring states,
none is as attentive as mine.
Yet the people of neighboring states do not decrease,
and my people do not increase—
why is this?"
Mencius replied,
"Your Majesty loves war;
allow me to use war as an analogy.
When drums thunder and
weapons clash,
some soldiers abandon their armor and drag their weapons in flight.
Some stop after a hundred paces,
some after fifty paces.
If those who fled fifty paces laugh at those who fled a hundred paces,
what would you say?"
The king said,
"That will not do;
they simply did not go a hundred paces—
yet they also fled."
Mencius said,
"Since Your Majesty understands this,
do not expect your people to outnumber those of neighboring states.
If the farming seasons are not disrupted, grain will be inexhaustible;
if fine nets are not cast into ponds, fish and turtles will be inexhaustible;
if axes and hatchets enter the forests at the proper times, timber will be inexhaustible.
When grain, fish, and turtles are inexhaustible,
and timber is inexhaustible,
the people will have no regrets in nurturing the living and burying the dead.
When they have no such regrets—
that is the beginning of the Kingly Way.
On land of five mu, plant mulberry trees;
those of fifty years can wear silk.
Raise chickens, pigs, dogs, and sows, not missing their seasons;
those of seventy years can eat meat.
On a hundred mu of farmland, do not disrupt the seasons;
a household of several mouths will not suffer hunger.
Devote care to schooling,
and reinforce it with the duties of filial piety and brotherly respect;
then gray-haired people will not carry burdens on the roads.
When those of seventy wear silk and eat meat,
and the common people are neither hungry nor cold,
yet the ruler does not become a true king—
such a thing has never happened.
"When dogs and pigs eat people's food without restraint,
and on the roads there are people dying of hunger without relief;
when people die, you say,
'It is not I—it is the year.'
How is this different from stabbing a man to death and saying,
'It is not I—it is the weapon'?
If Your Majesty does not blame the year,
then the people of the world will come to you."
1.4 King Huì of Liáng said,
"I wish to receive your instruction with a tranquil mind."
Mencius replied,
"Is there any difference between killing a man with a club and with a blade?"
The king said,
"There is no difference."
Mencius said,
"Is there any difference between killing with a blade and with misgovernment?"
The king said, "There is no difference."
Mencius said,
"In your kitchen there is fat meat,
in your stables there are fat horses;
yet the people have a famished look,
and in the wilds there are those who die of hunger.
This is driving beasts to devour men.
When beasts devour one another,
men still detest it;
yet as the parent of the people,
when you administer government
and cannot avoid driving beasts to devour men,
where is the 'parent of the people' in this?
Confucius said,
'The first maker of clay figurines for burial—
how he should have no descendants!'
Because they used things that resembled men.
How much worse, then,
to cause the people to die of hunger?"
1.5 King Huì of Liáng said,
"The state of Jìn
was once the strongest in the world—
as you, sir, well know.
But in my time,
I was defeated to the east by Qí,
and my eldest son died there;
to the west, I lost seven hundred li of territory to Qín;
to the south, I was humiliated by Chǔ.
I am ashamed of this,
and wish to avenge the dead once and for all.
What can I do to achieve this?"
Mencius replied,
"With a territory of a hundred li square,
one can become a true king.
If Your Majesty will practice benevolent government among the people,
reduce punishments,
lighten taxes,
and ensure deep plowing and timely weeding;
let the able-bodied in their free time cultivate filial piety, brotherly respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness;
serving their fathers and elder brothers at home,
and their elders and superiors abroad—
then you can make them, armed with clubs, strike down the strong armor and sharp weapons of Qín and Chǔ.
"Those states steal their people's farming seasons,
preventing them from plowing and weeding
to support their parents.
Their parents suffer cold and hunger;
brothers, wives, and children are scattered.
Those rulers plunge their people into misery.
If Your Majesty then goes forth to punish them,
who will oppose you?
Therefore it is said:
'The benevolent have no match.'
Let Your Majesty have no doubts!"
1.6 Mencius went to see King Xiāng of Liáng.
After he came out,
he said to others,
"Looking at him from a distance, he did not appear like a ruler;
approaching him, I saw nothing to inspire awe.
Suddenly he asked,
'How can the world be settled?'
I replied,
'It will be settled when unified.'
'Who can unify it?'
I replied,
'One who does not delight in killing men can unify it.'
'Who will follow him?'
I replied,
'There is no one in the world who would not follow him.'
Do you understand the nature of seedlings?
During a drought in the seventh and eighth months,
the seedlings wither.
When the sky suddenly gathers clouds,
and a copious rain falls,
the seedlings spring up vigorously.
Under such circumstances,
who can stop them?
Now, among the rulers of the world,
there is none who does not delight in killing people.
If there were one who did not delight in killing people,
then the people of the world would all crane their necks and look toward him.
If this were truly so,
the people would turn to him
like water flowing downward,
rushing forth—who could stop them?’”
1.7 King Xuān of Qí asked,
“May I hear about the deeds of Duke Huán of Qí and Duke Wén of Jìn?”
Mèngzǐ replied,
“Among the disciples of Zhòngní,
none spoke of the deeds of Duke Huán and Duke Wén.
Thus they have not been transmitted to later generations,
and I have not heard of them.
If you insist, then shall we speak of true kingship?”
The King said,
“What kind of virtue
must one possess to become a true king?”
Mèngzǐ said,
“Protect the people and become a true king—
no one can stop you.”
The King said,
“Can a person like me protect the people?”
Mèngzǐ said,
“Yes.”
The King said,
“How do you know I can?”
Mèngzǐ said,
“I heard from Hú Hé that
while you were seated in the hall,
a man passed below leading an ox.
You saw him and asked,
‘Where is the ox going?’
He replied,
‘It will be used to consecrate a bell with blood.’
You said,
‘Spare it!
I cannot bear its trembling,
as if it were an innocent being led to death.’
He asked,
‘Then shall we cancel the consecration of the bell?’
You said,
‘How can it be cancelled?
Replace it with a sheep!’
Was this so?”
The King said,
“Yes, it was.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“This heart is sufficient to become a true king.
The common people all think you were being stingy,
but I knew that you could not bear it.”
The King said,
“That is so;
indeed, there are such people.
Though Qí is narrow and small,
why would I be stingy about one ox?
I simply could not bear its trembling,
as if it were an innocent being led to death,
so I replaced it with a sheep.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“Do not be surprised that the people thought you were stingy.
Replacing a large animal with a small one—
how could they understand?
If you pitied its being innocent and led to death,
then what difference is there between an ox and a sheep?”
The King laughed and said,
“What indeed was in my heart?
It was not that I valued the wealth and replaced it with a sheep.
But it is fitting that the people say I was stingy.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“It does not matter.
This is a technique of benevolence—
you saw the ox but not the sheep.
A gentleman, regarding animals,
cannot bear to see them live
and then see them die;
he cannot bear to hear their cries
and then eat their flesh.
Therefore, a gentleman keeps away from the kitchen.”
The King was pleased and said,
“The *Odes* say,
‘Another person’s heart—
I can measure it.’
This describes you, Master.
I did the act,
but when I reflected on it,
I could not understand my own heart.
When you spoke of it,
it stirred something in my heart.
Why does this heart accord with the way of kingship?”
Mèngzǐ said,
“If someone reported to you,
‘My strength is enough to lift a hundred jūn,
but not enough to lift one feather;
my eyesight is sharp enough to examine the tip of an autumn hair,
but I cannot see a cartload of firewood’—
would you believe him?”
The King said,
“No.”
“Now your kindness extends to animals,
but its effects do not reach the people—
why is this alone so?
Thus, not lifting one feather
is a matter of not using strength;
not seeing a cartload of firewood
is a matter of not using eyesight;
the people not being protected
is a matter of not using kindness.
Therefore, your not becoming a true king
is a case of not doing it,
not of being unable to do it.”
The King said,
“How does the form of ‘not doing’ differ from that of ‘being unable’?”
Mèngzǐ said,
“To carry Mount Tài under your arm and leap over the North Sea—
if you said to someone,
‘I cannot do it,’
this is truly being unable.
To break a branch for an elder—
if you said to someone,
‘I cannot do it,’
this is not doing it,
not being unable.
Thus, your not becoming a true king
is not a matter of carrying Mount Tài under your arm and leaping over the North Sea;
your not becoming a true king
is a matter of breaking a branch.
“Treat your elders as elders, and extend it to the elders of others;
treat your young as young, and extend it to the young of others.
The world can be turned in the palm of your hand.
The *Odes* say,
‘Set an example for your wife,
extend it to your brothers,
and thereby govern your family and state.’
This means take this heart and apply it to others.
Thus, extending kindness is enough to protect all within the four seas;
not extending kindness is not enough to protect your wife and children.
The reason ancient people greatly surpassed others
is none other than this—they were good at extending what they did.
Now your kindness extends to animals,
but its effects do not reach the people—
why is this alone so?
“Weigh it, then you know lightness and heaviness;
measure it, then you know length and shortness.
This is true of all things,
but the heart is most so.
I ask you, King, to weigh it!
“Or is it that you raise troops,
endanger your officers and subjects,
and incur the enmity of the feudal lords—
only then do you feel pleasure in your heart?”
The King said,
“No;
how could I find pleasure in this?
I do it to seek what I greatly desire.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“May I hear what you greatly desire?”
The King smiled and did not speak.
Mèngzǐ said,
“Is it because rich and sweet food is not enough for your mouth?
Light and warm clothing is not enough for your body?
Or is it because brilliant colors are not enough for your eyes?
Sounds and music are not enough for your ears?
Or favored attendants are not enough to serve before you?
Your various officials are all sufficient to provide these—
how could you, King, be after these?”
The King said,
“No;
I am not after these.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“Then what you greatly desire can be known:
you wish to expand your territory,
have Qín and Chǔ come to court,
rule over the Central States
and pacify the four barbarian tribes.
To seek what you desire by such means
is like climbing a tree to find fish.”
The King said,
"Is it as extreme as that?"
The reply was,
"It is even more extreme.
Climbing a tree to seek fish,
although you may not catch the fish,
there will be no disaster afterwards.
But with what you are doing
to seek what you desire,
if you do it with all your heart and strength,
afterwards there will surely be disaster."
The King said,
"May I hear about this?"
The reply was,
"If the men of Zōu fought with the men of Chǔ,
which side would Your Majesty think would win?"
The King said,
"The men of Chǔ would win."
The reply was,
"Thus the small indeed cannot match the large,
the few cannot match the many,
the weak cannot match the strong.
Within the four seas,
the lands of a thousand lǐ square number nine,
and Qí together holds one of them.
To subdue eight with one,
how is this different from Zōu confronting Chǔ?
Why not return to the root of the matter?
"Now if Your Majesty will issue decrees and practice benevolence,
causing all officials under Heaven to wish to stand in Your Majesty's court,
all farmers to wish to plow in Your Majesty's fields,
all merchants to wish to store their goods in Your Majesty's markets,
all travelers to wish to go forth on Your Majesty's roads,
and all under Heaven who are suffering oppression from their rulers
to wish to come and complain to Your Majesty,
if this were so,
who could stop them?"
The King said,
"I am dull and confused,
and cannot advance to this level.
I wish you, Master, to assist my ambition,
and teach me clearly.
Although I am not intelligent,
allow me to try and practice this."
The reply was,
"As for those who have no constant means of support yet have a constant heart,
only scholars are capable of this.
As for the common people, if they have no constant means of support,
they will lack a constant heart.
If they lack a constant heart,
they will indulge in depravity and excess,
stopping at nothing.
When they fall into crime,
and then you follow and punish them,
this is to entrap the people.
How could a benevolent ruler on the throne
ever practice entrapping the people?
Therefore, an enlightened ruler regulates the people's means of support
so that, looking upward, they have enough to serve their parents,
and looking downward, enough to support their wives and children;
in good years they are always full,
and in bad years they escape death.
Only then does he drive them toward goodness,
and so the people follow him easily.
Now, when the people's means of support are regulated,
looking upward they lack enough to serve their parents,
and looking downward they lack enough to support their wives and children;
in good years they suffer all their lives,
and in bad years they cannot escape death.
Such people fear only to save themselves from death,
what leisure do they have to cultivate ritual and righteousness?
"If Your Majesty wishes to practice benevolence,
then why not return to the root of the matter?
Let five mǔ of land be planted with mulberry trees,
and those of fifty years can wear silk.
Raise chickens, pigs, and dogs at the proper times,
and those of seventy can eat meat.
With a hundred mǔ of land, if the farming seasons are not interrupted,
a family of eight can have no hunger.
Devote care to education in the village schools,
and inculcate the duty of filial piety and brotherly respect,
and those with gray hair will not carry burdens on the roads.
When the old wear silk and eat meat,
and the common people suffer neither hunger nor cold,
if the ruler does not become a true king,
that has never happened."
2.1 Zhuàng Bào had an audience with Mencius, and said,
"When Bào was presented to the King,
the King spoke to Bào about his love of music,
and Bào had no answer to give."
He said,
"What about the love of music?"
Mencius said,
"If the King's love of music is great,
then the state of Qí is nearly well-governed!"
Another day,
when he had an audience with the King, he said,
"Your Majesty once spoke to Zhuāngzǐ about your love of music—
was there such a thing?"
The King changed color, and said,
"I am not capable of loving the music of the former kings;
I only love the music of the common age."
The reply was,
"If Your Majesty's love of music is great,
then Qí is nearly well-governed!
The music of today is similar to the music of ancient times."
The King said,
"May I hear about this?"
The reply was,
"Taking pleasure alone in music,
or taking pleasure in music with others—
which is more joyful?"
The King said,
"It is not as good as with others."
The reply was,
"Taking pleasure in music with few,
or taking pleasure in music with many—
which is more joyful?"
The King said,
"It is not as good as with many."
"I, your servant, beg to speak to the King about music.
Now suppose the King were to make music here,
and the common people heard the sound of Your Majesty's bells and drums,
and the notes of your pipes,
they would all raise their heads, knit their brows, and say to one another,
'That our King loves to make music—
but why does he drive us to such extremes?
Fathers and sons do not see each other;
brothers, wives, and children are separated.'
Now suppose the King were to hunt here,
and the common people heard the sound of Your Majesty's chariots and horses,
and saw the beauty of your feathered banners,
they would all raise their heads, knit their brows, and say to one another,
'That our King loves to hunt—
but why does he drive us to such extremes?
Fathers and sons do not see each other;
brothers, wives, and children are separated.'
This has no other cause—
it is that he does not share his pleasures with the people.
"Now suppose the King were to make music here,
and the common people heard the sound of Your Majesty's bells and drums,
and the notes of your pipes,
they would all delightedly show joy and say to one another,
'Our King is likely free from illness,
for how else could he make music?'
Now suppose the King were to hunt here,
and the common people heard the sound of Your Majesty's chariots and horses,
and saw the beauty of your feathered banners,
they would all delightedly show joy and say to one another,
'Our King is likely free from illness,
for how else could he hunt?'
This has no other cause—
it is that he shares his pleasures with the people.
Now if the King shares his pleasures with the people, then he becomes a true king."
2.2 King Xuān of Qí asked,
"The park of King Wén was seventy lǐ square—
was there such a thing?"
Mencius replied,
"It is recorded in the histories."
The King said,
"Was it as large as that?"
The reply was,
"The people still considered it small."
The King said,
"My park is forty lǐ square,
and the people still consider it large—
why is this?"
The reply was,
"King Wén's park was seventy lǐ square,
and grass-cutters and wood-gatherers went there,
and hunters of pheasants and hares went there—
he shared it with the people.
That the people considered it small,
is this not fitting?
When I, your servant, first reached the borders,
I inquired about the great prohibitions of the state,
and only then dared to enter.
I heard that within the suburban gates
there is a park forty lǐ square,
and that killing a deer there
is treated as a crime equal to killing a man.
That is a forty-lǐ-square trap set up in the state.
That the people consider it large, is this not fitting?"
2.3 King Xuān of Qí asked,
"Is there a Way for dealing with neighboring states?"
Mencius replied,
"There is.
Only the benevolent are able to serve the small with the great,
therefore Tāng served Gé,
and King Wén served the Róng of Hùn.
Only the wise are able to serve the great with the small,
therefore King Tài served the Xūnyù,
and Gōujiàn served Wú.
To serve the small with the great is to delight in Heaven;
to serve the great with the small is to stand in awe of Heaven.
Those who delight in Heaven protect all under Heaven;
those who stand in awe of Heaven protect their own state."
The *Odes* say:
"Revere the awe of Heaven,
and thus preserve it."
The King said:
"Great is this saying!
I have a flaw:
I am fond of valor."
Mencius replied:
"I beg you, O King, not to be fond of petty valor.
For a man who grasps his sword, glares fiercely, and says,
'How dare anyone oppose me!'
— this is the valor of a common fellow,
fit only to contend with a single person.
I beg you, O King, to enlarge it!
The *Odes* say:
'The King blazed with anger,
then marshaled his troops,
to stop the invaders of Jǔ,
to strengthen the blessings of Zhōu,
and to respond to the expectations of all under Heaven.'
This is the valor of King Wén.
With one blaze of anger, King Wén
brought peace to the people of all under Heaven.
"The *Book of History* says:
'Heaven sent down the common people,
making rulers for them,
making teachers for them,
saying that they are to assist Heaven and cherish them.
Whether the four quarters have guilt or innocence, I alone am responsible;
who under Heaven would dare to overstep their will?'
When one man acted violently throughout all under Heaven,
King Wǔ considered it a disgrace.
This is the valor of King Wǔ.
And King Wǔ, with one blaze of anger,
brought peace to the people of all under Heaven.
Now if you, O King, with one blaze of anger,
bring peace to the people of all under Heaven,
the people will only fear that you are not fond of valor."
2.4. King Xuān of Qí received Mencius in the Snow Palace.
The King said:
"Does a worthy person also have such pleasure?"
Mencius replied:
"Yes.
If a person does not obtain it,
they blame their superiors.
To blame one's superiors when not obtaining it
is wrong;
but for those who are over the people not to share their pleasures with the people
is also wrong.
Those who rejoice in the people's joys,
the people will also rejoice in their joys;
those who worry about the people's sorrows,
the people will also worry about their sorrows.
To rejoice with all under Heaven,
to worry with all under Heaven,
and yet not become a true king —
such a thing has never happened.
"In former times, Duke Jǐng of Qí asked Yàn Zǐ:
'I wish to make an inspection tour to Zhuǎnfù and Cháowǔ,
following the coast southward,
as far as Lángyé.
What must I cultivate to be worthy of comparing with the inspection tours of the former kings?'
"Yàn Zǐ replied:
'An excellent question!
When the Son of Heaven visits the feudal lords, it is called a "tour of inspection."
A tour of inspection means inspecting what they guard.
When the feudal lords attend court before the Son of Heaven, it is called "reporting duties."
Reporting duties means reporting what they administer.
None of this is without purpose.
In spring, he examines the plowing and supplements deficiencies;
in autumn, he examines the harvesting and aids those in need.
A summer proverb says:
"If our king does not travel,
how can we rest?
If our king does not visit,
how can we receive aid?
One travel, one visit,
becomes the standard for the feudal lords."
Now it is not so:
the army moves and consumes provisions,
the hungry do not eat,
the weary do not rest.
With sidelong glances, they slander each other,
and the people turn to evil.
Defying commands and oppressing the people,
feasting and drinking as freely as flowing water.
It is drifting, lingering, wildness, and dissipation —
these are the sorrows of the feudal lords.
To follow the current downstream without turning back
is called "drifting";
to go upstream without turning back
is called "lingering";
to pursue game without satiety
is called "wildness";
to delight in wine without satiety
is called "dissipation."
The former kings had no pleasure of drifting or lingering,
nor conduct of wildness or dissipation.
It is for you, my lord, to decide which path to follow.'
"Duke Jǐng was pleased.
He made great preparations in the capital,
and went out to lodge in the suburbs.
Then he began to issue grain and supplement the deficient.
He summoned the Grand Musician and said:
'Compose for me music of mutual delight between lord and minister!'
And thus the *Zhǐzhāo* and *Juězhāo* were created.
Their poem says:
'What fault is there in cherishing the lord?'
To cherish the lord
is to love the lord."
2.5. King Xuān of Qí asked:
"Everyone tells me to destroy the Hall of Light.
Should I destroy it, or stop?"
Mencius replied:
"The Hall of Light is the hall of a true king.
If you wish to practice kingly government,
then do not destroy it."
The King said:
"May I hear about kingly government?"
Mencius replied:
"In former times, when King Wén governed Qí,
the farmers paid one-ninth of their produce,
officials received hereditary salaries,
at passes and markets there was inspection but no taxation,
fishing weirs and sluices were not prohibited,
and criminals' families were not punished.
The old without wives are called 'widowers';
the old without husbands are called 'widows';
the old without children are called 'the solitary';
the young without fathers are called 'orphans.'
These four kinds
are the poorest and most destitute among all under Heaven, with none to turn to.
When King Wén issued his government and practiced benevolence,
he always gave priority to these four.
The *Odes* say:
'Well-off are the rich,
but pity these solitary ones!'"
The King said:
"Excellent words!"
Mencius said:
"If you, O King, consider them excellent,
why do you not practice them?"
The King said:
"I have a flaw:
I am fond of wealth."
Mencius replied:
"In former times, Duke Liú was fond of wealth.
The *Odes* say:
'He stored grain in stacks and barns,
he packed dry provisions,
in bags and sacks.
Gathering his people, he brought glory.
Bows and arrows were prepared,
shields, spears, and halberds were raised,
and so he began his march.'
Therefore, those who remained had stored grain in barns,
and those who marched had provisions in bags.
Only then could he 'begin his march.'
If you, O King, are fond of wealth,
share it with the people —
what obstacle is that to kingly rule?"
The King said:
"I have a flaw:
I am fond of beauty."
Mencius replied:
"In former times, King Tài was fond of beauty,
and loved his consort.
The *Odes* say:
'Gǔgōng Dǎnfù, at dawn he galloped his horse,
along the western riverbank, as far as the foot of Mount Qí,
and there with the Lady Jiāng, he came to inspect the site.'
At that time,
within the palace there were no resentful women,
outside the palace there were no bachelors.
If you, O King, are fond of beauty,
share it with the people —
what obstacle is that to kingly rule?"
2.6. Mencius said to King Xuān of Qí:
"If one of your Majesty's ministers entrusted his wife and children to a friend
and went on a journey to Chǔ,
and when he returned,
found his wife and children cold and starving,
what should be done about it?"
The King said:
"Dismiss him."
Mencius said:
"If the chief judge cannot govern his subordinates,
what should be done about it?"
The King said:
"Remove him."
Mencius said:
"If within the four borders of the state there is no order,
what should be done about it?"
The King turned to his attendants and spoke of other matters.
2.7 Mencius had an audience with King Xuān of Qí and said:
"What is called an ancient state
is not meant to refer to having tall trees,
but to having hereditary ministers.
Your Majesty has no trusted ministers close to you;
those whom you promoted in the past
are now gone, and you do not even know where they have vanished."
The king said:
"How can I recognize the incapable and discard them?"
Mencius replied:
"When a ruler promotes the worthy, it is as if he has no choice—
he will have to let the lowly surpass the noble,
and the distant surpass the close.
Can this be done without caution?
If all those on your left and right say someone is worthy,
do not accept it;
if all the high officials say he is worthy,
do not accept it;
if all the people of the state say he is worthy,
then examine him;
when you see that he is worthy,
then employ him.
If all those on your left and right say someone is unsuitable,
do not listen;
if all the high officials say he is unsuitable,
do not listen;
if all the people of the state say he is unsuitable,
then examine him;
when you see that he is unsuitable,
then dismiss him.
If all those on your left and right say someone deserves death,
do not listen;
if all the high officials say he deserves death,
do not listen;
if all the people of the state say he deserves death,
then examine him;
when you see that he deserves death,
then execute him.
Therefore it is said: the people of the state execute him.
Only by acting in this way
can you be a parent to the people."
2.8 King Xuān of Qí asked:
"Tāng banished Jié,
and King Wǔ attacked Zhòu—
did such things happen?"
Mencius replied:
"They are recorded in the historical records."
The king said:
"Is it permissible for a minister to assassinate his ruler?"
Mencius replied:
"One who harms benevolence
is called a 'robber';
one who harms righteousness
is called a 'destroyer.'
A person who is a destroyer and a robber
is called 'a solitary fellow.'
I have heard of the execution of the solitary fellow Zhòu,
but I have not heard of the assassination of a ruler."
2.9 Mencius said to King Xuān of Qí:
"If you wish to build a great mansion,
you must certainly have the chief carpenter seek large timber.
When the chief carpenter finds large timber,
the king is pleased,
considering him capable of fulfilling his task.
But if the carpenter hews it and makes it smaller,
then the king becomes angry,
considering him incapable of fulfilling his task.
Now, a person studies in youth
and wishes to practice what he has learned when grown;
if the king says:
'Put aside what you have learned for now and follow me,'
what would happen?
Suppose there is an uncut jade here;
though it is worth ten thousand yì,
you must have a jade carver cut and polish it.
When it comes to governing the state,
you say:
'Put aside what you have learned for now and follow me'—
how is that different from teaching the jade carver to cut jade?"
2.10 The people of Qí attacked Yān and defeated it.
King Xuān asked:
"Some tell me not to take it,
others tell me to take it.
With a state of ten thousand chariots attacking another of ten thousand chariots,
I conquered it in fifty days;
human effort alone could not have achieved this.
If I do not take it, Heaven will surely send disaster.
What do you think of taking it?"
Mencius replied:
"If taking it would make the people of Yān happy,
then take it.
Among the ancients, there was one who did this:
King Wǔ was such a case.
If taking it would not make the people of Yān happy,
then do not take it.
Among the ancients, there was one who did this:
King Wén was such a case.
When a state of ten thousand chariots attacks another of ten thousand chariots,
and the people come with baskets of food and jugs of drink to welcome Your Majesty's army—
could there be any other reason?
They are fleeing from water and fire.
If the water becomes even deeper,
and the fire becomes even hotter,
then they will simply shift elsewhere."
2.11 The people of Qí attacked Yān
and took it.
The feudal lords were planning to rescue Yān.
King Xuān said:
"Many feudal lords are planning to attack me;
how should I deal with them?"
Mencius replied:
"I have heard of one who, with territory of seventy lǐ, ruled over all under Heaven—
Tāng was such a case.
I have never heard of one with a thousand lǐ being afraid of others.
The Book of History says:
'Tāng's first campaign
began with Gé.'
All under Heaven trusted him.
When he campaigned to the east,
the western tribes complained;
when he campaigned to the south,
the northern tribes complained,
saying:
'Why does he put us last?'
The people looked to him
as they look for clouds and rainbows in a great drought.
Those going to market did not stop;
those tilling the fields did not change their ways.
He punished their rulers and comforted their people,
like a timely rain falling.
The people were greatly delighted.
The Book of History says:
'We wait for our lord;
when our lord comes, we will revive.'
Now Yān is oppressing its people.
Your Majesty went and attacked them,
and the people thought you would rescue them from water and fire,
so they brought baskets of food and jugs of drink to welcome your army.
But if you kill their fathers and elder brothers,
bind their sons and younger brothers,
destroy their ancestral temples,
and remove their precious vessels—
how can that be right?
The whole world already fears Qí's strength;
now you have doubled your territory
without practicing benevolent government—
this is to stir up the armies of the world.
If Your Majesty quickly issues orders,
returns their elderly and young,
stops moving their precious vessels,
consults with the people of Yān,
establishes a ruler for them and then withdraws—
then it may still be possible to stop the attack."
2.12 Zōu and Lǔ were in conflict.
Duke Mù asked:
"Thirty-three of my officers died,
but none of the people died for them.
If I execute them,
I cannot execute all of them;
if I do not execute them,
I am angered that they watched their superiors die without rescuing them.
What should I do?"
Mencius replied:
"In years of famine and poor harvest,
the old and weak of Your Grace's people perished in ditches and gullies,
while the strong scattered in all directions—numbering nearly a thousand.
Yet Your Grace's granaries are full,
and your treasuries are well stocked.
None of the officers reported this to you;
this is to be negligent above and to oppress below.
Master Zēng said:
'Beware, beware!
What goes out from you
will return to you.'
Now the people have had the chance to return it.
Your Grace should not blame them!
If Your Grace practices benevolent government,
then these people will love their superiors
and die for their leaders."
2.13 Duke Wén of Téng asked:
"Téng is a small state,
situated between Qí and Chǔ.
Should I serve Qí?
Or serve Chǔ?"
Mencius replied:
"This plan is beyond my ability.
If you insist,
there is one way:
Dig this moat,
build this wall,
and defend it with the people.
If you are willing to die for it and the people do not leave,
then this can be done."
2.14 Duke Wén of Téng asked:
"The people of Qí are about to build a wall at Xuē.
I am very afraid.
What should I do?"
Mencius replied,
"Formerly, when King Tài dwelt in Bīn,
the Di tribes invaded it.
He left it and dwelt below Mount Qí.
He did not choose this place deliberately,
but was compelled by circumstances.
If one practices goodness,
then in later generations, one's descendants will surely have one who becomes a true king.
The noble person establishes a foundation and transmits a legacy,
so that it can be carried on.
As for achieving success,
that lies with Heaven.
What can you do [against such circumstances]?
Simply strive to do good."
2.15 Duke Wén of Téng asked,
"Téng is a small state.
Though we exhaust our strength to serve the great states,
we cannot avoid disaster.
What can be done?"
Mencius replied,
"Formerly, when King Tài dwelt in Bīn,
the Di tribes invaded it.
He served them with skins and silks,
but could not avoid disaster;
he served them with dogs and horses,
but could not avoid disaster;
he served them with pearls and jade,
but could not avoid disaster.
Then he gathered the elders and told them,
'What the Di desire is our land.
I have heard that
a noble person does not harm others with what is meant to nourish them.
Why should you worry about having no ruler?
I will leave this place.'
He left Bīn, crossed Mount Liáng,
and established a settlement below Mount Qí, where he dwelt.
The people of Bīn said,
'He is a benevolent man.
We must not lose him.'
Those who followed him were like crowds going to market.
Others said,
'This is a land that has been held for generations.
It is not something one can act on one's own.
We would rather die than leave.'
'Please choose between these two options.'
2.16 Duke Píng of Lǔ was about to go out.
His favorite, Zāng Cāng, asked,
'Other days when you go out,
you always inform the officials of your destination.
Now the carriage has been harnessed,
yet the officials do not know where you are going.
I venture to ask.'
The Duke said,
'I am going to see Mencius.'
Zāng Cāng said,
'Why, my lord, do you demean yourself to go and see a common man first?
Do you consider him worthy?
Ritual and righteousness come from the worthy;
but Mencius' funeral for his mother exceeded that for his father.
Do not go to see him!'
The Duke said,
'Very well.'
Yuèzhèngzǐ entered to see the Duke and said,
'Why did you not go to see Mencius?'
The Duke said,
'Someone told me,
"Mencius' funeral for his mother exceeded that for his father,"
and so I did not go.'
Yuèzhèngzǐ said,
'What do you mean by "exceeded"?
Earlier he buried his father as a scholar, later he buried his mother as a high official;
earlier he used three tripods, later he used five tripods — is that it?'
The Duke said,
'No;
I refer to the excellence of the inner and outer coffins, grave clothes, and shrouds.'
Yuèzhèngzǐ said,
'That is not what is meant by "exceeded,"
but only a difference in wealth and poverty.'
Yuèzhèngzǐ saw Mencius and said,
'I told the lord about you,
and he was going to come to see you.
But his favorite, Zāng Cāng, prevented him,
and so in the end he did not come.'
Mencius said,
'Going may be prompted by some force;
staying may be obstructed by some force.
Going and staying are not within human control.
That I did not meet with the Marquis of Lǔ
is due to Heaven.
How could that son of Zāng
cause me not to meet him?'
3.1 Gōngsūn Chǒu asked,
'Master, if you were to gain influence in Qí,
could the achievements of Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Zǐ be revived?'
Mencius said,
'You are indeed a man of Qí,
knowing only Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Zǐ.
Someone once asked Zēng Xī,
"Which is worthier, you or Zǐlù?"
Zēng Xī, looking uneasy, said,
"My late father held Zǐlù in awe."
The questioner said,
"Then which is worthier, you or Guǎn Zhòng?"
Zēng Xī, looking displeased, said,
"How can you compare me with Guǎn Zhòng?
Guǎn Zhòng had his ruler's exclusive trust,
governed the state for so long,
yet his achievements were so mean.
How can you compare me with him?" '
Mencius continued,
'What Zēng Xī would not do,
do you think I would desire it?'
Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
'Guǎn Zhòng made his ruler hegemon,
and Yàn Zǐ made his ruler illustrious.
Are Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Zǐ still not worth emulating?'
Mencius said,
'To make Qí a true king
is as easy as turning over one's hand.'
Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
'If so,
then I am even more perplexed.
With King Wén's virtue,
he lived to a hundred years and then died,
yet still he did not fully spread it throughout the realm.
Kings Wǔ and the Duke of Zhōu carried on his work,
and only then did it greatly prevail.
Now you speak of making a king as if it were so easy.
Is King Wén then not worth emulating?'
Mencius said,
'How can King Wén be equaled?
From Tāng to Wǔ Dīng,
worthy and sage rulers arose six or seven times,
and the realm had long been under the rule of Yīn.
When something is long-standing, it is hard to change.
Wǔ Dīng made the feudal lords pay court to him,
and possessed the realm as if turning it in the palm of his hand.
Zhòu was not far removed from Wǔ Dīng;
the old families, the lingering customs, the prevalent good ways, and the fine government were still preserved.
Moreover, there were Wēizǐ, Wēizhòng, Prince Bǐgān, Jīzǐ, and Jiāo Gé —
all worthy men.
They assisted and supported him,
and so it was long before he lost [the realm].
Not a foot of land was not his;
not a single person was not his subject.
Yet King Wén rose from a territory of a hundred square li,
and so it was difficult.
The people of Qí have a saying:
"Though one has wisdom,
it is better to seize the opportunity;
though one has a hoe,
it is better to wait for the season."
Now the time is easy:
In the flourishing ages of the Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu dynasties,
the territory never exceeded a thousand li,
yet Qí already has such territory;
the crowing of cocks and barking of dogs are heard
throughout the four borders,
and Qí already has such a population.
The territory need not be further expanded;
the people need not be further gathered.
Practicing benevolent government to become a true king,
none can stop it.
Moreover, never has the absence of a true king
been so prolonged as at this time;
never has the suffering of the people under oppressive government
been so severe as at this time.
The hungry are easily fed;
the thirsty are easily given drink.
Confucius said,
"The spread of virtue
is swifter than the transmission of orders by post stations."
At this time,
if a state of ten thousand chariots practices benevolent government,
the people's delight in it
will be like being rescued from hanging upside down.
Therefore, with half the effort of the ancients,
the achievement will be double theirs.
Only at this time is it so.'
3.2 Gōngsūn Chǒu asked,
'Master, if you were to hold the post of minister in Qí,
and could put your Way into practice,
even achieving hegemony or kingship would not be surprising.
If so, would your mind be moved [or disturbed]?'
Mencius said,
'No;
at forty I had an unmoved mind.'
Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
'If so,
then you far surpass Mèng Bēn.'
Mencius said,
'That is not difficult.
Gàozǐ had an unmoved mind before I did.'
Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
'Is there a way to have an unmoved mind?'
Mencius said,
'Yes.'
Běigōng Yóu nurtured his courage in this way:
he did not yield his skin;
he did not avoid with his eyes;
if he thought he had been humiliated by one hair's breadth by another,
it was to him like being flogged in the marketplace or in the court;
he would not submit to a coarse-garmented commoner,
nor would he submit to a lord of a ten-thousand-chariot state;
he regarded stabbing a lord of a ten-thousand-chariot state,
as if stabbing a coarse-garmented commoner;
he had no awe for the feudal lords;
if harsh words came to him,
he would surely retaliate.
Mèng Shīshè nurtured his courage in this way,
saying:
"I regard being unable to win as if it were winning;
to measure the enemy and then advance,
to consider victory and then engage,
this is to be afraid of the three armies.
How could Shè be certain of victory?
It is only that he is able to be without fear."
Mèng Shīshè resembled Zēngzǐ,
Běigōng Yóu resembled Zǐxià.
As for the courage of these two men,
I do not know which was superior,
yet Mèng Shīshè grasped the essential.
Formerly, Zēngzǐ spoke to Zǐxiāng, saying:
"Do you delight in courage, Sir?
I once heard about great courage from the Master:
If on self-examination I find myself not upright,
then even a coarse-garmented commoner,
I will surely be fearful of him;
if on self-examination I find myself upright,
then even if there be thousands and ten-thousands, I will go forward."
Mèng Shīshè's guarding of his qi,
yet was inferior to Zēngzǐ's grasping the essential.
[The disciple] said:
"I venture to ask,
about the Master's unperturbed mind and Gàozǐ's unperturbed mind,
may I hear about them?"
[Mèngzǐ] said: "Gàozǐ said:
'If you do not attain it in words,
do not seek it in the mind;
if you do not attain it in the mind,
do not seek it in the qi.'
If you do not attain it in the mind,
do not seek it in the qi—
that is acceptable;
if you do not attain it in words,
do not seek it in the mind—
that is not acceptable.
Now, the will is the commander of the qi,
and the qi is that which fills the body.
The will reaches its utmost,
and the qi follows after it;
therefore it is said:
'Hold fast to your will,
and do not violently agitate your qi.'"
[The disciple] said: "Since you say: 'The will reaches its utmost,
and the qi follows after it,'
you also say:
'Hold fast to your will,
and do not violently agitate your qi'—
why is this?"
[Mèngzǐ] said:
"If the will is concentrated, it moves the qi;
if the qi is concentrated, it moves the will.
Now, those who stumble and those who run,
this is the qi [acting],
yet it in turn moves the mind."
[The disciple] said: "I venture to ask, in what does the Master excel?"
[Mèngzǐ] said:
"I understand words,
and I am skilled in nurturing my vast, flowing qi."
[The disciple] said: "I venture to ask, what is meant by 'vast, flowing qi'?"
[Mèngzǐ] said:
"It is difficult to speak of.
As for this qi,
it is supremely great and supremely unyielding;
if one nurtures it with uprightness and does not harm it,
then it fills the space between Heaven and Earth.
As for this qi,
it is matched with righteousness and the Dao;
without these, it becomes starved.
It is produced by the accumulation of righteous deeds,
not obtained by occasional acts of righteousness.
If one's actions are not satisfactory in the mind,
then it becomes starved."
Therefore I say:
"Gàozǐ never understood righteousness,
because he treated it as external.
One must constantly be engaged in it,
yet without being fixated on it;
let the mind not forget it,
and do not help it grow.
Do not be like the man of Sòng:
There was a man of Sòng who, worried that his seedlings were not growing, pulled them up;
he returned home in a weary state,
and said to his family:
'Today I am exhausted!
I have helped the seedlings grow!'
His son rushed out to look at them,
and the seedlings were withered."
In the world, those who do not help seedlings grow are few.
Those who abandon them as useless,
these are the ones who do not weed the seedlings;
those who help them grow,
these are the ones who pull up the seedlings—
this is not only useless,
but also harms them.
"What is meant by 'understanding words'?"
[Mèngzǐ] said:
"From one-sided words, I know what they conceal;
from excessive words, I know what they are trapped in;
from depraved words, I know what they deviate from;
from evasive words, I know what they are exhausted in.
When these arise in the mind,
they harm government;
when they are manifested in government,
they harm affairs.
If a sage were to arise again,
he would surely follow my words."
[The disciple said:] "Zǎiwǒ and Zǐgòng were skilled in persuasive speech;
Rǎn Niú, Mǐnzǐ, and Yányuān were skilled in speaking of virtuous conduct.
Kǒngzǐ combined these,
saying:
'As for eloquence in speech,
I am not capable.'
Then, Master, are you already a sage?"
[Mèngzǐ] said:
"Alas!
What are these words?
Formerly, Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
'Master, are you a sage?'
Kǒngzǐ said:
'I am not capable of being a sage;
I study without satiety and teach without weariness.'
Zǐgòng said:
'To study without satiety—
that is wisdom;
to teach without weariness—
that is benevolence.
Being benevolent and wise,
Master, you are indeed a sage.'
Now, even the sage Kǒngzǐ did not claim that status—
what are these words?"
[The disciple said:] "Formerly I heard it said:
Zǐxià, Zǐyóu, and Zǐzhāng
each had one part of the sage's body,
while Rǎn Niú, Mǐnzǐ, and Yányuān
had the whole form but in a lesser degree.
I venture to ask where you would place yourself."
[Mèngzǐ] said:
"Let us set this aside for now."
[The disciple] said:
"What about Bóyí and Yī Yǐn?"
[Mèngzǐ] said:
"Their paths were different.
He would not serve a ruler who was not his own,
nor command people who were not his own;
in order, he would advance,
in disorder, he would withdraw—
that was Bóyí.
What ruler could he not serve?
What people could he not command?
In order, he would advance,
in disorder, he would also advance—
that was Yī Yǐn.
He would take office when it was proper to take office,
stop when it was proper to stop,
remain long when it was proper to remain long,
leave quickly when it was proper to leave quickly—
that was Kǒngzǐ.
All were ancient sages;
I have not been able to act like them;
as for what I wish,
it is to learn from Kǒngzǐ."
[The disciple said:] "Are Bóyí and Yī Yǐn, in relation to Kǒngzǐ,
fully comparable?"
[Mèngzǐ] said:
"No;
since the birth of mankind,
there has never been such a one as Kǒngzǐ."
[The disciple said:] "Yet is there something in common?"
[Mèngzǐ] said:
"Yes.
If they were granted a hundred li of territory and established as rulers,
they could all bring the feudal lords to court and possess the world;
but to commit one unjust act,
to kill one innocent person,
and thereby gain the world—
none of them would do it.
In this they are the same."
He said:
"May I venture to ask what distinguishes them?"
The reply was:
Zài Wǒ, Zǐ Gòng, and Yǒu Ruò
had wisdom sufficient to recognize a sage,
and they were not so base as to flatter those they admired.
Zài Wǒ said:
'In my view of our Master,
he is far superior to Yáo and Shùn.'
Zǐ Gòng said:
'By seeing the rites of a state, one knows its government;
by hearing its music, one knows its virtue.
From a hundred generations hence,
ranking the kings of a hundred generations,
none can surpass him.
Since the birth of mankind,
there has been no one like our Master.'
Yǒu Ruò said:
'Is it only among men?
The qílín among beasts,
the fènghuáng among birds,
Mount Tài among mounds,
rivers and seas among puddles—
they are of the same kind.
The sage among men
is also of the same kind.
Yet he rises above his kind,
stands out from the multitude.
Since the birth of mankind,
there has been none more excellent than Confucius.'"
3.3 Mencius said:
"He who uses force as a pretext for benevolence is a hegemon;
a hegemon must possess a large state.
He who practices benevolence through virtue becomes a true king;
a true king does not depend on size—
Tāng ruled with seventy lǐ,
King Wén with a hundred lǐ.
"When force subdues others,
they do not submit willingly;
they submit because their strength is insufficient.
When virtue subdues others,
they are delighted in their hearts and truly submit,
as the seventy disciples submitted to Confucius.
The Book of Odes says:
'From west to east,
from south to north,
no one is unwilling to submit.'
This is what is meant."
3.4 Mencius said:
"Benevolence brings honor;
lack of benevolence brings disgrace.
Now to dislike disgrace yet dwell in lack of benevolence
is like disliking dampness yet living in a low place.
If you dislike it,
nothing is better than to value virtue and honor scholars,
placing the worthy in office
and the capable in positions.
While the state is at peace,
take that time to clarify its policies and penalties.
Even a large state
will surely stand in awe of you.
The Book of Odes says:
'Before the sky darkens with rain,
strip the mulberry roots,
bind tight the windows and doors.
Now those below,
who dares to insult me?'
Confucius said:
'The one who made this ode
understood the Way!
If one can govern his state,
who dares to insult him?'
But when the state is at peace,
if one indulges in pleasure and idleness,
that is to seek misfortune for oneself.
Good fortune and misfortune are never not sought by oneself.
The Book of Odes says:
'Ever reflect on matching Heaven's decree,
and seek much good fortune for yourself.'
The Grand Oath says:
'When Heaven brings calamity,
it can still be escaped;
when you bring calamity yourself,
you cannot survive.'
This is what is meant."
3.5 Mencius said:
"Honor the worthy and employ the capable,
and let outstanding men hold office,
then all scholars under Heaven will be delighted and wish to stand in your court.
If the marketplaces levy tax on storage but not on goods,
or regulate without taxing storage,
then all merchants under Heaven will be delighted and wish to store goods in your markets.
If at borders only inspection is made without taxation,
then all travelers under Heaven will be delighted and wish to travel on your roads.
If farmers assist in public fields but are not taxed,
then all farmers under Heaven will be delighted and wish to farm your lands.
If there is no levy of corvée or fines on dwellings,
then all people under Heaven will be delighted and wish to become your subjects.
If you truly can practice these five things,
then the people of neighboring states will look up to you as a parent.
To lead their children to attack their parent—
since the birth of mankind, no one has succeeded in such an endeavor.
Thus,
you will be invincible under Heaven.
Being invincible under Heaven is being a minister of Heaven.
Yet if one does not become a true king,
this has never happened."
3.6 Mencius said:
"All men have a heart that cannot bear to see others suffer.
The ancient kings had this heart,
and so they had a government that could not bear to see others suffer.
With such a heart,
practicing such a government,
governing the world is like turning it in the palm of the hand.
Why do I say all men have this heart?
Now, if someone suddenly sees a child about to fall into a well,
they will all feel alarm and compassion—
not to gain favor with the child's parents,
not to seek praise from neighbors and friends,
not because they dislike the child's cry.
From this we see:
without a compassionate heart,
one is not human;
without a heart of shame,
one is not human;
without a heart of deference,
one is not human;
without a heart of right and wrong,
one is not human.
The compassionate heart is the beginning of benevolence;
the heart of shame is the beginning of righteousness;
the heart of deference is the beginning of propriety;
the heart of right and wrong is the beginning of wisdom.
Having these four beginnings
is like having four limbs.
To have these four beginnings yet claim inability
is to harm oneself;
to claim one's ruler cannot do it
is to harm one's ruler.
All who have these four beginnings within themselves
know to expand and fill them,
like a fire just kindled,
like a spring just breaking through.
If you can fill them,
they will be enough to protect the four seas;
if you do not fill them,
they will not be enough to serve your parents."
3.7 Mencius said:
"Is the arrow-maker less benevolent than the armor-maker?
The arrow-maker only fears not harming others,
the armor-maker only fears harming others.
The shaman and the coffin-maker are similar.
Thus one must be careful in choosing one's craft.
Confucius said:
'Living in benevolence is beautiful.
If you choose not to dwell in benevolence,
how can you be wise?'
Benevolence is Heaven's noble title
and man's peaceful dwelling.
To be un-benevolent when nothing prevents it
is to be unwise.
To lack benevolence and wisdom,
to lack propriety and righteousness,
is to be a servant of others.
To be a servant yet be ashamed of serving
is like a bow-maker ashamed of making bows,
or an arrow-maker ashamed of making arrows.
If you are ashamed,
nothing is better than practicing benevolence.
The benevolent person is like an archer:
the archer corrects himself before shooting;
if he shoots and misses,
he does not blame those who surpass him,
but seeks the cause within himself."
3.8 Mencius said:
"Zǐ Lù,
when told of his faults, rejoiced.
Yǔ, upon hearing good words, bowed.
Great Shùn went further:
he shared goodness with others,
cast aside his own views to follow others,
and delighted in taking from others to practice goodness.
From his days of plowing, making pottery, and fishing
to becoming emperor,
there was nothing he did not take from others.
Taking from others to practice goodness
is to help others practice goodness.
Thus the greatest thing for a junzi is to help others practice goodness."
3.9 Mencius said:
"Bó Yí would serve no ruler he deemed unworthy,
and befriend no friend he deemed unworthy.
He would not stand in the court of an evil man,
nor speak with an evil man.
To stand in an evil man's court
or speak with an evil man
was to him like sitting in mud and ashes in court robes and cap."
Extending this aversion to evil,
if he thought of standing with a fellow villager,
whose cap was not properly adjusted,
he would leave him with a cold look,
as if he would be defiled.
Therefore, although a feudal lord might come with commendable words and invitations,
he would not accept them.
Not accepting them,
this was because he would not stoop to associate with them.
Liǔ Xiàhuì was not ashamed of a foul prince,
nor did he disdain a lowly office.
When promoted, he did not conceal his virtue,
but always acted according to the Way.
When passed over and left unused, he did not complain.
When reduced to straits and poverty, he was not distressed.
Therefore he said:
"You are you,
and I am I.
Even if you stand naked and uncovered beside me,
how can you defile me?"
Therefore, he would freely associate with others
without losing himself.
If someone pulled him to stop, he would stop.
Pulling him to stop and he stopping,
this was because he would not stoop to leave.
Mencius said:
"Bóyí was too narrow-minded,
Liǔ Xiàhuì was not respectful.
Narrow-mindedness and lack of respect
are not what a gentleman follows."
4.1 Mencius said:
"Heaven's timing is not as good as Earth's advantage;
Earth's advantage is not as good as human harmony.
A city of three lǐ,
with a walled suburb of seven lǐ,
invested and attacked, yet not overcome.
To invest and attack it,
one must have obtained Heaven's timing;
yet if it is not overcome,
this is because Heaven's timing is not as good as Earth's advantage.
The walls are not low,
the moats are not shallow,
the weapons and armor are not weak and ineffective,
the grain and provisions are not scarce;
yet they abandon and flee,
this is because Earth's advantage is not as good as human harmony.
Therefore it is said:
To delimit the people is not by borders;
to secure the state is not by the danger of mountains and streams;
to awe the world is not by the sharpness of weapons.
One who gains the Way has many helpers;
one who loses the Way has few helpers.
At the extreme of few helpers,
even relatives rebel against him;
at the extreme of many helpers,
the whole world follows him.
Using what the whole world follows,
to attack what relatives rebel against;
therefore the gentleman either does not fight,
or if he fights, he is sure to win."
4.2 Mencius was about to go to court to see the king,
when the king sent a messenger, saying:
"I was intending to come and see you,
but I have a cold,
and cannot expose myself to the wind.
In the morning, I will hold court;
I do not know if I may be permitted to see you then?"
The reply was:
"Unfortunately I am ill,
and cannot come to court."
The next day, he went out to offer condolences at the Dōngguō family.
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"Yesterday you excused yourself on grounds of illness,
but today you go to offer condolences;
perhaps this is not proper?"
Mencius said:
"Yesterday I was ill;
today I am recovered.
Why should I not offer condolences?"
The king sent a messenger to inquire after his illness,
and a physician came.
Mèng Zhòngzǐ replied:
"Yesterday, when the king's command came,
he was suffering from a minor ailment,
and could not come to court.
Today he is somewhat better,
and has hurried to court;
I do not know if he has arrived or not."
He then sent several men to intercept him on the road, saying:
"Please by all means do not go home,
but proceed to court!"
Forced to do so, Mencius went to spend the night at Jǐng Chǒu's place.
Jǐngzǐ said:
"Within the family, there is the relationship of father and son;
outside, there is the relationship of prince and minister.
These are the great human relationships.
Between father and son, affection is paramount;
between prince and minister, respect is paramount.
I see that the king respects you,
but I do not see how you respect the king."
Mencius said:
"Oh! What words are these!
Among the people of Qí, there is none who speak of benevolence and righteousness to the king.
Do they think benevolence and righteousness are not good?
In their hearts, they say:
'Is he worth speaking to about benevolence and righteousness?' — that is all.
Then there is no disrespect greater than this.
I dare not set before the king anything but the Way of Yáo and Shùn.
Therefore none in Qí respects the king as I do."
Jǐngzǐ said:
"No; that is not what I mean.
The Book of Rites says:
When a father calls,
one does not say 'yes' but goes;
when the prince summons, one does not wait for the carriage.
You had intended to go to court,
but hearing the king's command, you did not go.
This seems not to accord with the rules of propriety."
Mencius said:
"Is that what you mean?
Zēngzǐ said:
'The wealth of Jìn and Chǔ cannot be attained;
they have their wealth,
and I have my benevolence;
they have their rank,
and I have my righteousness.
Why should I feel inferior?'
Would Zēngzǐ have said this
if it were not righteous?
This represents another principle.
In the world, there are three universally honored things:
rank is one,
age is one,
virtue is one.
At court, nothing surpasses rank;
in the village, nothing surpasses age;
in assisting the world and ruling the people, nothing surpasses virtue.
How can one possess only one of these and slight the other two?
Therefore a prince who is about to accomplish great deeds
must have ministers he does not summon;
if he wishes to consult them, he goes to them.
To honor virtue and delight in the Way, unless he acts thus,
he is not fit for great achievement.
Thus Tāng with respect to Yī Yǐn
first learned from him and then made him his minister;
therefore he became king without effort.
Duke Huán with respect to Guǎn Zhòng
first learned from him and then made him his minister;
therefore he became hegemon without effort.
Now the territories of the world are equal and their virtues alike;
none can excel over another.
This is for no other reason
than that they like to have those whom they teach as ministers,
and do not like to have those from whom they learn as ministers.
Tāng with respect to Yī Yǐn
and Duke Huán with respect to Guǎn Zhòng
dared not summon them.
Even Guǎn Zhòng could not be summoned,
how much less one who is not even as good as Guǎn Zhòng?"
4.3 Chén Zhēn asked:
"Formerly in Qí,
the king gave you a gift of one hundred yì of fine gold, and you did not accept;
in Sòng,
the gift was seventy yì, and you accepted;
in Xuē,
the gift was fifty yì, and you accepted.
If your not accepting before was right,
then your accepting today is wrong;
if your accepting today is right,
then your not accepting before is wrong.
Master, you must fall into one of these cases."
Mencius said:
"Both were right.
When I was in Sòng,
I was about to travel far;
those who travel must be given travel expenses;
the giver said:
'A gift for traveling expenses.'
Why should I not accept it?
When I was in Xuē,
I had concerns about safety;
the giver said:
'Hearing that you are taking precautions,
I give this for purchasing weapons.'
Why should I not accept it?
But in Qí,
there was no such reason.
Giving a gift without reason
is to bribe me.
How can a gentleman be taken by bribery?"
4.4 Mencius went to Pínglù and
said to its governor:
"If one of your soldiers armed with halberds
left his post three times in a single day,
would you dismiss him or not?"
Mencius said,
"There is no need to wait for three instances (to remove them)."
"Then you yourself have been absent from your post many times.
In years of famine and scarcity,
the old and weak among your people have perished in the ditches and gullies,
and the strong have scattered to the four directions —
nearly a thousand people."
Mencius replied,
"This is not something I, Jùxīn, could have prevented."
Mencius said,
"Now, if a man accepts another's cattle and sheep
to herd them for him,
he must surely seek pasture and fodder for them.
If he seeks pasture and fodder and cannot obtain them,
does he return them to their owner?
Or does he stand by and watch them die?"
Jùxīn said,
"This is indeed my fault."
Another day, when he was seen by the king, he said:
"Among those whom your Majesty entrusts with cities,
I know five men.
Only Kǒng Jùxīn
is aware of his fault."
He then recited this to the king.
The king said,
"This is indeed my fault."
4.5 Mencius said to Qí Wā:
"Your resignation from Língqiū
to request the office of Chief Judge
seems proper,
because you could then speak (on matters).
Now several months have passed,
can you still not speak?"
Qí Wā remonstrated with the king but was not heeded,
so he resigned his office and left.
A man of Qí said:
"What he did for Qí
Wā was good;
but what he did for himself —
I do not understand."
Gōngdūzǐ reported this.
Mencius said:
"I have heard this:
Those who hold office
should leave if they cannot fulfill their duties;
those who have the responsibility to speak
should leave if they cannot get their words adopted.
I hold no office,
I have no duty to speak,
so my advancing or withdrawing
— is it not free and easy with abundant leeway?"
4.6 Mencius served as a minister in Qí.
He went on a diplomatic mission to Téng,
and the king sent the Grandee of Gài, Wáng Huān, as his assistant.
Wáng Huān saw Mencius morning and evening,
and on the entire road between Qí and Téng,
Mencius never discussed matters of state with him.
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked:
"The rank of a minister in Qí
is not small;
the road between Qí and Téng
is not short;
and yet on going and returning
you never discussed matters with him —
why?"
Mencius said:
"If he had managed things himself,
what would I have to say?"
4.7 Mencius went from Qí to bury his mother in Lǔ.
On returning to Qí,
he stopped at Yíng.
Chōng Yú asked:
"Before, not knowing my inadequacy,
you entrusted me with supervising the burial work.
It was urgent,
so I dared not ask.
Now I would venture to ask:
The wood seemed too fine."
Mencius said:
"In ancient times, there were no fixed standards for inner and outer coffins.
In the middle antiquity, the inner coffin was seven inches thick,
with the outer coffin corresponding.
From the Son of Heaven down to commoners,
this was not merely for display of beauty,
but to fulfill the heart's desire.
If one could not obtain it,
one could not be content;
if one lacked wealth,
one could not be content.
If one could obtain it and had the wealth,
the ancients all used it;
why should I alone be different?
Moreover, to prevent
the earth from touching the flesh of the deceased —
is this alone not soothing to the human heart?
I have heard:
The noble person does not skimp on their parent for the sake of the world."
4.8 Shěn Tóng asked on his own behalf:
"May Yàn be attacked?"
Mencius said:
"Yes;
Zǐ Kuài had no right to give Yàn to another,
and Zǐ Zhī had no right to receive Yàn from Zǐ Kuài.
If there were an officer here
whom you favored,
and without telling the king
you privately gave him your rank and salary;
and if that officer,
also without the king's command, privately received them from you —
would that be acceptable?
How is this different?"
The men of Qí attacked Yàn.
Someone asked:
"You urged Qí to attack Yàn —
is that so?"
Mencius said:
"No;
Shěn Tóng asked, 'May Yàn be attacked?'
and I answered,
'Yes.'
He then acted on it and attacked.
If he had said, 'Who may attack it?'
I would have answered,
'One who is a minister of Heaven
may attack it.'
Now, if there is a murderer,
and someone asks,
'May this man be killed?'
I would answer, 'Yes.'
If he then said,
'Who may kill him?'
I would answer,
'The Chief Judge
may kill him.'
Now, when Yàn attacks Yàn,
how could I have urged that?"
4.9 The people of Yàn rebelled.
The king said:
"I am deeply ashamed before Mencius."
Chén Jiǎ said:
"Let the king not worry.
Does the king consider himself, compared with the Duke of Zhōu,
who is more benevolent and wise?"
The king said:
"Alas!
What words are these!"
Chén Jiǎ said:
"The Duke of Zhōu appointed Guǎn Shū to oversee Yīn.
Guǎn Shū then used Yīn to rebel.
If the Duke knew this and appointed him,
that would be unkind.
If he did not know and appointed him,
that would be unwise.
Benevolence and wisdom —
the Duke of Zhōu did not fully possess them;
how much less so for the king?
Allow me to see him and explain this."
When he saw Mencius, he asked:
"What manner of man was the Duke of Zhōu?"
Mencius said:
"An ancient sage."
Chén Jiǎ said:
"He appointed Guǎn Shū to oversee Yīn,
and Guǎn Shū used Yīn to rebel — is this so?"
Mencius said:
"Yes."
Chén Jiǎ said:
"Did the Duke know that he would rebel
and still appoint him?"
Mencius said:
"He did not know."
Chén Jiǎ said: "Then did even a sage err?"
Mencius said:
"The Duke of Zhōu was the younger brother;
Guǎn Shū was the elder brother.
The Duke of Zhōu's error —
was it not fitting?
Moreover, the noble men of old
corrected their errors when they made them;
the noble men of today
persist in their errors.
The noble men of old,
when they erred, it was like an eclipse of the sun or moon —
all the people saw it;
but when they changed,
all the people looked up to them.
The noble men of today
not only persist in their errors,
but also devise explanations for them."
4.10 Mencius resigned from his office and prepared to return home.
The King went to see Mencius,
and said:
"Previously, I wished to see you but could not obtain that privilege;
being able to have you in the court together was a great joy.
Now you abandon me again and return;
I do not know whether after this I may still hope to see you."
Mencius replied:
"I dare not ask for it,
but it is indeed my wish."
Another day, the King spoke to Shí Zǐ:
"I wish to give Mencius a house in the center of the state,
and to support his disciples with a salary of ten thousand zhōng;
let all the great officers and the people have someone they can look up to and imitate.
Why do you not speak to him about it for me!"
Shí Zǐ then, through Chén Zǐ, informed Mencius,
and Chén Zǐ told Mencius what Shí Zǐ had said.
Mencius said:
"So;
how could that Shí Zǐ know that it is improper?
If I desired wealth,
would I have refused one hundred thousand and accepted ten thousand?
Would that be seeking wealth?
Jì Sūn said:
'How strange
is Zǐ Shū Yí!
He himself tried to govern,
but was not employed;
then he stopped,
yet he then had his younger brother and son made ministers.
Who does not desire wealth and honor?
But only in the midst of wealth and honor
is there a private monopolizing of profit.'
In ancient times markets were established,
to exchange what one had
for what one did not have;
the authorities merely supervised them.
There was a base fellow,
who always sought a high vantage point and climbed up on it,
looking left and right,
to corner all the market profit.
Everyone considered him base,
so they levied taxes on him accordingly.
The taxing of merchants
began with this base fellow."
4.11 Mencius left Qí and lodged in Zhòu.
Someone who wished to retain the King's guest sat down and spoke with him.
Mencius did not respond,
but reclined on his armrest and lay down.
The guest, displeased, said:
"I fasted and purified myself before daring to speak;
you lie down and do not listen;
I dare not presume to see you again."
Mencius said:
"Sit down!
I will clearly tell you.
Formerly, Duke Mù of Lǔ
had no one by the side of Zǐ Sī,
and thus could not keep Zǐ Sī at ease;
Xiè Liǔ and Shēn Xiáng
had no one by the side of Duke Mù,
and thus could not keep themselves secure.
You consider the elders,
but do not reach the standard of Zǐ Sī;
is it you who cut off the elder,
or the elder who cuts off you?"
4.12 Mencius left Qí.
Yǐn Shì said to others:
"Not knowing that the King could not become a Tāng or Wǔ,
that was a lack of insight;
knowing that he could not,
yet still coming,
that was seeking favor.
He traveled a thousand lǐ to see the King;
not meeting with his acceptance he left,
but lingered for three nights before leaving Zhòu—
why such hesitation?
I am displeased with this."
Gāo Zǐ reported this.
Mencius said:
"How could Yǐn Shì understand me?
Traveling a thousand lǐ to see the King,
that was what I desired;
not meeting with acceptance and therefore leaving,
how could that be what I desired?
I had no choice.
I lingered three nights before leaving Zhòu;
in my heart I still thought it too hasty—
perhaps the King might change!
If the King should change,
then he would certainly call me back.
When I left Zhòu
and the King did not pursue me,
only then did I have a grand resolve to go home.
But even so,
how could I abandon the King!
The King is still capable of being good;
if the King should employ me,
then would it only be the people of Qí who would be at peace?
The people of all the realm would be at peace.
Perhaps the King might change!
I daily hoped for it!
Would I act like those petty men?
When their remonstrances with their ruler are not accepted,
they become angry,
and their displeasure shows in their faces;
when they leave, they travel a full day's journey before stopping?"
Yǐn Shì, hearing this,
said:
"I am indeed a petty man."
4.13 Mencius left Qí.
Chōng Yú asked him on the road:
"You, Master, seem to have a displeased look.
Previously I heard you say:
'The noble man does not complain against Heaven
nor blame others.'"
Mencius said:
"That was one time,
this is another.
Every five hundred years, a true king is sure to arise;
and in between, there must be men renowned in their age.
From the Zhōu dynasty down to now,
more than seven hundred years have passed.
In terms of the cycle, it has passed;
in terms of the times, it is due.
Heaven
does not yet wish to bring peace to the world;
if it wished to bring peace,
in this present age,
who besides me could do it?
Why should I be displeased?"
4.14 Mencius left Qí and stayed in Xiū.
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked:
"Is serving in office without accepting salary
the way of antiquity?"
Mencius said:
"No;
at Chóng,
when I had an audience with the King,
I already formed the intention to leave;
I did not wish to change this,
so I did not accept it.
Then a military campaign was ordered,
and I could not request leave.
Staying long in Qí
was not my intention."
5.1 Duke Wén of Téng, as heir apparent,
was going to Chǔ;
passing through Sòng, he saw Mencius.
Mencius spoke of the goodness of human nature,
and in his words always cited Yáo and Shùn.
When the heir apparent returned from Chǔ,
he again saw Mencius.
Mencius said:
"Do you, heir apparent, doubt my words?
The Way is one and only one.
Chéng Jiàn said to Duke Jǐng of Qí:
'He is a man,
I am a man;
why should I be afraid of him?'
Yán Yuān said:
'What kind of man was Shùn?
What kind of man am I?
Those who act can also become like him.'
Gōngmíng Yí said:
'King Wén is my teacher;
how could Zhōu Gōng deceive me?'
Now Téng, cutting off the long and supplementing the short,
will be about fifty lǐ;
yet it can still become a good state.
The Book of History says:
'If the medicine does not cause dizziness,
the disease will not be cured.'"
5.2 Duke Dìng of Téng died.
The heir apparent said to Rán Yǒu:
"Previously, Mencius spoke with me in Sòng,
and my heart has never forgotten it.
Now, unfortunate as it is, this great bereavement has come;
I wish to send you to ask Mencius,
and then proceed with the rites."
Rán Yǒu went to Zōu
to ask Mencius.
Mencius said:
"How excellent!
In mourning for parents, one indeed does his utmost.
Zēng Zǐ said:
'While alive,
serve them according to ritual;
when dead,
bury them according to ritual,
and sacrifice to them according to ritual—
this may be called filial piety.'"
As for the rites of the feudal lords,
I have not studied them;
nonetheless,
I have heard of them.
The three-year mourning period,
the garments of hempen cloth and coarse silk,
and the eating of congee —
from the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
the Three Dynasties all shared this practice."
Ranyou returned with the reply,
and the three-year mourning was established.
The elder nobles and all the officials were displeased,
so they said:
"Our ancestral state of Lǔ never practiced this under its former rulers,
nor did our former rulers practice it.
For you, in your own person, to reverse this
is unacceptable.
Moreover, the Record says:
'In mourning and sacrifice, follow the ancestors.'
And it says:
'I have received this (tradition) from them.'"
[The heir apparent] said to Ranyou:
"In the past, I never studied or learned,
but was fond of galloping horses and testing swords.
Now the elder nobles and officials are dissatisfied with me,
fearing that I may not be able to fully carry out the great affair.
You, sir, go and consult Mencius for me!"
Ranyou went again to Zōu
to consult Mencius.
Mencius said:
"Yes;
this is not a matter that can be sought from others.
Confucius said:
'When the ruler dies,
the chief minister takes charge of affairs,
the heir sips congee,
his face turns deep black,
he takes his place and wails,
and all the officials and officers
dare not show a lack of grief —
this is because he leads them by example.'
If those above have a fondness for something,
those below will surely go even further.
The virtue of the gentleman
is like the wind;
the virtue of the petty man
is like the grass.
When the wind blows over the grass, the grass must bend.
This depends on the heir apparent."
Ranyou returned with the reply.
The heir apparent said:
"Yes;
this indeed rests with me."
For five months he dwelt in the mourning hut,
issuing no commands or prohibitions.
All the officials and clan members
approved,
calling him enlightened.
When the time came for the burial,
people from all quarters came to watch,
and the mournfulness of his expression
and the sorrow of his weeping
greatly pleased the mourners.
5.3 Duke Wén of Téng asked about governing the state.
Mencius said:
"The affairs of the people cannot be delayed."
The Book of Odes says:
'By day you gather thatch,
By night you twist ropes;
Hasten to repair the roof,
For soon you will begin sowing the hundred grains.'
The way of the people is this:
those with constant property have constant hearts,
while those without constant property lack constant hearts.
If they lack constant hearts,
they will abandon themselves to depravity, perversity, evil, and excess,
and will stop at nothing.
When they fall into crime,
and then you punish them,
that is entrapping the people.
How could a benevolent person in power
ever allow such entrapment of the people?
Therefore, a worthy ruler must be respectful, frugal, and courteous to his subordinates,
taking from the people according to fixed regulations.
Yáng Hǔ said:
'He who seeks wealth is not benevolent,
and he who seeks benevolence is not wealthy.'
Under the Xià dynasty, [the tax] on fifty mǔ was 'gòng' [tribute];
under the Yīn dynasty, on seventy mǔ it was 'zhù' [aid];
under the Zhōu dynasty, on one hundred mǔ it was 'chè' [extraction];
in all cases, it was one-tenth.
'Chè' means
extraction;
'zhù' means
borrowing [labor].
Lóngzǐ said:
'In managing land, nothing is better than the aid system,
and nothing is worse than the tribute system.'
With the tribute system,
