one calculates the average output of several years as the fixed norm.
In a bountiful year,
grain is scattered everywhere,
and taking more would not be oppressive,
yet one takes less;
in a bad year,
the yield does not even cover the manure spent on the fields,
yet one demands the full amount.
As the parents of the people,
to make the people strain their eyes [in anxiety],
so that throughout the year they toil and struggle
and cannot support their parents,
and moreover borrow to make up the tax,
causing the old and young to be cast into the ditches and gullies —
wherein lies their role as parents of the people?
As for hereditary salaries,
Téng has long practiced this.
The Book of Odes says:
'May rain fall on our public fields,
and then reach our private fields.'
It is only under the aid system that public fields exist.
From this perspective,
even the Zhōu dynasty used the aid system."
"Set up 'xiáng', 'xù', 'xué', and 'xiào' [schools] to educate them.
'Xiáng' means nourishing;
'xiào' means teaching;
'xù' means archery [drilling].
Under the Xià dynasty, it was called 'xiào';
under the Yīn dynasty, 'xù';
under the Zhōu dynasty, 'xiáng';
as for 'xué' [higher learning], all three dynasties shared it —
all were means to illuminate human relationships.
When human relationships are made clear on high,
the common people below will be affectionate.
When a true king arises,
he will surely come to take this as his model,
and thus you will be a teacher to the true king."
"The Book of Odes says:
'Zhōu, though an old state,
received a new mandate.'
This refers to King Wén.
If you, sir, vigorously practice this,
you too will renew your state!"
He sent Bì Zhàn to ask about the well-field system.
Mencius said:
"Your ruler is about to practice benevolent government,
and he has chosen and sent you, sir;
you must exert yourself to it!
Benevolent government must begin with the land boundaries.
If the boundaries are not correct,
the well-fields will not be equal,
and the grain salaries will not be fair.
Therefore, oppressive rulers and corrupt officials always neglect the boundaries.
Once the boundaries are corrected,
the division of fields and the regulation of salaries
can be settled without effort."
"Now Téng's territory is small and limited.
There are gentlemen [rulers] to be served,
and there are countrymen [laborers] to be employed.
Without gentlemen, there would be no one to govern the countrymen;
without countrymen, there would be no one to support the gentlemen.
In the countryside,
adopt the nine-parts-one system of aid;
in the capital city,
let [the people] pay one-tenth as a self-imposed tax.
Officials from the ministers down must have their sacrificial fields,
each of fifty mǔ;
younger sons [of the house] receive twenty-five mǔ.
In death or removal, none should leave the village.
The village fields share the same well,
and in going out and coming in, people befriend one another,
guard and watch over each other,
and support each other in illness —
thus the hundred surnames become intimate and harmonious.
One square lǐ forms a well-field,
and the well-field covers nine hundred mǔ,
with the central part being the public field.
Eight families each possess one hundred mǔ of private land,
and together they cultivate the public field;
only after the public work is done
do they dare attend to their private affairs —
this is how to distinguish the countrymen.
This is the general outline;
as for refining and adjusting it,
that lies with you and your ruler."
5.4 There came to Téng a man named Xú Xíng, who professed the doctrines of Shénnóng.
From Chǔ he arrived in Téng,
and at the gate he addressed Duke Wén, saying:
"I, a man from a distant region,
have heard that you, sir, practice benevolent government,
and I wish to receive a dwelling place and become your subject."
Duke Wen of Teng provided a place for Xu Xing to live.
His followers numbered several dozen,
all dressed in coarse hemp clothing,
making sandals and weaving mats for a living.
Chen Liang’s disciple, Chen Xiang, along with his younger brother Xin,
carried plowshares and hoes on their backs and went from Song to Teng.
They said:
“We hear that you, ruler, practice the governance of a sage;
you too are a sage,
and we wish to become subjects of a sage.”
When Chen Xiang met Xu Xing, he was greatly delighted,
completely abandoned what he had learned, and studied under him.
Chen Xiang came to see Mencius,
and related Xu Xing’s words, saying:
“The ruler of Teng is indeed a worthy ruler.
Nevertheless,
he has not yet heard of the Way.
Worthy rulers plow and eat alongside the people,
preparing their morning and evening meals while governing.
But now Teng has granaries and treasuries,
which means he oppresses the people to support himself.
How can he be called worthy?”
Mencius said:
“Does Master Xu necessarily plant grain before he eats?”
Chen Xiang replied:
“Yes.”
“Does Master Xu necessarily weave cloth before he wears clothes?”
He replied:
“No;
Master Xu wears coarse hemp clothing.”
“Does Master Xu wear a cap?”
He replied:
“Yes.”
Mencius said:
“What kind of cap?”
He replied:
“A plain cap.”
Mencius said:
“Did he weave it himself?”
He replied:
“No;
he traded grain for it.”
Mencius said:
“Why did Master Xu not weave it himself?”
He replied:
“It would interfere with his plowing.”
Mencius said:
“Does Master Xu use a cauldron and a steamer for cooking,
and iron tools for plowing?”
He replied:
“Yes.”
“Did he make them himself?”
He replied:
“No;
he traded grain for them.”
“Trading grain for tools and utensils
does not harm the potters and smiths;
and when potters and smiths trade their tools and utensils for grain,
does that harm the farmers?
Moreover, why does Master Xu not become a potter and smith himself,
so that he could take everything from his own home for use?
Why does he busily engage in trade with all the craftsmen?
Why does Master Xu not find this troublesome?”
He replied:
“The work of the various craftsmen
indeed cannot be done while plowing.”
“Then
can governing the world alone be done while plowing?
There is the work of great men,
and there is the work of small men.
Moreover, with a single person,
the products of all craftsmen are required;
if one must make everything oneself before using it,
that would lead the whole world to exhaustion.
Therefore it is said:
‘Some labor with their minds,
others labor with their strength;
those who labor with their minds govern others,
those who labor with their strength are governed by others;
those who are governed by others feed others,
those who govern others are fed by others—
this is the universal principle of the world.’
“In the time of Yao,
the world was not yet settled;
the floodwaters overflowed,
spreading across the world;
vegetation grew thick and lush,
birds and beasts multiplied,
the five grains did not ripen,
birds and beasts threatened the people,
and paths made by animal tracks and bird claws
crisscrossed the Central Plains.
Yao alone worried about this,
and raised up Shun to bring order to it.
Shun appointed Yi to take charge of fire;
Yi burned the mountains and marshes,
and the birds and beasts fled into hiding.
Yu dredged the nine rivers,
channeled the Ji and Ta rivers into the sea,
diverted the Ru and Han rivers,
and drained the Huai and Si rivers into the Yangtze,
after which the people of the Central Plains could grow grain.
At that time,
Yu spent eight years outside,
passing his own gate three times without entering.
Even if he had wanted to plow,
could he have done so?
“Hou Ji taught the people agriculture,
planting the five grains;
when the five grains ripened, the people were nourished.
The Way of human beings is such that
if they are full of food, warmly clothed,
and live in idleness without instruction,
they come close to the birds and beasts.
The sage was worried about this,
and appointed Xie to be Minister of Education,
teaching the people human relations:
affection between father and son,
righteousness between ruler and subject,
distinction between husband and wife,
order between elder and younger,
and trust between friends.
Fang Xun said:
‘Encourage them, lead them,
correct them, straighten them,
assist them, protect them,
so that they acquire it themselves,
and then further help and guide them with virtue.’
The sage’s concern for the people was like this—
and yet would he have leisure to plow?
“Yao worried that he could not get Shun;
Shun worried that he could not get Yu and Gao Yao.
The one who worries that his hundred mu of land are not well cultivated
is a farmer.
Sharing wealth with others is called generosity;
teaching others goodness is called loyalty;
finding worthy men for the world is called benevolence.
Therefore giving the world to another is easy,
but finding the right man for the world is hard.
Confucius said:
‘How great
was Yao as a ruler!
Only Heaven is great,
and only Yao matched it.
Vast and boundless—the people could not name it!
What a true ruler was Shun!
Lofty and majestic—he possessed the world but did not hold it for himself!’
When Yao and Shun governed the world,
did they use no effort of mind?
They simply did not apply it to plowing.
“I have heard of using the Chinese to transform the barbarians,
but never of being transformed by barbarians.
Chen Liang
was a native of Chu;
he delighted in the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius,
and studied in the north, in the Central States.
Among the scholars of the north,
no one surpassed him.
He was what is called a man of outstanding talent.
You and your brother
served him for decades;
when your teacher died, you then turned against him!
In the past, when Confucius passed away,
after three years,
his disciples packed up their belongings and prepared to return;
they went in to bid farewell to Zi Gong,
and faced each other and wept,
all losing their voices,
and then left.
Zi Gong returned,
built a hut by the grave,
and lived alone for three more years,
and then left.
On another day, Zi Xia, Zi Zhang, and Zi You,
thinking You Ruo resembled the sage,
wanted to serve him as they had served Confucius,
and pressed Zeng Zi to agree.
Zeng Zi said:
‘No;
just as the Jiang and Han rivers wash him clean,
and the autumn sun dries him white,
he is so pure and bright that nothing can surpass him.’
Now this southern barbarian with his jargon,
who slanders the Way of the former kings,
you turn against your teacher and study under him—
this is indeed different from Zeng Zi.
I have heard of coming out from a dark valley
and moving to a tall tree,
but never of descending from a tall tree and entering a dark valley.
The Lu Hymns say:
‘The Rong and Di are smitten,
the Jing and Shu are punished.’
The Duke of Zhou would smite them;
and you learn from them—
this is indeed a poor transformation.”
"If we follow Master Xu's way,
then market prices would not differ,
and there would be no deceit within the state.
Even if we sent a five-foot lad to the market,
no one would cheat him.
When cloth and silk are of the same length,
their prices would be similar;
when hemp, flax, silk floss, and wadding are of the same weight,
their prices would be similar;
when the five grains are of the same quantity,
their prices would be similar;
when shoes are of the same size,
their prices would be similar."
Mencius said:
"That things are not equal
is their natural condition.
Some are twice, some five times,
some ten or a hundred times,
some a thousand or ten thousand times.
If you equalize them by comparison,
this is to throw the world into confusion.
If large and small shoes were the same price,
would anyone make them?
To follow Master Xu's way
is to lead one another into deceit.
How could it govern a state?"
5.5 The Mohist Yī Zhī
sought an audience with Mencius through Xú Pì.
Mencius said:
"I certainly wish to see him,
but now I am still ill.
When I recover,
I will go to see him.
Let Master Yī not come!"
Another day, Yī Zhī again sought an audience.
Mencius said:
"Now I can see him.
If I am not straightforward, the Way will not be evident.
I will be straightforward.
I have heard that Master Yī is a Mohist.
In conducting funerals, Mohists
take frugality as their Way.
Master Yī thinks to change the world with this;
did he consider that without this nothing is valuable?
Yet Master Yī buried his parents richly,
thus he served his parents with what he despises."
Xú Zǐ reported this to Yī Zhī.
Yī Zhī said:
"The Way of the Ruists says
that the ancients
'treated the people as if protecting an infant.'
What does this saying mean?
I take it to mean that love is without gradation,
but its practice begins with one's parents."
Xú Zǐ reported this to Mencius.
Mencius said:
"Does Master Yī truly
believe that a person loves his brother's child
as he loves his neighbor's infant?
That saying has its specific reference.
When an infant crawls toward a well,
it is not the infant's fault.
Moreover, when Heaven produces creatures,
it gives them a single root,
but Master Yī gives them two roots.
In ancient times, there were those who did not bury their parents.
When a parent died,
they carried them out and threw them into a ditch.
Later, passing by,
foxes and wolves were eating them,
flies and gnats were biting at them.
Sweat broke out on their foreheads.
They averted their eyes and would not look.
This sweat
was not for others' sake;
it issued from their hearts and reached their faces.
So they went home, took up baskets and spades, and buried them.
To bury them
was indeed correct.
Then the filial son and benevolent person's burying their parents
must also have its Way."
Xú Zǐ reported this to Yī Zhī.
Yī Zhī was lost in thought for a while, then said:
"I have been instructed."
6.1 Chén Dài said:
"Not to see the feudal lords
seems rather petty.
If you see them once,
in a great matter you might become king,
in a lesser matter, a hegemon.
Moreover, the Record says:
'To bend a foot and straighten a yard—
this seems something that can be done.'"
Mencius said:
"Formerly, Duke Jǐng of Qí went hunting.
He summoned the gamekeeper with a pennant,
but he did not come,
and was about to have him killed.
'A man of ambition does not forget ending up in a ditch;
a brave man does not forget losing his head.'
What did Confucius take from this?
He took the refusal to go when not summoned properly.
If one goes without waiting to be summoned properly,
what then?
Moreover, speaking of 'bending a foot and straightening a yard'
is done from the perspective of profit.
If we speak in terms of profit,
then bending a yard and straightening a foot for profit—
can this also be done?
Formerly, Zhào Jiǎnzǐ
sent Wáng Liáng to drive for the favorite Xī.
They drove all day and caught no birds.
The favorite Xī reported back:
'He is the worst charioteer in the world.'
Someone told Wáng Liáng.
Wáng Liáng said:
'Let me try again.'
After being pressed, he agreed,
and in one morning they caught ten birds.
The favorite Xī reported back:
'He is the best charioteer in the world.'
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ said:
'I will put him in charge of driving for you.'
He spoke to Wáng Liáng.
Wáng Liáng would not accept,
saying:
'When I drove for him following the rules,
urging the horses forward,
we caught none all day;
when I drove crookedly for him,
in one morning we caught ten.
The Odes say:
"Without losing his driving,
he loosed his arrows and hit as if breaking."
I am not used to driving for a petty man.
I beg to resign.'
The charioteer was ashamed to be associated with the archer.
Even if, by associating, they caught animals
piled up like hills,
he would not do it.
If I were to bend the Way and follow them,
what would that be?
Moreover, you are mistaken:
One who bends himself
has never been able to straighten others."
6.2 Jǐng Chūn said:
"Are Gōngsūn Yǎn and Zhāng Yí
not truly great men?
When they grow angry, the feudal lords tremble;
when they are at peace, the world is calm."
Mencius said:
"How can these be called great men?
Have you not studied the rites?
When a man comes of age,
his father instructs him;
when a woman marries,
her mother instructs her,
escorting her to the door and
warning her, saying:
'Go to your husband's home,
be respectful and careful,
do not disobey your husband!'
To take obedience as the norm
is the way of concubines and women.
To dwell in the broad house of the world,
to stand in the correct position of the world,
to walk the great path of the world;
when successful, to share it with the people;
when unsuccessful,
to walk one's own path alone.
Wealth and honor cannot corrupt him,
poverty and lowliness cannot move him,
power and force cannot bend him—
this is called a great man."
6.3 Zhōu Xiāo asked:
"Did the gentlemen of old seek office?"
Mencius said:
"They did."
The Records say:
'If Confucius went three months without a ruler,
he became anxious and unsettled,
and when he left the state he always carried his token of introduction.'
Gōngmíng Yí said:
'In ancient times,
if a man went three months without a ruler,
he would be condoled with.'"
"If one is condoled with after three months without a ruler,
is that not too urgent?"
Mencius said:
"When a scholar loses his position,
it is like a feudal lord losing his state.
The Book of Rites says:
"The feudal lords personally plow and assist
to supply the grain for the sacrificial vessels;
their consorts tend silkworms and reel silk
to make ceremonial garments.
If the sacrificial animals are not perfect,
the grain offerings are not pure,
or the garments are not complete,
they dare not offer sacrifices.
Only if a scholar-official has no land
does he then not sacrifice."
If the sacrificial animals, vessels, and garments are not complete,
one dares not offer sacrifices,
then one dares not feast joyfully—
is this not sufficient cause for mourning?
"Why must one always carry a gift of introduction when leaving one's state?"
(Someone) asked.
(Mencius) replied:
"A scholar-official's taking office
is like a farmer's plowing;
would a farmer abandon his plow and hoe
just because he leaves his state?"
(The questioner) said:
"The state of Jìn is also a place where one can serve in office,
yet I have never heard that seeking office is so urgent.
If seeking office is so urgent,
why is it that the gentleman is so reluctant to take office?"
(Mencius) answered:
(Mencius) said:
"A young man, when born, wishes to have a wife;
a young woman, when born, wishes to have a husband;
the feelings of parents
are present in everyone.
Without waiting for the parents' command
or the matchmaker's words,
to bore holes in walls to peek at each other,
or to climb over walls to follow each other—
then parents and fellow countrymen would all despise them.
The ancients were never unwilling to take office,
but they also detested taking it by improper means.
To go into office by improper means
is like drilling holes and peeping—it is of the same kind."
6.4 Péng Gēng asked, saying:
"With dozens of chariots following behind
and several hundred followers,
to go from one feudal lord to another and be fed—
is this not excessive?"
Mencius said:
"If it is not according to the Way,
then one should not accept even a single basket of food from others;
if it is according to the Way,
then Shùn receiving the entire realm from Yáo
was not considered excessive—
do you consider it excessive?"
(Péng Gēng) said:
"No;
but a scholar-official eating without working—
that is not acceptable."
(Mencius) said:
"If you do not exchange labor and trade goods,
using surplus to supplement deficiency,
then the farmer will have surplus grain
and the woman will have surplus cloth;
if you do facilitate exchange,
then carpenters, wheelwrights, and cart-makers can all get their food from you.
Here there is a person
who at home is filial
and abroad is fraternal,
who upholds the way of the former kings
to instruct future students,
yet he cannot obtain food from you—
why do you honor carpenters, wheelwrights, and cart-makers
but despise those who practice benevolence and righteousness?"
(Péng Gēng) said:
"Carpenters, wheelwrights, and cart-makers—
their intention is to seek food;
when the gentleman pursues the Way,
is his intention also to seek food?"
(Mencius) said:
"Why do you pay attention only to intention?
If someone has merit for you,
and is worthy of being fed, then you feed him.
Moreover, do you feed based on intention
or based on achievement?"
(Péng Gēng) said:
"Based on intention."
(Mencius) said:
"Here is a man
who smashes tiles and paints over walls—
his intention is to seek food—
would you feed him?"
(Péng Gēng) said:
"No."
(Mencius) said:
"Then it is not intention by which you feed,
but achievement."
6.5 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying:
"Sòng
is a small state;
now it is about to practice kingly government,
and Qí and Chǔ, being hostile, are attacking it—
what should be done?"
Mencius said:
"When Tāng lived in Bó,
he was neighbor to Gé,
and the Earl of Gé was unruly and did not offer sacrifices.
Tāng sent someone to ask him:
'Why do you not offer sacrifices?'
(The Earl) replied:
'I have no animals for sacrifice.'
Tāng sent him cattle and sheep.
The Earl of Gé ate them
and still did not use them for sacrifice.
Tāng again sent someone to ask him:
'Why do you not offer sacrifices?'
(The Earl) replied:
'I have no grain for the offerings.'
Tāng sent the people of Bó to go and plow for him,
and the old and weak brought food.
The Earl of Gé led his people
to waylay those who had wine, grain, millet, and rice
and seize them;
those who did not hand them over
were killed.
There was a boy who brought millet and meat as provisions;
(the Earl) killed him and seized the food.
The Book of History says:
'The Earl of Gé treated the food-bringers as enemies.'
This is what is meant.
Because he killed that boy, (Tāng) attacked him;
all within the four seas said:
'It is not for coveting the world,
but to avenge the common men and women.'
'Tāng's first campaign
began with Gé.'
After eleven campaigns, he was invincible in the world.
When he campaigned in the east,
the western tribes complained;
when he campaigned in the south,
the northern tribes complained,
saying:
'Why does he leave us for last?'
The people looked for him
as in a great drought they look for rain.
Those going to market did not stop;
the weeders did not change their work;
he executed their rulers
and comforted their people—
like a timely rain descending.
The people were greatly delighted.
The Book of History says:
'Wait for our sovereign;
when our sovereign comes, there will be no punishment!'
'There were those who would not submit to Zhōu;
(King Wǔ) campaigned in the east
to pacify the men and women;
they wrapped up their silks and black and yellow fabrics,
to greet our King of Zhōu and receive his favor—
they submitted to the great state of Zhōu.'
Their gentlemen filled baskets with black and yellow silks
to welcome the gentlemen of Zhōu;
their common people brought baskets of food and vessels of broth
to welcome the commoners of Zhōu;
(Zhōu) rescued the people from fire and water
and removed their oppressors.
The Great Declaration says:
'We display our martial might,
invade his territory,
seize the oppressor,
spread the execution and punishment,
and outshine even Tāng.'
If (Sòng) does not practice kingly government, that is one thing;
but if it does practice kingly government,
all within the four seas will lift their heads
and look to it,
desiring to make its ruler their sovereign;
though Qí and Chǔ be great,
what is there to fear?"
6.6 Mencius said to Dài Bùshèng:
"Do you wish your king to be good?
Let me explain to you plainly.
Here is a high official of Chǔ
who wishes his son to speak the language of Qí.
Should he have a man of Qí teach him?
Or a man of Chǔ teach him?"
(Dài Bùshèng) said:
"Have a man of Qí teach him."
(Mencius) said:
"If one man of Qí teaches him
while a crowd of Chǔ men babble around him,
though you beat him daily and demand that he speak Qí,
it will not be achieved;
but if you take him and place him in the marketplace of Zhuāng Yuè for several years,
though you beat him daily and demand that he speak Chǔ,
it will likewise not be achieved."
The Master said, "If one takes Xue Juzhou
as a fine officer,
and has him reside at the king's court,
then if those at the king's court,
whether old or young, humble or noble, are all like Xue Juzhou,
with whom would the king do what is not good?
If those at the king's court,
whether old or young, humble or noble, are none of them like Xue Juzhou,
with whom would the king do what is good?
A single Xue Juzhou,
how can he alone affect the King of Song?"
6.7 Gongsun Chou asked,
"Not to see the feudal lords—
what is the principle in this?"
Mencius replied,
"In antiquity, those who were not ministers did not see them.
Duan Gammu jumped over a wall to avoid them;
Xie Liu shut his gate and refused to admit them.
These actions were excessive;
when pressed,
one may indeed see them.
Yang Hu wished to see Confucius
but disliked any breach of propriety.
When a high officer made a gift to an officer,
if the officer could not receive it at his own home,
he had to go to the officer's gate to bow in thanks.
Yang Hu, having observed that Confucius was out,
sent him a steamed pig.
Confucius, also observing when Yang Hu was out,
went to bow in thanks.
At that time,
if Yang Hu had taken the initiative,
how could Confucius have failed to see him?
Zengzi said,
'Hunching one's shoulders and putting on a flattering smile,
this is more painful than working in the fields in summer.'
Zilu said,
'To speak with someone without being of one mind,
and seeing his face
turn red with shame—
this is something I do not condone.'
From this we may see
what the cultivation of a gentleman
truly consists of."
6.8 Dai Yingzhi said,
"A tax of one part in ten,
and abolishing the levies at passes and markets—
this year we cannot yet do it.
I beg to reduce them,
and wait until next year,
then stop altogether.
How does that sound?"
Mencius replied,
"Now suppose there is a man who daily steals his neighbor's chickens.
Someone tells him,
'This is not the way of a gentleman.'
He says,
'I beg to reduce it—
steal one chicken a month,
and wait until next year,
then stop.'
If you know it is not right,
you must stop at once—
why wait until next year?"
6.9 Gongduzi said,
"Outsiders all say that you, Master, love disputation.
I venture to ask why."
Mencius said,
"Do I indeed love disputation?
I have no choice.
The world has been in existence for a long time,
now orderly, now chaotic.
In the time of Yao,
the waters flowed backward,
flooding the Central Kingdoms,
where snakes and dragons dwelled,
and the people had no settled place.
Those in low places made nests
in trees; those in high places built cave dwellings.
The *Book of History* says,
'The torrent waters warn me.'
The 'torrent waters' are the floodwaters.
Yao had Yu control them.
Yu dug channels and drained them into the sea;
he drove the snakes and dragons into the marshes;
the waters flowed through the channels in the earth,
as the Yangzi, Huai, Yellow, and Han rivers do.
Once the dangers were removed,
the harmful birds and beasts vanished,
and the people could dwell on the level ground.
"After Yao and Shun passed away,
the way of the sages declined,
and tyrannical kings arose one after another.
They destroyed houses to make ponds,
so that the people had no place for rest;
they abandoned fields to make gardens and parks,
so that the people could not get food and clothing.
Heretical doctrines and violent deeds arose again;
gardens, parks, ponds, and marshes multiplied,
and wild animals returned.
By the time of Zhou,
the world fell into great chaos again.
The Duke of Zhou assisted King Wu
in punishing Zhou, attacking Yan
for three years to punish its ruler;
he drove Fei Lian to the seashore and executed him;
he destroyed fifty states;
and drove away tigers, leopards, rhinoceroses, and elephants far off—
and the whole world rejoiced greatly.
The *Book of History* says,
'How bright was the plan of King Wen!
How well was the achievement of King Wu carried on!
They guided and enlightened us who came after,
ensuring all was correct and without flaw.'
"When the age declined and the Way became obscured,
heretical doctrines and violent deeds arose again.
There were cases of ministers killing their rulers,
and sons killing their fathers.
Confucius was alarmed,
and he composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals*—this is the task of the Son of Heaven.
Therefore Confucius said,
'Those who understand me
will do so through the *Spring and Autumn Annals*!
Those who blame me
will do so through the *Spring and Autumn Annals*!'
When sage kings no longer arose,
the feudal lords indulged in license,
and recluses voiced wild opinions.
The words of Yang Zhu and Mo Di filled the world.
The doctrines of the world
either fell under Yang or under Mo.
Yang's principle is 'for oneself'—
this means denying the ruler;
Mo's principle is 'universal love'—
this means denying the father.
To deny father and ruler
is to be like beasts.
Gongming Yi said,
'In the kitchen there is fat meat,
and in the stables there are fat horses;
but the people have starving faces,
and in the wilds there are those who die of hunger—
this is leading beasts to devour men.'
If the ways of Yang and Mo do not cease,
the way of Confucius will not shine forth.
This is because heretical doctrines deceive the people
and block the path of benevolence and righteousness.
When benevolence and righteousness are blocked,
then beasts are led to devour men,
and men will devour one another.
I am alarmed by this,
and I defend the way of the former sages,
oppose Yang and Mo, and refute their excessive words,
so that heretical doctrines cannot arise.
If they arise in the mind,
they will harm one's affairs;
if they arise in affairs,
they will harm governance.
Even if a sage were to arise again,
he would not change my words.
"In ancient times, Yu curbed the floodwaters
and the world was peaceful;
the Duke of Zhou united the barbarians,
drove away the wild beasts,
and the people were secure;
Confucius completed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
and rebellious ministers and villainous sons were afraid.
The *Book of Poetry* says,
'The Rong and Di are smitten,
the Jing and Shu are punished—
then no one dares to oppose us.'
Those who deny father and ruler
are what the Duke of Zhou smote.
I also wish to rectify people's minds,
to stop heretical doctrines,
to oppose perverse deeds,
and to refute excessive words,
so as to carry on the work of the three sages.
Do I love disputation?
I have no choice.
Those who can speak to oppose Yang and Mo
are disciples of the sages."
6.10 Kuang Zhang said,
"Is Chen Zhongzi not truly a man of incorruptible integrity?
Living in Wuling,
he went three days without food,
so that his ears could not hear
and his eyes could not see.
On a well there was a plum,
of which the worms had eaten more than half.
Crawling to it, he tried to eat it;
after three swallows,
then his ears could hear and his eyes could see."
Mencius said,
“Among the scholars of Qi,
I must consider Zhongzi the thumb of this group.
Nevertheless,
how can Zhongzi be considered incorruptible?
To fulfill Zhongzi’s principles to the utmost,
one would have to become an earthworm before it could be done.
For an earthworm feeds above on dry soil,
and drinks below from the yellow springs.
As for the house where Zhongzi dwells,
was it built by Bo Yi?
Or was it built by Robber Zhi?
As for the grain he eats,
was it planted by Bo Yi?
Or was it planted by Robber Zhi?
This cannot be known.”
Someone said,
“What harm is there in that?
He himself weaves sandals, and his wife twists hemp,
to exchange for them.”
Mencius said,
“Zhongzi
comes from a great hereditary family in Qi;
his elder brother Dai
receives a stipend of ten thousand zhong from Gai;
yet considering his brother’s stipend as unjust,
he does not eat it,
and considering his brother’s house as unjust,
he does not dwell in it.
He avoids his brother and leaves his mother,
dwelling in Wuling.
One day, when he returned,
someone had presented his brother with a live goose.
Zhongzi frowned and said,
‘What use is this cackling thing?’
Another day, his mother killed that goose
and gave it to him to eat.
His brother came from outside
and said,
‘This is the flesh of that cackling thing.’
Zhongzi went out and vomited it.
He would not eat what came from his mother,
but he ate what came from his wife;
he would not dwell in his brother’s house,
but he dwells in Wuling.
Can this be considered
fully extending his standard to all similar cases?
As for one like Zhongzi,
only after becoming an earthworm could he fully fulfill his principles.”
7.1. Mencius said,
“With the clear vision of Li Lou
and the skill of Gongshuzi,
without the compass and square,
one cannot form squares or circles;
with the keen hearing of Shi Kuang,
without the six pitch-pipes,
one cannot correct the five notes;
with the Way of Yao and Shun,
without benevolent government,
one cannot pacify and order the world.
Now, if there is a ruler with a benevolent heart and a reputation for benevolence,
yet the people do not receive his beneficence,
and he cannot be a model for later generations,
it is because he does not practice the ways of the former kings.
Therefore it is said,
‘Goodness alone is insufficient for government;
law alone cannot put itself into practice.’
The Book of Odes says,
‘Do not err, do not forget,
follow the old statutes.’
To err while following the laws of the former kings
has never happened.
When the sages exhausted the power of their eyesight,
they followed it up with the compass, square, level, and plumb line,
to produce squares, circles, level surfaces, and straight lines,
and these were used inexhaustibly;
when they exhausted the power of their hearing,
they followed it up with the six pitch-pipes to correct the five notes,
and these were used inexhaustibly;
when they exhausted the power of their thoughts,
they followed it up with a government that could not bear to see suffering,
and then benevolence covered the world.
Therefore it is said,
To build high, one must rely on the hills and mountains;
to build low, one must rely on the rivers and marshes;
to govern
without relying on the ways of the former kings—
can this be called wisdom?
Therefore only the benevolent should be in high positions.
If the unbenevolent are in high positions,
this is to spread their evils among the multitude.
When those above have no moral principles to measure by,
those below have no laws to uphold,
when the court does not believe in the Way,
when artisans do not trust their measures,
when gentlemen violate righteousness,
when small men violate punishments,
for a state to survive under such conditions
is a matter of luck.
Therefore it is said,
‘If city walls are not complete,
if weapons and armor are insufficient,
these are not disasters for a state;
if fields are not cultivated,
if goods and wealth are not accumulated,
these are not harms for a state.
If those above have no ritual,
if those below have no learning,
if rebellious people arise,
then ruin is not far off.’
The Book of Odes says,
‘Heaven is about to shake things up,
do not be so remiss!’
‘Remiss’
is the same as ‘negligent.’
To serve one’s lord without righteousness,
to advance or withdraw without ritual,
to speak and slander the ways of the former kings—
this is to be like the negligent.
Therefore it is said,
‘To urge one’s ruler to do what is difficult is called respect;
to set forth what is good and block what is evil is called reverence;
to say that one’s lord cannot do it is called robbery.’
7.2. Mencius said,
“The compass and square
are the ultimate standards for squares and circles;
the sage
is the ultimate standard for human relations.
If one wishes to be a lord,
he must fully exhaust the Way of the lord;
if one wishes to be a minister,
he must fully exhaust the Way of the minister.
Both simply take Yao and Shun as their model.
If one does not serve his lord in the way Shun served Yao,
he is disrespectful to his lord;
if one does not govern the people in the way Yao governed the people,
he is a robber of his people.
Confucius said,
‘There are only two ways,
benevolence and unbenevolence.’
If a ruler oppresses his people severely,
then he will be killed and his state will perish;
if not severely,
then his person will be endangered and his state weakened,
and he will be given the epithets
‘Dark’ or ‘Cruel,’
and even with filial sons and loving grandsons,
for a hundred generations it cannot be changed.
The Book of Odes says,
‘The mirror of Yin is not far away,
it is in the age of the Xia sovereigns.’
This is what is meant.”
7.3. Mencius said,
“The Three Dynasties won the world through benevolence,
and lost the world through lack of benevolence.
The rise and fall, survival and ruin of states are likewise.
If the Son of Heaven is not benevolent,
he cannot protect the four seas;
if the feudal lords are not benevolent,
they cannot protect their altars of soil and grain;
if the high ministers and grandees are not benevolent,
they cannot protect their ancestral temples;
if the scholars and common people are not benevolent,
they cannot protect their four limbs.
Now, to hate death
yet delight in unbenevolence
is like hating drunkenness
yet forcing oneself to drink.”
7.4. Mencius said,
“If you love others and they are not close to you,
reflect on your own benevolence;
if you govern others and they are not well ordered,
reflect on your own wisdom;
if you are courteous to others and they do not respond,
reflect on your own reverence.
When your actions fail to achieve their purpose,
always turn inward and seek the cause in yourself.
When your own self is correct,
the whole world will turn to you.
The Book of Odes says,
‘Everlasting is the mandate of Heaven;
seek your own many blessings.’”
7.5. Mencius said,
“People have a common saying, they all say,
‘The world, the state, the family.’
The root of the world is in the state;
the root of the state is in the family;
the root of the family is in the self.”
7.6. Mencius said,
“Government is not difficult—
it is simply not offending the great families.
What the great families admire,
the whole state will admire;
what the whole state admires,
the whole world will admire;
thus, their virtuous teaching overflows throughout the four seas.”
7.7 Mencius said,
"When the Way prevails in the world,
those of lesser virtue serve those of greater virtue,
and those of lesser worth serve those of greater worth.
When the Way does not prevail in the world,
the small serve the large,
and the weak serve the strong.
These two situations
are determined by Heaven.
Those who follow Heaven survive;
those who defy Heaven perish.
Duke Jǐng of Qí said,
'If one can neither command
nor accept commands,
that is to be cut off from all relations.'
With tears flowing, he married his daughter to the ruler of Wú.
Now, small states take the great states as their models
yet are ashamed to receive commands from them.
This is like a disciple being ashamed to receive commands from his master.
If they are ashamed of this,
nothing is better than taking King Wén as their model.
If they take King Wén as their model,
a great state will, within five years,
and a small state within seven years,
surely come to rule over the world.
The Book of Odes says,
'The descendants of the Shāng,
their numbers were beyond counting.
But when the High God gave His command,
they all submitted to Zhōu.
They all submitted to Zhōu,
for Heaven's mandate is not constant.
The officers of Yīn, fine and intelligent,
assisted in the libation at the capital of Zhōu.'
Confucius said,
'Benevolence cannot be overcome by numbers.
If a ruler loves benevolence,
he will have no rivals in the world.'
Now, if one desires to have no rivals in the world
yet does not practice benevolence,
this is like holding something hot without cooling it in water.
The Book of Odes says,
'Who can hold something hot
without cooling it in water?'"
7.8 Mencius said,
"Can one speak with
the unkind?
They are at ease in danger and profit from calamity,
delighting in what leads to their ruin.
If the unkind could be spoken
to,
how could there be ruined states and destroyed families?
There was a child singing,
'When the water of Cāng Láng is clear,
I can wash my cap-strings;
when the water of Cāng Láng is muddy,
I can wash my feet.'
Confucius said,
'Listen, my disciples!
When clear, wash the cap-strings;
when muddy, wash the feet.
This is determined by the water itself.'
A man must first bring disgrace upon himself,
and then others disgrace him.
A family must first destroy itself,
and then others destroy it.
A state must first attack itself,
and then others attack it.
The Tài Jiǎ says,
'If Heaven sends calamity,
it may still be avoided;
but if one brings calamity upon oneself,
there is no escape.'
This is what is meant."
7.9 Mencius said,
"When Jié and Zhòu lost their states,
it was because they lost their people;
losing their people
meant losing their hearts.
There is a way to gain the world:
gain the people, and you gain the world;
there is a way to gain the people:
gain their hearts, and you gain the people;
there is a way to gain their hearts:
gather for them what they desire,
and
do not impose
what they dislike—that is all.
The people's turning to benevolence
is like water flowing downward
or beasts running to the wilds.
Thus, the one who drives fish into the deep pool
is the otter;
the one who drives birds into the thicket
is the hawk;
the one who drove the people to Tāng and Wǔ
was Jié and Zhòu.
If today there is a ruler in the world who loves benevolence,
then all the feudal lords will drive their people to him.
Even if he wished not to become king, he could not avoid it.
Those who now wish to become king
are like one with a seven-year illness
seeking wormwood that has been aged for three years.
If they do not store it up,
they will never get it in their lifetime.
If they do not set their hearts on benevolence,
they will be forever troubled and disgraced,
until they sink into death.
The Book of Odes says,
'How can they achieve good?
They will all drown together.'
This is what is meant."
7.10 Mencius said,
"With those who do violence to themselves
one cannot speak;
with those who abandon themselves
one cannot act.
To speak in a way that slanders propriety and righteousness—
this is called doing violence to oneself.
To say 'I am unable to abide in benevolence or follow righteousness'—
this is called abandoning oneself.
Benevolence
is the peaceful abode of man;
righteousness
is the proper path of man.
To leave the peaceful abode empty and not dwell in it,
to abandon the proper path and not follow it—
how sad!"
7.11 Mencius said,
"The Way is near
yet people seek it far away;
matters are simple
yet people seek them in difficulty.
If everyone loves their parents and respects their elders,
the world will be at peace."
7.12 Mencius said,
"If one is in a low position
and does not gain the trust of his superior,
he cannot govern the people.
There is a way to gain the trust of one's superior:
if one is not trusted by his friends,
he will not gain the trust of his superior.
There is a way to be trusted by friends:
if serving one's parents does not please them,
one will not be trusted by friends.
There is a way to please one's parents:
if one examines himself and finds no sincerity,
he will not please his parents.
There is a way to be sincere in oneself:
if one does not understand what is good,
he will not be sincere in himself.
Therefore, sincerity
is the Way of Heaven;
to seek sincerity
is the Way of man.
That someone with utmost sincerity does not move others
has never happened;
without sincerity,
there has never been anyone who could move others."
7.13 Mencius said,
"Bó Yí fled from Zhòu
and lived by the coast of the North Sea.
Hearing that King Wén had arisen, he rose and
said,
'Why not go back!
I hear that the Western Chief is good at caring for the elderly.'
Tài Gōng fled from Zhòu
and lived by the coast of the East Sea.
Hearing that King Wén had arisen, he rose and
said,
'Why not go back!
I hear that the Western Chief is good at caring for the elderly.'
These two elders
were the greatest elders in the world, and they went to him—
this was like the fathers of the world going to him.
When the fathers of the world go to him,
where can their sons go?
If a feudal lord implements the policies of King Wén,
within seven years
he will surely come to rule over the world."
7.14 Mencius said,
"Qiú
served as steward of the Jì family,
but he could not change their virtue,
and he doubled the grain tax compared to before.
Confucius said,
'Qiú
is not my disciple.
You disciples may beat the drum and attack him.'
From this we see,
if a ruler does not practice benevolent government
and yet one enriches him,
such a person is rejected by Confucius—
how much more so those who fight fierce battles for him?
For the sake of land, they fight,
killing people until the fields are filled;
for the sake of cities, they fight,
killing people until the cities are filled—
this is what is called leading the land to devour human flesh,
a crime for which death is insufficient punishment."
Therefore, those skilled in war should suffer the severest punishment;
those who form alliances with other feudal lords come next;
those who clear away the grass and weeds,
and those who exploit the land come next.”
7.15 Mencius said:
“In examining a person,
nothing is better than looking into his eyes.
The eyes cannot conceal his evil.
If his heart is upright,
then his eyes are clear and bright;
if his heart is not upright,
then his eyes are dim and dull.
When you listen to his words,
and observe his eyes,
how can a person hide himself?”
7.16 Mencius said:
“A respectful person does not insult others;
a frugal person does not seize from others.
A ruler who insults and seizes from others
would only fear that others will not obey him;
how can he be called respectful and frugal?
Can respect and frugality be achieved through merely pleasant speech and a smiling face?”
7.17 Chún Yú Kūn said:
“That men and women should not touch each other when giving or receiving things—
is this ritually proper?”
Mencius said:
“It is ritually proper.”
The other said:
“If one’s sister-in-law is drowning, should one rescue her with one’s hand?”
Mencius said:
“If one does not rescue a drowning sister-in-law,
that is to be a wolf or a jackal.
That men and women should not touch each other when giving or receiving things is a general rule;
this is the ritual norm.
To rescue a drowning sister-in-law with one’s hand,
that is an expedient adaptation.”
The other said:
“Now the whole world is drowning,
yet you, Master, do not rescue it—
why is this?”
Mencius said:
“When the world is drowning,
one rescues it with the Way;
when a sister-in-law is drowning,
one rescues her with one’s hand.
Do you wish me to rescue the world with my hand?”
7.18 Gōng Sūn Chǒu said:
“That a gentleman does not teach his own son—
why is this?”
Mencius said:
“Because the situation makes it impossible.
A teacher must use correctness;
when using correctness does not work,
anger follows.
When anger follows,
then there is injury.
‘You, Master, teach me with correctness,
but you yourself have not come from correctness.’
Thus father and son injure each other.
When father and son injure each other, that is terrible.
In ancient times, people exchanged sons and taught each other’s sons.
Between father and son, one does not demand goodness.
Demanding goodness leads to estrangement;
estrangement is the greatest of misfortunes.”
7.19 Mencius said:
“Of services, which is the greatest?
Serving one’s parents is the greatest.
Of guarding, which is the greatest?
Guarding oneself is the greatest.
I have heard of those who, without losing their own person,
were able to serve their parents;
I have never heard of one who,
having lost his own person,
was able to serve his parents.
Who does not serve?
Serving one’s parents
is the foundation of service.
Who does not guard?
Guarding oneself
is the foundation of guarding.
Zēngzǐ supported Zēng Xī,
always having wine and meat;
when about to clear the dishes,
he would always ask to whom the leftovers should be given;
when asked if there were any left,
he would always say ‘Yes.’
When Zēng Xī died,
Zēng Yuán supported Zēngzǐ,
always having wine and meat;
when about to clear the dishes,
he did not ask to whom the leftovers should be given;
when asked if there were any left,
he said:
‘There is none,’
intending to present them again.
This is called merely nourishing the mouth and body.
As for Zēngzǐ,
one could say he nourished the will.
To serve one’s parents as Zēngzǐ did—
that is acceptable.”
7.20 Mencius said:
“One cannot be satisfied by simply pointing out errors in men;
nor can one find fault merely with government policies.
Only a great person can correct what is wrong in the ruler’s mind.
If the ruler is benevolent, no one will be unbenevolent.
If the ruler is righteous, no one will be unrighteous.
If the ruler is upright, no one will be crooked.
Once the ruler is corrected, the state will be settled.”
7.21 Mencius said:
“There is unexpected praise,
and there is perfection-seeking criticism.”
7.22 Mencius said:
“When a person speaks lightly,
it is because he has no sense of responsibility.”
7.23 Mencius said:
“The trouble with people
is that they like to be teachers of others.”
7.24 Yuè Zhèngzǐ followed Zǐ Áo to Qí.
Yuè Zhèngzǐ came to see Mencius.
Mencius said:
“Have you come to see me as well?”
Yuè Zhèngzǐ replied:
“Why does the Master speak this way?”
Mencius said:
“How many days have you been here?”
Yuè Zhèngzǐ said:
“Since yesterday.”
Mencius said:
“Since yesterday,
then my speaking this way
is not inappropriate, is it?”
Yuè Zhèngzǐ said:
“My lodging had not yet been settled.”
Mencius said: “Have you heard that one should
settle his lodging
before seeking an audience with an elder?”
Yuè Zhèngzǐ said:
“I am at fault.”
7.25 Mencius said to Yuè Zhèngzǐ:
“Your coming here following Zǐ Áo
is merely for eating and drinking.
I did not expect that you, having studied the Way of the ancients,
would come just for eating and drinking.”
7.26 Mencius said:
“There are three unfilial acts;
having no posterity is the greatest.
Shùn married without informing his parents
because if he had not, he would have had no posterity.
Thus the noble person considers that his informing was as good as doing so.”
7.27 Mencius said:
“The substance of benevolence
is serving one’s parents.
The substance of righteousness
is obeying one’s elder brother.
The substance of wisdom
is knowing these two and not departing from them.
The substance of ritual
is regulating and adorning these two.
The substance of music
is taking joy in these two;
when joy arises,
how can it be stopped?
And if it cannot be stopped,
then one will unconsciously dance with his feet
and gesture with his hands.”
7.28 Mencius said:
“When the whole world was greatly delighted
and was about to turn to him,
he regarded the world’s turning to him with delight
as mere straw and grass.
Only Shùn was capable of this.
If one cannot get along with his parents,
he cannot be considered a true person;
if one cannot obey his parents,
he cannot be considered a true son.
Shùn exhausted the Way of serving his parents,
and so Gǔ Sǒu was brought to joy;
when Gǔ Sǒu was brought to joy,
the whole world was transformed.
When Gǔ Sǒu was brought to joy,
the relationship between fathers and sons throughout the world was settled.
This is what is called great filial piety.”
8.1 Mencius said:
“Shùn was born in Zhū Féng,
moved to Fù Xià,
and died in Míng Tiáo—he was a man from the eastern barbarian regions.
King Wén was born in Qí Zhōu,
and died in Bì Yǐng—he was a man from the western barbarian regions.
The distance between their territories
was over a thousand lǐ;
the difference between their generations
was over a thousand years.
Yet when they achieved their ambitions and acted in the Central States,
it was like matching the two halves of a tally.
The former sage and the later sage
followed the same standard.”
8.2 Zichǎn was in charge of the government of Zhèng.
He used his own carriage to ferry people across the Zhēn and the Wěi rivers.
Mèngzǐ said:
"This shows kindness, but he does not understand governance.
In the eleventh month of the year, footbridges are built;
in the twelfth month, carriage bridges are constructed,
and the people will no longer suffer from crossing.
A noble person brings order to his government,
and if he goes out and has people clear the way, that is acceptable—
how could he ferry every single person one by one?
Thus, for those who govern,
if they try to please each individual,
they would not have enough days in the year."
8.3 Mèngzǐ told King Xuān of Qí:
"If the ruler regards his ministers as his hands and feet,
then the ministers regard the ruler as their belly and heart;
if the ruler regards his ministers as dogs and horses,
then the ministers regard the ruler as a stranger;
if the ruler regards his ministers as dirt and grass,
then the ministers regard the ruler as a bandit and foe."
The King said:
"According to ritual,
one wears mourning for a former ruler.
Under what circumstances can one wear mourning for him?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"If one’s remonstrances are followed and one’s words are heeded,
and blessings and favors reach the people;
and if one leaves due to some reason,
then the ruler sends someone to guide him out of the realm,
and also prepares the way in advance for where he is going;
if the departed does not return for three years,
only then does the ruler take back his fields and homestead.
This is called observing the three acts of ritual.
Under these circumstances,
one would wear mourning for him.
Nowadays, for a minister,
if his remonstrances are not followed,
and his words are not heeded;
blessings and favors do not reach the people;
and if he leaves due to some reason,
then the ruler seizes and arrests him,
and also pushes him to the extreme in the place he goes;
on the day he departs,
he immediately takes back his fields and homestead.
This is called treating him as a bandit and foe.
If he is a bandit and foe, what mourning can there be?"
8.4 Mèngzǐ said:
"If a scholar is killed without crime,
then a grandee may leave;
if a commoner is executed without crime,
then a scholar may migrate."
8.5 Mèngzǐ said:
"If the ruler is benevolent, none will be unbenevolent;
if the ruler is righteous, none will be unrighteous."
8.6 Mèngzǐ said:
"Rituals that are not ritual,
righteousness that is not righteousness—
the great person does not practice them."
8.7 Mèngzǐ said:
"Those who are centered nurture those who are not centered;
those who are talented nurture those who are not talented.
Thus, people delight in having worthy fathers and elder brothers.
If the centered abandon the uncentered,
and the talented abandon the untalented,
then the distance between the worthy and the unworthy
cannot be measured by even an inch."
8.8 Mèngzǐ said:
"Only if a person refrains from doing some things
can he then accomplish something."
8.9 Mèngzǐ said:
"To speak of others’ faults—
what about the consequences that follow?"
8.10 Mèngzǐ said:
"Zhòngní did not go to extremes."
8.11 Mèngzǐ said:
"The great person
does not necessarily keep every word,
nor does he necessarily follow through on every action—
he only acts according to righteousness."
8.12 Mèngzǐ said:
"The great person
is one who does not lose his childlike heart."
8.13 Mèngzǐ said:
"Caring for the living
is not enough to be considered a great matter;
only seeing off the dead can be considered a great matter."
8.14 Mèngzǐ said:
"The noble person penetrates deeply into the Way through proper methods,
desiring to attain it himself.
When attained by himself, he dwells in it securely;
dwelling in it securely, he draws from it deeply;
drawing from it deeply, he finds its source everywhere he turns.
Thus the noble person desires to attain it himself."
8.15 Mèngzǐ said:
"To learn broadly and explain it in detail
is in order to return and explain it simply."
8.16 Mèngzǐ said:
"No one has ever been able to subdue others by using goodness to compel them;
but by using goodness to nurture others,
one can then subdue all under heaven.
For one who has not won the hearts of all under heaven to become a true king—
such a thing has never happened."
8.17 Mèngzǐ said:
"Speech without substance
is inauspicious.
Those who block the worthy will bear the consequences of such inauspiciousness."
8.18 Xúzǐ said:
"Zhòngní often praised water, saying:
'Water indeed!
Water indeed!'
What did he find to admire in water?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"A spring gushes forth ceaselessly,
never stopping day or night;
it fills every hollow before advancing,
and flows onward to the four seas.
That which has a source is like this—
this is what he admired.
But if there is no source,
during the seventh and eighth months,
when rain gathers,
ditches and channels fill up;
but their drying up
can be waited for in a moment.
Thus, when reputation exceeds reality,
the noble person is ashamed of it."
8.19 Mèngzǐ said:
"What distinguishes humans from beasts
is slight—
the common people discard it,
the noble person preserves it.
Shùn understood all things,
and discerned human relationships;
he acted from benevolence and righteousness,
not merely performing benevolent and righteous acts."
8.20 Mèngzǐ said:
"Yǔ disliked fine wine but loved good words.
Tāng held to the mean
and promoted the worthy without partiality.
King Wén regarded the people as if they were wounded,
and looked upon the Way as if he had not yet seen it.
King Wǔ did not slight those near
and did not forget those far away.
The Duke of Zhōu thought to combine
the three kings
to practice their four undertakings;
when something did not accord with them,
he looked up and pondered it,
continuing day and night;
fortunate enough to attain it,
he sat waiting for dawn."
8.21 Mèngzǐ said:
"When the traces of the true kings faded
and the Odes were lost,
the Odes being lost,
then the Spring and Autumn Annals were composed.
The Records of Jìn,
the Taowu of Chǔ,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals of Lǔ
are of the same kind:
their events concern Duke Huán of Qí
and Duke Wén of Jìn,
and their style is that of history.
Confucius said:
'Their righteous principles I, Qiū, have taken for myself.'"
8.22 Mèngzǐ said:
"The influence of a noble person
ends after five generations;
the influence of a petty person
also ends after five generations.
I was not able to become a disciple of Confucius,
but I have learned from him privately through others."
8.23 Mèngzǐ said:
"When one can take,
and also can refrain from taking,
taking harms integrity;
when one can give,
and also can refrain from giving,
giving harms kindness;
when one can die,
and also can refrain from dying,
dying harms courage."
8.24 Páng Méng learned archery from Yì;
he mastered all of Yì's arts,
thought that only Yì in the world surpassed him
and so killed Yì.
Mèngzǐ said:
"This is also Yì's fault."
Gōngmíng Yí said:
"It seems he should be without fault."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Slightly so, he says—
how could he be without fault?"
A man of Zheng sent Zizhuo Ruzi to invade Wei.
Wei sent Yugong Zhisi to pursue him.
Zizhuo Ruzi said:
"Today my illness has struck;
I cannot hold my bow.
I am as good as dead!"
He asked his charioteer:
"Who is the one pursuing me?"
His charioteer said:
"It is Yugong Zhisi."
He said:
"I will live."
His charioteer said:
"Yugong Zhisi is
a fine archer of Wei.
You, Master, say you will live—
what does this mean?"
He said:
"Yugong Zhisi studied archery
under Yigong Zhita,
and Yigong Zhita studied archery under me.
Now, Yigong Zhita
is a man of integrity,
so the friends he chooses must also be upright."
When Yugong Zhisi arrived,
he said:
"Why are you not holding your bow, Master?"
He said:
"Today my illness has struck;
I cannot hold my bow."
Yugong Zhisi said:
"I learned archery from Yigong Zhita,
and Yigong Zhita learned archery from you, Master.
I cannot bear to use your teaching
to harm you in return.
Nevertheless, today's affair
is a matter of my lord's service,
and I dare not neglect it."
He drew an arrow, struck it against the wheel,
removed its metal tip,
shot four arrows, and then withdrew.
8.25 Mencius said:
"If the beautiful Xishi were covered with filth,
people would all pass her by holding their noses.
But even if a person is ugly,
if they fast and bathe,
they can offer sacrifices to the Lord on High."
8.26 Mencius said:
"When people in the world discuss human nature,
they merely consider its 'old course.'
This 'old course'
has benefit as its foundation.
What is disliked in cleverness
is that it tends to be forced.
If the clever
were like Yu in directing water,
then there would be no dislike of cleverness.
Yu's directing of water
involved doing nothing that seemed forced.
If the clever also do nothing forced,
their cleverness would be great indeed.
Heaven is high,
and the stars are distant,
but if we seek their old course,
then the solstices of a thousand years
can be calculated while sitting."
8.27 Gonghangzi was in mourning for his son.
The Right Commander-in-Chief went to offer condolences.
Upon entering the gate,
some stepped forward to speak with the Right Commander-in-Chief,
and others went to his seat
to speak with him.
Mencius did not speak with the Right Commander-in-Chief.
The Right Commander-in-Chief, displeased, said:
"All you gentlemen speak with me, Huan;
Mencius alone does not speak with me, Huan—
this is showing me disrespect."
Mencius, hearing of this,
said:
"According to ritual,
in the court one does not step across positions to speak with another,
nor does one cross the steps to bow to another.
I wished to observe ritual,
but Ziao considers me disrespectful—
is this not strange?"
8.28 Mencius said:
"What distinguishes the noble man from others
lies in what he keeps in his heart.
The noble man keeps benevolence in his heart
and keeps ritual in his heart.
The benevolent love others,
and the ritually proper respect others.
Those who love others
are constantly loved by others;
those who respect others
are constantly respected by others.
If there is a person
who treats me with perversity and unreasonableness,
the noble man will certainly examine himself:
'I must have been unbenevolent,
I must have been without ritual—
why else would this happen?'
If, after self-examination, he finds he is benevolent
and has acted according to ritual,
yet the perversity continues,
the noble man will certainly examine himself again:
'I must have been unfaithful.'
If, after self-examination, he finds he is faithful,
yet the perversity continues,
the noble man will say:
'This is merely a deluded person.
In such a case, what difference is there between him and a beast?
And what difficulty is there in dealing with a beast?'
Therefore the noble man has lifelong anxiety,
but no sudden calamity.
As for what he is anxious about, it is this:
Shun was a man;
I, too, am a man.
Shun became a model for all under Heaven,
transmittable to later generations;
I, on the other hand, still remain as a common man—
this is what is worrisome.
What should be done about this anxiety?
Only to become like Shun—that is all.
As for what the noble man might suffer, there is none.
He does nothing that is not benevolent,
and performs no action that is not ritually proper.
If a sudden calamity befalls him,
the noble man does not suffer from it."
8.29 Yu and Ji lived in a peaceful age,
yet they passed by their own doors three times without entering.
Confucius praised them.
Yanzi lived in a chaotic age,
dwelling in a narrow lane,
with a single bamboo dish of food
and a single gourd dipper of drink.
Others could not bear the hardship,
but Yanzi did not change his joy.
Confucius praised him.
Mencius said:
"Yu, Ji, and Yan Hui shared the same Way.
Yu thought that anyone drowning under Heaven
was as if he himself had drowned them;
Ji thought that anyone starving under Heaven
was as if he himself had starved them.
Thus
they were so urgent.
If Yu, Ji, and Yanzi had exchanged places,
they would all have acted the same.
Now, if someone from the same house is fighting,
you go to rescue him,
even if it means going with disheveled hair and wearing a cap incorrectly tied—
that is acceptable.
But if a neighbor from the same village is fighting,
going to rescue him with disheveled hair and a cap incorrectly tied
would be foolish;
even shutting the door is acceptable."
8.30 Gongduzi said:
"Kuang Zhang—
the whole state calls him unfilial,
yet you, Master, associate with him,
and moreover treat him with courtesy and politeness.
May I ask why?"
Mencius said:
"What the world commonly calls unfilial consists of five things:
laziness of the four limbs,
neglecting the support of parents—
this is the first unfilial act.
Gambling and games, fondness for drinking,
neglecting the support of parents—
this is the second unfilial act.
Fondness for wealth and goods,
selfish devotion to wife and children,
neglecting the support of parents—
this is the third unfilial act.
Following the desires of ears and eyes,
thereby bringing disgrace to parents—
this is the fourth unfilial act.
Fondness for bravery, quarreling, and violence,
thereby endangering parents—
this is the fifth unfilial act.
Does Zhangzi have even one of these?
Now, Zhangzi's case is that
between father and son, they urged goodness upon each other
but could not reach an understanding.
Urging goodness
is the Way between friends;
if father and son urge goodness upon each other,
it greatly harms their natural affection.
Now, Zhangzi—
would he not desire the ties of husband and wife, parent and child?
But because he offended his father,
he cannot approach him,
so he sent away his wife and kept his children at a distance,
not supporting them for life.
He designed his mind to think that
if he did not do so,
his offense would be even greater.
That is all there is to Zhangzi."
8.31 Once, when Zēng Zǐ was living in Wǔchéng,
there was an incursion by the Yuè people.
Someone said to him:
"The bandits have come;
why not leave this place?"
Zēng Zǐ replied:
"Do not lodge anyone in my house,
lest they damage the firewood and trees."
When the bandits withdrew,
he then said:
"Repair my walls and house,
for I shall return."
The bandits withdrew,
and Zēng Zǐ returned.
His followers said:
"The people of this place treated you, Sir, with such
loyalty and respect.
When the bandits came,
you were the first to leave, setting an example for the people;
when the bandits withdrew, you returned.
This seems hardly proper."
Shěn Yóu Xíng said:
"This is not something you understand.
In former times,
when Shěn Yóu suffered the calamity of the fuel-gatherers,
those who followed our Master were seventy men,
but none of them got involved."
Zǐ Sī was living in Wèi,
when the Qí attacked.
Someone said:
"The bandits have come;
why not leave?"
Zǐ Sī said:
"If I, Jí, leave,
with whom will the ruler defend the city?"
Mencius said:
"Zēng Zǐ and Zǐ Sī followed the same principle.
Zēng Zǐ was a teacher,
a father and elder brother;
Zǐ Sī was a minister,
of lowly status.
Had Zēng Zǐ and Zǐ Sī exchanged places,
each would have acted in the same way."
8.32 Chú Zǐ said:
"The king sent someone to spy on you, Master. Does he indeed have something that makes him different from others?"
Mencius said:
"How am I different from others?
Yáo and Shùn were the same as other men."
8.33 A man of Qí had a wife and a concubine, and they lived together.
When their husband went out,
he would always return full of wine and meat.
His wife asked who he ate and drank with,
and he said they were all wealthy and noble men.
The wife told the concubine:
"When our husband goes out,
he always returns full of wine and meat;
when I ask who he eats and drinks with,
they are all wealthy and noble men.
Yet no distinguished person has ever come here.
I will spy on where our husband goes."
Rising early,
she stealthily followed her husband to where he went.
Throughout the whole city, no one stood and talked with him.
Finally, he went to the Eastern outskirts to the graves among the tombs,
approached those making offerings,
and begged for their leftovers;
not getting enough,
he looked around and went to others.
This was the way he managed to get his fill.
His wife returned home,
and told the concubine, saying:
"A husband is someone
we look up to and rely on for life,
and now he is like this!"
She and the concubine reviled their husband,
and wept together in the courtyard.
But the husband, not knowing this,
came swaggering in from outside,
putting on airs before his wife and concubine.
From the perspective of a gentleman,
as for the ways men seek wealth, honor, profit, and advancement,
few indeed are those whose wives and concubines would not feel shame and weep together.
9.1 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying:
"When Shùn went to the fields,
he wept and cried out to the compassionate Heaven.
Why did he weep and cry out?"
Mencius said:
"It was because of resentment and longing."
Wàn Zhāng said:
"When parents love you,
rejoice and never forget it;
when parents hate you,
work hard and do not resent them.
Then did Shùn resent his parents?"
Mencius said:
"Cháng Xī asked Gōngmíng Gāo, saying:
'As for Shùn going to the fields,
I have already received your instruction;
but when he wept and cried out to the compassionate Heaven and to his parents,
I do not understand.'
Gōngmíng Gāo said:
'This is not something you can understand.'
Now, Gōngmíng Gāo considered that a filial son's heart
could not be so indifferent as this:
'I strive to till the fields,
and fulfill my duties as a son—that is all.
If my parents do not love me,
what blame is that to me?'
The Di (Emperor) sent his nine sons and two daughters,
along with the various officers, oxen and sheep, grain and storehouses, all prepared,
to serve Shùn in the midst of the fields.
Many scholars of the world came to join him,
and the Di intended to cede the whole world to him and transfer it
But because he could not please his parents,
he felt like a poor man with no place to turn.
To be loved by the world's scholars
is what men desire,
yet it was not enough to relieve his sorrow;
love of beauty is what men desire,
yet marrying the Di's two daughters
was not enough to relieve his sorrow;
wealth
is what men desire,
yet possessing the whole world's wealth
was not enough to relieve his sorrow;
honor
is what men desire,
yet being honored as the Son of Heaven
was not enough to relieve his sorrow.
Being loved, beauty, and wealth and honor—
none of these were enough to relieve his sorrow.
Only by pleasing his parents
could his sorrow be relieved.
In youth, one longs for parents;
when one knows love of beauty, one longs for a young and attractive partner;
when one has a wife and children, one longs for them;
when one takes office, one longs for the ruler;
if one cannot gain the ruler's favor, one's heart burns within.
Great filial piety means longing for one's parents throughout life.
As for one who at fifty still longed for them,
I have seen this in Great Shùn."
9.2 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying:
"The Book of Odes says:
'How should one take a wife?
One must inform one's parents.'
If this saying is to be believed,
no one should have followed it more than Shùn.
Why did Shùn take a wife without informing his parents?"
Mencius said:
"If he had informed them, he would not have been able to marry.
The relationship between man and woman in the home
is one of the great bonds of human life.
If he had informed them, he would have abandoned this great bond,
thus incurring the resentment of his parents.
Therefore, he did not inform them."
Wàn Zhāng said:
"As for Shùn not informing his parents and taking a wife,
I have already received your instruction.
But why did the Di give his daughters as wives to Shùn without informing Shùn's parents?"
Mencius said:
"The Di also knew that if he informed them,
he would not be able to give his daughters in marriage."
Wàn Zhāng said:
"Shùn's parents sent him to repair the granary,
then removed the ladder, and Gǔsǒu set fire to the granary.
They sent him to dig a well,
and when he came out, they covered him up.
Xiàng said:
'The plot to cover the lord of the city was all my achievement.
The oxen and sheep go to our parents,
the granaries go to our parents,
the shields and spears shall be mine,
the zither shall be mine,
the bow shall be mine,
and my two sisters-in-law shall be made to attend to my bed.'
Xiàng went into Shùn's palace,
and found Shùn on his bed playing the zither.
Xiàng said:
'I am so deeply thinking of you!'
He looked ashamed.
Shùn said:
'I think of these my ministers and people;
do you assist me in governing them.'
I do not know—did Shùn not know that Xiàng was about to kill him?"
He said,
"How could he not know?
When Xiàng was worried, Shùn was also worried;
when Xiàng was happy, Shùn was also happy."
(Someone) said,
"Then was Shùn feigning joy?"
He said,
"No.
Once, someone gave a live fish to Zǐchǎn of Zhèng.
Zǐchǎn ordered the pond-keeper to raise it in the pond.
The pond-keeper cooked it,
and reported back, saying:
'When it was first released, it was sluggish;
after a while, it swam freely;
then it vanished contentedly.'
Zǐchǎn said,
'It has found its place!
It has found its place!'
The pond-keeper came out and said,
'Who says Zǐchǎn is wise?
I have already cooked and eaten it,
and he says,
"It has found its place,
it has found its place!"'
Therefore, a gentleman may be deceived by what accords with his principles,
but it is difficult to mislead him with what is contrary to the Way.
He came with the way of loving his elder brother,
so (Shùn) truly believed and rejoiced in it.
How could it be feigned?"
9.3 Wàn Zhāng asked,
"Xiàng daily made it his business
to kill Shùn.
Yet when Shùn became Son of Heaven,
he banished him.
Why was that?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"He enfeoffed him;
some say it was banishment."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"Shùn banished Gòng Gōng to Yōuzhōu,
sent Huān Dōu to Chóngshān,
killed the ruler of Sān Miáo at Sānwēi,
and imprisoned Gǔn at Yǔshān.
When these four criminals were punished,
the whole world submitted.
This was punishing the unkind.
Xiàng was utterly unkind,
yet he was enfeoffed at Yǒubì.
What crime did the people of Yǒubì commit?
Is a kind person indeed like this—
punishing others,
yet enfeoffing his own brother?"
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"A kind person toward his brother
harbors no anger,
stores up no resentment.
He simply loves and cherishes him.
In cherishing him,
he wishes him to be noble;
in loving him,
he wishes him to be wealthy.
Enfeoffing him at Yǒubì
was making him noble and wealthy.
If he himself were Son of Heaven
and his brother remained a commoner,
could that be called loving and cherishing him?"
"May I ask,
as for what you said, 'some say it was banishment'—
what does that mean?"
He said,
"Xiàng could not act independently in his state.
The Son of Heaven sent officials to govern his state
and collect its tribute taxes.
Therefore it was called banishment.
How could he be allowed to oppress the people there?
Nevertheless,
(Shùn) wished to see him frequently,
so (Xiàng) came constantly.
'Not waiting for the tribute period,
but through government affairs, he had contact with Yǒubì.'
This is what that refers to."
9.4 Xiánqiū Méng asked,
"It is said,
'A man of abundant virtue
cannot be treated as a subject by a ruler,
nor as a son by a father.'
When Shùn faced south as ruler,
Yáo led the feudal lords facing north
to pay him court.
Gǔsǒu also faced north
to pay him court.
When Shùn saw Gǔsǒu,
his expression was uneasy.
Confucius said,
'At that time,
the world was in danger—
precarious indeed!'
I do not know: is this saying truly so?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"No.
This is not the words of a gentleman,
but the talk of wild people from eastern Qí.
When Yáo grew old, Shùn acted as regent.
The 'Canon of Yáo' says,
'After twenty-eight years,
Fāng Xūn passed away.
The people mourned as if for a parent.
For three years,
all within the four seas ceased all music.'
Confucius said,
'The heavens have no two suns;
the people have no two kings.'
If Shùn were already Son of Heaven,
and yet led the feudal lords of the world
to observe three years of mourning for Yáo,
that would make two Sons of Heaven."
Xiánqiū Méng said,
"That Shùn did not treat Yáo as a subject—
this I have already heard.
The Book of Odes says,
'Under the whole heaven,
every spot is the king's land;
to the shores of the land,
every man is the king's subject.'
Since Shùn was already Son of Heaven,
may I ask, what of Gǔsǒu not being a subject—
how is that?"
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"This ode
does not mean that.
It describes one who toiled in the king's service
and could not care for his parents.
It says,
'This is all the king's business,
yet I alone am worthy and toil.'
Therefore, when explaining odes,
do not let the words harm the phrase,
nor let the phrase harm the intent.
Use your understanding to meet the intent—
that is to grasp it.
If you only take the words literally,
the ode 'Yún Hàn' says,
'Of the remnant people of Zhōu,
not one remains.'
If you believed these words,
then Zhōu would have no surviving people.
The ultimate filial son
is nothing greater than honoring his parents;
the ultimate in honoring parents
is nothing greater than supporting them with the whole world.
Being the father of the Son of Heaven
is the utmost honor;
supporting him with the whole world
is the utmost support.
The Book of Odes says,
'Eternal filial thoughts,
filial thoughts as a model.'
This refers to that.
The Book of History says,
'Reverently he went to see Gǔsǒu,
trembling and reverent, solemn and cautious,
and Gǔsǒu was also truly compliant.'
Is this a case of a father not being able to treat him as a son?"
9.5 Wàn Zhāng said,
"That Yáo gave the world to Shùn—
was there such a thing?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"No.
The Son of Heaven cannot give the world to another."
"Then, since Shùn possessed the world,
who gave it to him?"
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"Heaven gave it to him."
"When Heaven gave it to him,
did it issue explicit commands?"
He said,
"No.
Heaven does not speak;
it reveals itself through deeds and events."
(Wàn Zhāng) said,
"As for revealing itself through deeds and events—
how is that?"
He said,
"The Son of Heaven can recommend a man to Heaven,
but cannot make Heaven give him the world.
A feudal lord can recommend a man to the Son of Heaven,
but cannot make the Son of Heaven give him a state.
A high minister can recommend a man to a feudal lord,
but cannot make the feudal lord give him a high post.
Formerly, Yáo recommended Shùn to Heaven,
and Heaven accepted him.
He presented him to the people,
and the people accepted him.
Therefore it is said,
'Heaven does not speak;
it reveals itself through deeds and events.'"
Wàn Zhāng said,
"May I ask, when Yao recommended Shun to Heaven,
Heaven accepted him;
when he presented him to the people, the people accepted him.
How did this happen?"
Mencius said,
"He had Shun preside over sacrifices,
and all the spirits enjoyed them—
this was Heaven accepting him.
He had Shun manage affairs,
and affairs were well ordered,
the hundred surnames were at peace with him—
this was the people accepting him.
Heaven gave it to him,
and people gave it to him.
Therefore it is said,
'The Son of Heaven cannot give the realm to another.'
Shun assisted Yao
for twenty-eight years—
this was not something any person could bring about;
it was Heaven.
When Yao died,
after the three-year mourning period was completed,
Shun withdrew from Yao's son
to the south of the Southern River.
The feudal lords of the realm who came to pay homage
did not go to Yao's son but went to Shun;
those who had lawsuits
did not go to Yao's son but went to Shun;
those who sang praises
did not sing praises of Yao's son but sang praises of Shun.
Therefore it is said,
'It was Heaven.
Only then did he go to the central capital
and ascend the throne of the Son of Heaven.
If he had dwelt in Yao's palace
and pressured Yao's son,
that would have been usurpation,
not a gift from Heaven.'
The "Great Declaration" says,
'Heaven sees as my people see;
