Heaven hears as my people hear'—
this is what is meant."
9.6 Wàn Zhāng asked,
"People say,
'When it came to Yǔ, virtue declined;
he did not transmit to the worthy
but transmitted to his son.'
Is this so?"
Mencius said,
"No,
this is not so.
If Heaven gives it to the worthy,
then it gives it to the worthy;
if Heaven gives it to the son,
then it gives it to the son.
In ancient times, Shun recommended Yǔ to Heaven.
Seventeen years later,
Shun died.
After the three-year mourning period was completed,
Yǔ withdrew from Shun's son
to Yángchéng.
The people of the realm followed him,
just as after Yao's death
they did not follow Yao's son but followed Shun.
Yǔ recommended Yì to Heaven.
Seven years later,
Yǔ died.
After the three-year mourning period was completed,
Yì withdrew from Yǔ's son
to the north of Jīshān.
Those paying homage
and those with lawsuits
did not go to Yì but went to Qǐ,
saying,
'He is our lord's son.'
Those who sang praises
did not sing praises of Yì but sang praises of Qǐ,
saying,
'He is our lord's son.'
Dānzhū was unworthy,
and Shun's son was also unworthy.
Shun's assisting Yao
and Yǔ's assisting Shun
spanned many years,
and they had long bestowed grace on the people.
Qǐ was worthy,
able to respectfully inherit and continue Yǔ's way.
Yì's assisting Yǔ
spanned few years,
and he had not long bestowed grace on the people.
The lengths of time Shùn, Yǔ, and Yì
were in office differed widely,
and the worthiness or unworthiness of their sons—
all this was Heaven,
not something any person could bring about.
What is done without anyone doing it
is Heaven;
what arrives without anyone bringing it
is fate.
For a common man to possess the realm,
his virtue must be like that of Shùn or Yǔ,
and he must be recommended by the Son of Heaven.
Therefore Confucius did not possess the realm.
For one who inherits the realm,
what Heaven abolishes
must be like Jié or Zhòu.
Therefore Yì, Yī Yǐn, and Zhōu Gōng
did not possess the realm.
Yī Yǐn assisted Tāng to rule over the realm as king.
Tāng died,
Tài Dīng was not established,
Wài Bǐng reigned two years,
Zhòng Rén four years.
Tài Jiǎ overturned Tāng's laws and standards.
Yī Yǐn exiled him to Tóng.
After three years,
Tài Jiǎ repented,
blamed himself and reformed.
In Tóng, he dwelt in benevolence and shifted to righteousness
for three years, listening to Yī Yǐn's admonitions to himself.
He then returned to Bó.
Zhōu Gōng's not possessing the realm
was like Yì's case with Xià
and Yī Yǐn's with Yīn.
Confucius said,
'Táng and Yú abdicated;
Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu passed on [the throne].
Their principle is one.'"
9.7 Wàn Zhāng asked,
"People say,
'Yī Yǐn used cutting meat and cooking to secure Tāng's favor.'
Is this so?"
Mencius said,
"No,
this is not so.
Yī Yǐn plowed in the wilds of Yǒu Shēn,
and delighted in the way of Yáo and Shùn.
If it was not righteous,
if it was not the Way,
even if the whole realm were offered as his salary, he would not look at it;
even if a thousand teams of horses were tied up, he would not glance at them.
If it was not righteous,
if it was not the Way,
he would not give a single straw to another,
nor take a single straw from another.
Tāng sent a messenger with gifts to invite him.
Casual and carefree, he said,
'What would I do with Tāng's invitation gifts?
Would I not rather stay in the fields,
thereby delighting in the way of Yáo and Shùn?'
Tāng sent three times to invite him.
Then, changing his mind, he said,
'Rather than staying in the fields,
thereby delighting in the way of Yáo and Shùn,
would it not be better to make this lord a lord like Yáo and Shùn?
Would it not be better to make these people people like Yáo and Shùn?
Would it not be better to see this accomplished in my own lifetime?
Heaven, in giving birth to these people,
causes those who know first to awaken those who know later,
and those who awaken first to awaken those who awaken later.
I
am one of Heaven's people who awakens first.
I shall use this Way to awaken these people.
If I do not awaken them, then who will?'
He thought that if any man or woman among the people of the realm
failed to receive the grace of Yáo and Shùn,
it was as if he himself had pushed them into a ditch.
So heavily did he take upon himself the burden of the realm.
Therefore he went to Tāng
and persuaded him
to punish Xià
and rescue the people.
I have never heard of someone who crooked himself but could straighten others,
let alone someone who humiliated himself to set the realm straight.
The conduct of sages is not uniform:
some keep distant, some keep near;
some leave, some do not leave;
they all return to keeping themselves pure.
I have heard of his using the way of Yáo and Shùn to seek Tāng's favor,
but not of using cutting meat and cooking.
The "Instructions of Yī" says,
'Heaven's punishment began in Mùgōng;
I began in Bó.'"
9.8 Wàn Zhāng asked,
"Some say
that Confucius in Wèi stayed with the healer,
and in Qí stayed with the eunuch, Jí Huán.
Is this so?"
Mencius said,
"No,
this is not so;
it is the fabrication of gossips.
In the state of Wei
[Confucius] lodged with Yán Chóuyóu.
Mí Zǐ's wife and Zǐlù's wife
were sisters.
Mí Zǐ said to Zǐlù:
"If Confucius lodges with me,
a ministerial post in Wei can be obtained."
Zǐlù reported this [to Confucius].
Confucius said:
"It is determined by fate."
Confucius advanced according to ritual,
and withdrew according to righteousness.
Whether he obtained [a position] or not, he said:
"It is determined by fate."
But lodging with Yōngjū and the eunuch Jí Huán,
that would be without righteousness and without fate.
Confucius was not pleased in Lu and Wei,
encountered Huán Sīmǎ of Song,
who planned to waylay and kill him,
so he changed his clothes and passed through Song.
At that time Confucius was in distress,
and lodged with Sīchéng Zhēnzǐ,
who was a minister of Chén Hóu Zhōu.
I have heard that to observe a close minister,
one looks at whom he lodges with;
to observe a distant minister,
one looks at with whom he lodges.
If Confucius had lodged with Yōngjū and the eunuch Jí Huán,
how could he be Confucius?"
9.9 Wàn Zhāng asked:
"Some say,
'Bǎilǐ Xī sold himself
to a cattle breeder in Qin
for five sheepskins, and fed cattle
to seek audience with Duke Mù of Qin.'
Is this true?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"No,
it is not so;
this was made up by those fond of meddling.
Bǎilǐ Xī
was a man of Yú.
The men of Jin, with the jade of Chuíjí
and the horses bred in Qū,
sought passage through Yu to attack Guo.
Gōng Zhīqí remonstrated,
but Bǎilǐ Xī did not remonstrate.
Knowing that the Duke of Yu could not be remonstrated with, he left and went to Qin,
and he was already seventy years old then;
if he did not know that feeding cattle to seek an audience with Duke Mù of Qin was disgraceful,
could that be called wisdom?
Not remonstrating when remonstrance was impossible,
can that be called unwisdom?
Knowing that the Duke of Yu was about to perish,
he left first,
so he cannot be called unwise.
When he was later promoted in Qin,
knowing that Duke Mù was someone with whom one could act
and becoming his minister,
can that be called unwise?
As minister of Qin,
he made his lord renowned throughout the world,
and could be passed down to later generations;
could anyone who was not worthy have done this?
Selling himself to perfect his lord,
even a man of the village who cares for his own integrity would not do it,
so could a worthy be said to do it?"
10.1 Mèngzǐ said:
"Bó Yí would not see evil sights,
nor hear evil sounds.
He would not serve a lord he did not regard as his lord,
nor command people he did not regard as his people.
When the state was well governed, he would advance;
when it was in disorder, he would retreat.
Where oppressive government issued,
where unruly people dwelt,
he could not bear to stay.
He considered being with a village man
like sitting in court robes and cap
amid mud and charcoal.
During the time of Zhòu,
he lived at the shore of the North Sea,
waiting for the world to become pure.
Therefore, those who heard the style of Bó Yí,
the covetous became honest,
and the weak-willed developed resolve.
Yī Yǐn said:
'What lord is not to be served?
What people are not to be commanded?'
In good government he advanced,
in disorder he also advanced,
saying:
'Heaven gave birth to these people,
causing those who first knew
to awaken those who later know,
causing those who first awakened
to awaken those who later awaken.
I
am one of Heaven's people who first awakened.
I will use this Way to awaken these people.'
He considered that if any man or woman among the people of the world
did not share in the benefits of Yáo and Shùn,
it was as if he himself had pushed them into a ditch.
Such was the weight he took on himself for the world.
Liǔ Xiàhuì
was not ashamed of a vile lord,
nor did he decline a small office.
In advancing, he did not conceal his worth,
always acting according to his Way.
When passed over, he did not resent;
when in distress, he did not worry.
Living with village men,
he was naturally at ease and could not bear to leave.
'You are you,
I am I;
even if you were to stand stark naked by my side,
how could you defile me?'
Therefore, those who heard the style of Liǔ Xiàhuì,
the narrow-minded became generous,
and the stingy became sincere.
"When Confucius left Qí,
he wrung out the water from his rice and set off;
when he left Lǔ,
he said:
'I am going slowly,
for this is the way to leave the state of one's parents.'
He could speed up when speed was called for,
and stay long when staying long was called for,
could be at rest when rest was called for,
and could serve in office when service was called for,
such was Confucius."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Bó Yí
was the saint of purity,
Yī Yǐn
was the saint of responsibility,
Liǔ Xiàhuì
was the saint of harmony,
and Confucius was the saint of timeliness.
Confucius can be said to have achieved the grand synthesis.
'Achieving the grand synthesis' means
like the metal sound being struck and the jade sound vibrating.
'The metal sound being struck'
is the beginning of orderly pattern;
'the jade sound vibrating'
is the completion of orderly pattern.
The beginning of orderly pattern
is a matter of wisdom;
the completion of orderly pattern
is a matter of sagehood.
Wisdom
is like skill;
sagehood
is like strength.
It is like shooting from a hundred paces away:
reaching the target
is due to your strength;
hitting the target
is not due to your strength."
10.2 Běigōng Qí asked:
"How did the house of Zhōu rank its offices and salaries?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"The details
cannot be heard now,
because the feudal lords disliked that [these records] harmed their interests,
and so they all destroyed the documents;
however, I, 'Kē,'
have heard the outline of it.
The Son of Heaven was one rank,
the Duke one rank,
the Marquis one rank,
the Earl one rank,
the Viscount and Baron were the same rank,
making five grades in total.
The lord [of a state] was one rank,
the Minister one rank,
the Great Officer one rank,
the Upper Scholar one rank,
the Middle Scholar one rank,
the Lower Scholar one rank,
making six grades [in the state].
The system for the Son of Heaven
had a territory of a thousand square li;
Dukes and Marquises each had a hundred square li;
Earls had seventy;
Viscounts and Barons had fifty,
making four grades [of territory].
A territory of less than fifty li
cannot have direct communication with the Son of Heaven.
It is attached to a feudal lord,
and is called an "appanage."
The ministers of the Son of Heaven
receive land equal to that of a marquis;
the great officers
receive land equal to that of an earl;
the principal officers
receive land equal to that of a viscount or baron.
The territory of a great state is one hundred li square.
The ruler's salary is ten times that of his chief minister;
the chief minister's salary is four times that of a great officer;
the great officer's salary is double that of a first-class officer;
the first-class officer's salary is double that of a middle-class officer;
the middle-class officer's salary is double that of a lower-class officer;
the lower-class officer's salary is the same as that of a commoner serving in office,
and this salary is enough to replace his income from farming.
The territory of a second-class state is seventy li square.
The ruler's salary is ten times that of his chief minister;
the chief minister's salary is three times that of a great officer;
the great officer's salary is double that of a first-class officer;
the first-class officer's salary is double that of a middle-class officer;
the middle-class officer's salary is double that of a lower-class officer;
the lower-class officer's salary is the same as that of a commoner serving in office,
and this salary is enough to replace his income from farming.
The territory of a small state is fifty li square.
The ruler's salary is ten times that of his chief minister;
the chief minister's salary is two times that of a great officer;
the great officer's salary is double that of a first-class officer;
the first-class officer's salary is double that of a middle-class officer;
the middle-class officer's salary is double that of a lower-class officer;
the lower-class officer's salary is the same as that of a commoner serving in office,
and this salary is enough to replace his income from farming.
As for the produce of a farmer,
one man receives one hundred mu;
when these hundred mu are fertilized,
an upper-class farmer can support nine people,
the next upper class supports eight,
the middle class supports seven,
the next middle class supports six,
and the lower class supports five.
For commoners serving in office,
their salaries are graded accordingly."
10.3 Wàn Zhāng asked,
"May I venture to ask about friendship?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Do not rely on seniority,
do not rely on nobility,
do not rely on brothers' influence when making friends.
Friendship is
befriending another's virtue,
and it cannot involve any reliance.
Mèng Xiànzǐ
was the head of a family with a hundred chariots;
he had five friends:
Yuèzhèng Qiú and Mù Zhòng;
as for the other three, I have forgotten them.
Xiànzǐ's friendship with these five men
was not based on his family's status.
If these five men had relied on Xiànzǐ's family,
then he would not have befriended them.
This was not only true for a family with a hundred chariots;
even the ruler of a small state had such friends.
Duke Huì of Fèi said,
'With Zǐsī,
I treated him as my teacher;
with Yán Bān,
I treated him as a friend;
as for Wáng Shùn and Zhǎng Xī,
they served me.'
This was not only true for the ruler of a small state;
even the ruler of a great state had such friends.
As for Duke Píng of Jìn and Hài Táng,
when told to enter, he entered;
when told to sit, he sat;
when told to eat, he ate;
although it was coarse rice and vegetable soup,
he never failed to eat his fill,
for he dared not not eat his fill.
But this was all.
He did not share the ruler's heavenly rank,
he did not administer the ruler's heavenly office,
and he did not partake of the ruler's heavenly salary.
This was a scholar's way of honoring the worthy,
not a king or duke's way of honoring the worthy.
Shùn once met the Emperor;
the Emperor lodged his son-in-law in a secondary chamber,
and also feasted Shùn;
they took turns as host and guest,
and this was the Son of Heaven
befriending a common man.
When the lowly honor the noble,
it is called 'honoring the noble';
when the noble honor the lowly,
it is called 'honoring the worthy.'
Honoring the noble and honoring the worthy
have the same principle."
10.4 Wàn Zhāng said,
"May I venture to ask about social interaction—
what intention should one have?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Respect."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"'To refuse a gift outright is disrespectful'—
why is that?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"When a superior gives a gift, if one says,
'Was the way he obtained it
righteous or unrighteous?'
and only then accepts it,
this is considered disrespectful,
so one does not refuse it."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"What if one does not refuse it with words,
but refuses it in one's heart, saying,
'He took it from the people unrighteously,'
and then uses some other excuse to avoid accepting—
would that not be acceptable?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"If the relationship is formed in the proper Way
and the interaction is conducted with propriety,
then even Confucius would accept such a gift."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"Suppose there is a robber outside the city gates,
and he forms a relationship in the proper Way
and offers a gift with propriety—
would it then be acceptable to accept the robber's gift?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"No;
the 'Announcement to Kāng' says:
'Those who kill and plunder,
reckless and unafraid of death,
are loathed by all the people.'
Such people are to be executed without awaiting instruction.
The Yīn received this from the Xià,
and the Zhōu received it from the Yīn;
there has been no objection.
In the present age, this is even more severe.
How could one accept gifts from them?"
Wàn Zhāng said,
"Today's feudal lords take from the people
just like robbers.
If they provide courteous interaction with propriety,
then the gentleman accepts their gifts—
may I ask how this is justified?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Do you think that if a true king arose,
he would punish all today's feudal lords in one fell swoop?
Or would he first instruct them, and only punish those who do not reform?
To call
taking what is not one's own
'robbery' is to stretch the analogy to its fullest extent.
When Confucius served in Lǔ,
the people of Lǔ competed in hunting,
and Confucius also competed in hunting.
If even competing in hunting was acceptable,
how much more so accepting gifts?"
Wàn Zhāng said,
"Then was Confucius's service
not for the sake of the Way?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"It was for the Way."
"If it was for the Way, why did he compete in hunting?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Confucius first rectified the sacrificial vessels according to records,
and did not use food from all directions to supply the rectified vessels."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"Why did he not leave then?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"He was giving a sign.
When the sign sufficed to show the Way could be practiced,
and yet it was not practiced,
then he left.
This is why he never stayed for a full three years in any state.
Confucius had service where he saw the Way could be practiced,
service where he was treated with courtesy,
and service where he was supported by the state.
With Jì Huánzǐ,
it was service where he saw the Way could be practiced;
with Duke Líng of Wèi,
it was service where he was treated with courtesy;
with Duke Xiào of Wèi,
it was service where he was supported by the state."
10.5 Mèngzǐ said,
"Service in office is not for the sake of poverty,
but sometimes it is for poverty;
taking a wife is not for the sake of support,
but sometimes it is for support.
For one who serves for poverty,
he should decline high office and take a low position,
decline riches and take poverty.
To decline high office and take a low position,
to decline riches and take poverty—
what is suitable?
Guarding the gates and striking the watchman's rattle."
Confucius once served as a minor grain official,
and said,
“I just made sure the accounts were correct.”
He once served as a herdsman,
and said,
“I just made sure the cattle and sheep grew strong
and were well-fed.”
“To hold a lowly position but speak of high matters is a fault;
to stand in a ruler’s court
and yet see the Way not put into practice
is a disgrace.”
10.6 Wan Zhang said,
“Why does a scholar not take up residence with a feudal lord?”
Mencius said,
“He dares not.
It is proper for a feudal lord who has lost his state to reside with another feudal lord;
but it is not proper for a scholar to reside with a feudal lord.”
Wan Zhang said,
“If the lord offers him grain, does he accept it?”
Mencius said,
“He accepts it.”
“On what principle does he accept it?”
Mencius said,
“A lord is expected to provide for the common people.”
Wan Zhang said,
“When he provides for him, he accepts; but when he bestows a gift, he does not accept. Why is that?”
Mencius said,
“He dares not.”
Wan Zhang said,
“May I ask why he dares not?”
Mencius said,
“Even gatekeepers and night watchmen have fixed duties and thus receive support from their superiors.
To receive a gift from a superior without having a fixed duty is considered disrespectful.”
Wan Zhang said,
“If the lord offers gifts, he accepts them. May I ask whether such gifts can be offered regularly?”
Mencius said,
“When Duke Mù treated Zǐsī,
he frequently inquired after him
and frequently sent him cooked meat.
Zǐsī was displeased.
Finally,
he drove the messenger out through the main gate,
faced north, bowed twice with his head to the ground, and refused the gift,
saying,
‘Now I know that you treat me like a dog or a horse!’
From then on, no gifts were sent.
If one admires worthiness but cannot promote it
nor support it,
can this be called admiring worthiness?”
Wan Zhang said,
“May I ask how a ruler who wishes to support a noble man can be said to truly support him?”
Mencius said,
“At first, he presents the gift with a royal command, and the recipient bows twice with head to the ground and accepts.
Afterward, the granary officer sends grain
and the cook sends meat,
but without the royal command.
Zǐsī thought that sending cooked meat
would make him bow again and again,
which is not the way to support a noble man.
When Yáo treated Shùn,
he had his nine sons serve him,
gave him two daughters in marriage,
and provided officials, cattle, sheep, granaries, and all necessities,
thus supporting Shùn while he was in the fields,
and later promoted him to the highest position.
Hence it is said: this is how kings and dukes honor the worthy.”
10.7 Wan Zhang said,
“May I ask what principle lies in not meeting with the feudal lords?”
Mencius said,
“In the state, one is called a subject of the marketplace, and in the countryside, a subject of the wilds—both are called commoners.
Commoners do not present a token of introduction to become ministers,
and so they dare not seek an audience with feudal lords—
this is proper.”
Wan Zhang said,
“When a commoner is summoned to do labor,
he goes;
but when a lord wishes to see him and summons him,
he does not go.
Why is that?”
Mencius said,
“Going to do labor is righteous;
going to seek an audience
is not righteous.
Moreover, why does the lord wish to see him?”
Wan Zhang said,
“Because of his extensive knowledge,
or because of his worthiness.”
Mencius said,
“If it is because of his extensive knowledge, even the Son of Heaven does not summon his teacher—
how much less would a feudal lord?
If it is because of his worthiness, I have never heard of summoning someone worthy to be seen.
Duke Mù frequently sought audiences with Zǐsī,
and said,
‘In ancient times, rulers of a thousand-chariot state befriended scholars—
what do you think of that?’
Zǐsī was displeased,
and said,
‘The ancients had a saying:
“One serves him, does one not—how can one call it befriending him?”’
Why was Zǐsī displeased?
Was it not because he thought,
‘In terms of rank, you are my ruler;
I am your subject—
how dare I befriend you?
In terms of virtue, you should serve me—
how can you befriend me?’
If a ruler of a thousand-chariot state could not gain his friendship,
how much less could he summon him?
Duke Jǐng of Qí once went hunting
and summoned a gamekeeper with a banner.
The gamekeeper did not come,
and the duke was about to kill him.
‘A man of志向 does not fear dying in a ditch; a brave man does not fear losing his head.’
What did Confucius approve in this?
He approved the fact that the gamekeeper refused to go when summoned with the wrong token.”
Wan Zhang said,
“May I ask how a gamekeeper should be summoned?”
Mencius said,
“With a leather cap; a commoner with a plain flag; a scholar with a pennoned flag; a great officer with a banner.
To summon a gamekeeper with a summons meant for a great officer,
the gamekeeper would rather die than go;
to summon a commoner with a summons meant for a scholar, would the commoner dare go?
How much less
when one summons a worthy person
with a token unfit for a worthy?
To wish to see a worthy man but not follow the proper Way
is like wishing him to enter but shutting the door against him.
Righteousness is the road;
ritual is the door.
Only a noble man can follow this road
and go in and out by this door.
The Book of Odes says:
‘The Way of Zhōu is like a whetstone, straight as an arrow; the noble man treads it, the commoner looks up to it.’”
Wan Zhang said,
“When Confucius was summoned by a ruler’s command,
he did not wait for his carriage to be yoked but set out immediately.
Was he then wrong?”
Mencius said,
“Confucius was in office with a set duty,
and he was summoned by virtue of his office.”
10.8 Mencius said to Wan Zhang,
“A good scholar of one village befriends the good scholars of that village;
a good scholar of one state befriends the good scholars of that state;
a good scholar of the world befriends the good scholars of the world.
If befriending the good scholars of the world is not enough,
he goes further to discuss the ancients.
He recites their poems and reads their books,
but can he do so without knowing what kind of men they were?
Therefore he examines their times.
This is befriending the ancients.”
10.9 King Xuān of Qí asked about ministers.
Mencius said,
"What kind of ministers does the King mean?"
The King said,
"Are ministers not the same?"
Mencius said,
"No, they are not.
There are ministers from the royal clan,
and there are ministers of different surnames."
The King said,
"May I ask about ministers from the royal clan?"
Mencius said,
"If the ruler has a great fault, they remonstrate;
if after repeated remonstrance he still does not listen,
then they replace him."
The King’s countenance suddenly changed.
Mencius said,
"Let not the King be surprised.
The King asked me,
and I dare not answer otherwise than truthfully."
The King’s expression settled,
and then he asked about ministers of different surnames.
Mencius said,
"If the ruler has a fault, they remonstrate;
if after repeated remonstrance he still does not listen,
then they leave."
11.1 The philosopher Gào said,
"Human nature is like the willow tree;
righteousness
is like cups and bowls.
To make human nature into benevolence and righteousness
is like making the willow tree into cups and bowls."
Mencius said,
"Can you follow the nature of the willow tree
and make it into cups and bowls?
Or will you mutilate the willow tree
and then make it into cups and bowls?
If you mutilate the willow tree
to make it into cups and bowls,
then must you also mutilate human beings to make them benevolent and righteous?
The one who leads all under Heaven to bring calamity to benevolence and righteousness
will surely be your words!"
11.2 The philosopher Gào said,
"Human nature
is like swirling water.
If a breach is made to the east, it flows east;
if a breach is made to the west, it flows west.
Human nature’s indifference to good and not-good
is like water’s indifference to east and west."
Mencius said,
"Water indeed is indifferent to east and west,
but is it indifferent to up and down?
The goodness of human nature
is like water’s tendency to flow downward.
There is no human being who does not tend toward good;
there is no water that does not tend downward.
Now, if you strike water and make it leap up,
you can make it go over your forehead;
if you dam it and force it,
you can make it go up a mountain.
Is this the nature of water?
It is the force of circumstances that does it.
That human beings can be made to do what is not good
is also like this in their nature."
11.3 The philosopher Gào said,
"Inborn nature is what is meant by 'nature'."
Mencius said,
"Does 'inborn nature is what is meant by nature'
mean the same as 'white is what is meant by white'?"
Gào said,
"Yes."
"Is the whiteness of a white feather
like the whiteness of white snow?
Is the whiteness of white snow
like the whiteness of white jade?"
Gào said,
"Yes."
"Then, is the nature of a dog
like the nature of an ox,
and the nature of an ox
like the nature of a human being?"
11.4 The philosopher Gào said,
"Appetite for food and sex
is nature.
Benevolence
is internal, not external;
righteousness
is external, not internal."
Mencius said,
"Why do you say that benevolence is internal and righteousness is external?"
Gào said,
"That elder I treat as elder
is not because there is an elder in me;
it is like that white I treat as white,
following its whiteness from outside;
therefore I call it external."
Mencius said,
"The whiteness of a white horse
is no different from the whiteness of a white person;
but I do not know if the respect for an old horse
is no different from the respect for an old man?
Moreover, do you say that the elder is righteous,
or that he who treats him as elder is righteous?"
Gào said,
"I love my own younger brother,
but I do not love the younger brother of a man of Qín;
this is because I myself am the one pleased,
so I call it internal.
I respect the elder of a man of Chǔ,
and I also respect my own elder;
this is because the elder is the one pleased,
so I call it external."
Mencius said,
"To relish the roast meat of a man of Qín
is no different from relishing my own roast meat;
with things there is also such a case.
Then does relishing roast meat also have something external?"
11.5 Mèng Jìzǐ asked Gōngdū Zǐ,
"Why do you say that righteousness is internal?"
Gōngdū Zǐ said,
"I practice my reverence,
so I call it internal."
Jìzǐ said, "If a fellow villager is one year older than your elder brother,
whom do you respect?"
Gōngdū Zǐ said,
"I respect my elder brother."
"When pouring wine, whom do you serve first?"
Gōngdū Zǐ said,
"I serve the fellow villager first."
"The one you respect is here,
the one you honor in practice is there;
indeed it is external,
not from within."
Gōngdū Zǐ could not answer,
and reported this to Mencius.
Mencius said,
"Do you respect your uncle,
or do you respect your younger brother?
He will say,
'I respect my uncle.'
Then you say,
'If the younger brother is acting as the impersonator of the dead,
whom do you respect then?'
He will say,
'I respect my younger brother.'
You say,
'Wherein lies the respect for your uncle?'
He will say,
'Because of his position.'
You also say,
'Because of his position.
The constant respect is for the elder brother,
the temporary respect is for the fellow villager.'"
When Jìzǐ heard this, he said,
"Respecting the uncle is respect;
respecting the younger brother is respect;
indeed it is external,
not from within."
Gōngdū Zǐ said,
"In winter we drink hot soup,
in summer we drink cold water.
Then does drinking and eating also lie in external things?"
11.6 Gōngdū Zǐ said,
"The philosopher Gào said,
'Human nature is neither good nor not-good.'
Some say,
'Human nature can become good,
and can become not-good;
thus when King Wén and King Wǔ arose,
the people loved goodness;
when King Yōu and King Lì arose,
the people loved violence.'
Others say,
'There is a nature that is good,
and a nature that is not good;
thus with Yáo as ruler there was Xiàng;
with Gǔsǒu as father there was Shùn;
with Zhòu as nephew of the ruler,
and even as ruler,
there were Wēizǐ Qǐ and Prince Bígān.'
Now you say, 'Human nature is good.'
Then are all these wrong?"
Mencius said,
"As for the genuine feelings of human nature,
they can become good—
that is what I mean by goodness.
As for becoming not-good,
it is not the fault of the innate capacity."
The feeling of compassion
is possessed by all men;
the feeling of shame and dislike
is possessed by all men;
the feeling of reverence and respect
is possessed by all men;
the feeling of right and wrong
is possessed by all men.
The feeling of compassion
is benevolence (Rén);
the feeling of shame and dislike
is righteousness (Yì);
the feeling of reverence and respect
is propriety (Lǐ);
the feeling of right and wrong
is wisdom (Zhì).
Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom
are not infused into us from without;
we inherently have them,
only we do not reflect on them.
Hence it is said:
'Seek and you will find them;
let them go and you will lose them.'
Some differ by twice, five times, or beyond calculation
simply because they cannot fully develop their natural capacity.
The Book of Odes says:
'Heaven generates the multitudes of people;
for every thing there is a rule.
The people hold fast to the constant nature;
they love this excellent virtue.'
Confucius said:
'The one who made this ode
indeed understood the Way (Dào)!
For each thing there must be its rule;
the people hold fast to the constant nature;
therefore they love this excellent virtue.' "
11.7 Mencius said:
"In years of plenty,
most young men are good;
in years of famine,
most young men are violent.
It is not that the natural endowment from Heaven differs in this way;
it is because their hearts are sunk and lost that they become so.
Now consider the wheat:
after sowing and covering it,
if the ground is the same,
and the time of planting is the same,
it grows vigorously,
and by the summer solstice
it all ripens.
Yet there may be differences
due to the richness or poorness of the soil,
the nourishment from rain and dew,
and the unequal human care.
Therefore, all things of the same kind
are generally similar;
why then doubt it only in the case of humans?
The sage is of the same kind as I am.
Hence the Master Lóng said:
'In making sandals without knowing the feet,
I know they will not be woven as baskets.'
The similarity of sandals
is because all feet under heaven are the same.
The mouth likes flavors
and has the same preferences;
Yìyá first grasped what our mouths prefer.
If the mouth's liking for flavors
differed from man to man in nature,
as a horse or dog differs from me in kind,
then why would all under heaven
follow Yìyá in taste?
In matters of taste,
all under heaven look to Yìyá,
meaning all mouths under heaven are similar.
The ear is also like this.
In matters of sound,
all under heaven look to Shīkuàng,
meaning all ears under heaven are similar.
The eye is also like this.
In the case of Zǐdū,
no one under heaven fails to recognize his beauty.
Those who do not recognize Zǐdū's beauty
are those without eyes.
Hence it is said:
The mouth in tasting flavors
has the same preferences;
the ear in hearing sounds
has the same hearing;
the eye in seeing colors
has the same sense of beauty.
Then when it comes to the heart,
alone does it have nothing in common?
What is it that the heart holds in common?
It is, I say, principle (Lǐ)
and righteousness (Yì).
The sage first grasps
what my heart holds in common.
Hence principle and righteousness delight my heart
just as meat delights my mouth."
11.8 Mencius said:
"The trees of Ox Mountain were once beautiful;
but being on the outskirts of a great state,
they were cut down by axes and hatchets.
Could they remain beautiful?
Yet, through the rest and growth of day and night
and the nourishment of rain and dew,
it was not that sprouts and shoots did not grow;
but then cattle and sheep came to graze on them,
and so it became so barren.
People see its barrenness
and think it never had timber;
but is this the nature of the mountain?
Even with what is preserved in humans,
can there be no heart of benevolence and righteousness?
The reason they let go their good heart
is like the axe and hatchet to the trees:
if it is cut down day after day,
can it remain beautiful?
Through the rest and growth of day and night,
the morning air,
their likes and dislikes are barely close to those of others;
but what they do during the day
again fetters and destroys it.
If this fettering is repeated,
then the night air is not enough to preserve it;
if the night air is not enough to preserve it,
then they are not far from beasts.
People see their beastly nature
and think they never had natural capacity;
but is this the true state of humans?
Therefore, if something is properly nurtured,
nothing will not grow;
if it loses its nurture,
nothing will not perish.
Confucius said:
'Hold it, and it remains;
let it go, and it vanishes;
it comes and goes without fixed time,
no one knows its dwelling.'
Is this not about the heart?"
11.9 Mencius said:
"No wonder the king is not wise!
Even with the easiest-to-grow plant in the world,
if you expose it to the sun for one day
and then cool it for ten days,
nothing will grow.
I see him but rarely;
when I withdraw,
those who cool him arrive;
what can I do with his sprouting?
Now consider the art of Go (Yì);
it is a minor art;
without single-minded devotion,
one cannot master it.
Yì Qiū
is the best Go player in the whole state.
Suppose Yì Qiū teaches two men to play Go:
one of them gives his whole mind to it,
listening only to Yì Qiū.
The other, though he listens,
has his mind on a swan about to arrive,
thinking of taking his bow and arrow to shoot it.
Although he studies together with the other,
he does not match him.
Is it because his intelligence is inferior?
I say:
'It is not.' "
11.10 Mencius said:
"Fish
is what I desire;
bear's paw
is also what I desire;
if I cannot have both,
I will forgo the fish and take the bear's paw.
Life
is what I desire;
righteousness
is also what I desire;
if I cannot have both,
I will forgo life and take righteousness.
Life is what I desire,
but what I desire is more than life,
so I do not cling to it improperly;
death is what I hate,
but what I hate is more than death,
so there are calamities I do not avoid.
If what people desire were nothing more than life,
then why would they not use any means to preserve it?
If what people hated were nothing more than death,
then why would they not do anything to avoid calamity?
Thus there are cases where one could live by such means
yet chooses not to use them,
and cases where one could avoid harm by such means
yet chooses not to do so.
Therefore, there are desires greater than life
and aversions greater than death.
It is not only the worthy who have this heart;
all people possess it,
but the worthy are able not to lose it.
A single basket of food,
a single bowl of soup,
if obtained, one lives;
if not, one dies.
If offered with abuse,
even a wayfarer will not accept it;
if offered with trampling,
even a beggar disdains it.
Yet for a salary of ten thousand zhōng, one accepts it without discerning ritual and righteousness.
What benefit is ten thousand zhōng to me?
Is it for the beauty of palaces and halls,
the service of wives and concubines,
or the gratitude of the poor and needy I know?
Formerly, one would rather die than accept;
now, for the beauty of palaces and halls, one does it.
Formerly, one would rather die than accept;
now, for the service of wives and concubines, one does it.
Formerly, one would rather die than accept;
now, for the gratitude of the poor and needy I know, one does it.
Should this not also be stopped?
This is called losing one's original heart."
11.11 Mencius said:
"Benevolence
is the human heart;
righteousness
is the human path.
To abandon the path
and not follow it,
to lose the heart
and not seek it —
how lamentable!
When people let a chicken or dog stray,
they know to seek it;
when they lose their heart,
they do not know to seek it.
The way of learning is nothing else:
it is merely seeking the lost heart."
11.12 Mencius said:
"Now, if there is a nameless finger
bent and cannot straighten,
it does not cause pain or hinder tasks,
yet if someone can straighten it,
one would not consider the Qín-Chǔ road too far,
because the finger is inferior to others.
When a finger is inferior to others,
one knows to dislike it;
when the heart is inferior to others,
one does not know to dislike it.
This is called failing to recognize categories."
11.13 Mencius said:
"For a tóng-zǐ tree of a handspan or armspan girth,
if one wishes it to grow,
one knows how to nurture it.
As for oneself,
one does not know how to nurture oneself.
Does one not love oneself as much as the tóng-zǐ tree?
It is extreme thoughtlessness."
11.14 Mencius said:
"In regard to the body,
one loves every part.
Loving every part,
one nurtures every part.
There is no inch of skin not loved,
and thus no inch of skin not nurtured.
How does one examine what is good and not good?
Is there any other way?
One simply takes from oneself.
The body has noble and base parts,
great and small parts.
Do not harm the great with the small,
do not harm the noble with the base.
Nurturing the small part makes one petty;
nurturing the great part makes one great.
Now, there is a gardener
who neglects the wú-jiǎ
and nurtures the èr-jí;
he is a base gardener.
Nurturing one finger
while losing the shoulder and back,
unaware of it,
he is a man with disorder like a wolf.
A person devoted to eating and drinking
is despised by others,
because he nurtures the small
to the detriment of the great.
If a person devoted to eating and drinking
had no such loss,
then would the mouth and belly
be merely for the inch of skin?"
11.15 Gōngdū Zǐ asked:
"All are equally human,
yet some become great,
some become petty. Why?"
Mencius said:
"Following the greater part
makes one great;
following the smaller part
makes one petty."
[Gōngdū Zǐ] said:
"All are equally human,
yet some follow the greater part,
some follow the smaller part. Why?"
[Mencius] said:
"The offices of the ears and eyes do not think,
and are clouded by things.
When things interact with things,
they merely lead one astray.
The office of the heart is to think;
when it thinks, it attains it;
when it does not think, it does not attain it.
This is what Heaven has given us.
First establish the greater part,
and the smaller part cannot take it away.
This is all it means to be a great person."
11.16 Mencius said:
"There is a noble title of Heaven,
and a noble title of humanity.
Benevolence, righteousness,
loyalty, and trustworthiness,
delighting in good without tiring —
this is the noble title of Heaven.
Dukes, ministers, and high officials —
this is the noble title of humanity.
In ancient times, people
cultivated their noble title of Heaven,
and the noble title of humanity followed.
In modern times, people
cultivate their noble title of Heaven to seek the noble title of humanity;
once they obtain the noble title of humanity, they abandon their noble title of Heaven.
This is the height of delusion,
and in the end they will surely lose it."
11.17 Mencius said:
"To desire nobility
is common to all human hearts.
Everyone has something noble in themselves,
but they do not reflect on it.
What people ennoble
is not true nobility.
What Zhào Mèng ennobles,
Zhào Mèng can debase.
The Book of Odes says:
'Already drunk with wine,
already satiated with virtue.'
This means being full of benevolence and righteousness,
and therefore not desiring the rich flavors of others' fine meats;
having a good reputation and wide praise applied to one's person,
and therefore not desiring the embroidered silks of others."
11.18 Mencius said:
"The victory of benevolence over non-benevolence
is like water overcoming fire.
Those who practice benevolence nowadays
are like using a cup of water to save a cartload of burning firewood;
when the fire is not extinguished,
they say water cannot overcome fire.
This further abets those who are extremely non-benevolent,
and in the end they will surely lose it."
11.19 Mencius said:
"The five grains
are the finest of crops;
if they are not ripe,
they are worse than weeds.
Benevolence, too, depends on ripening."
11.20 Mencius said:
"When Yì taught archery,
he was always intent on drawing the bow to the full;
learners, too, must be intent on drawing to the full.
A great craftsman instructs people
always by the compass and square;
learners, too, must use the compass and square."
12.1 A man from Rén asked Wūlú Zǐ:
"Between ritual and food, which is weighty?"
[Wūlú Zǐ] said:
"Ritual is weighty."
"Between sex and ritual, which is weighty?"
[Wūlú Zǐ] said:
"Ritual is weighty."
[The man] said:
"If one follows ritual in eating, one starves to death;
if one does not follow ritual, one obtains food.
Must one still follow ritual?
If one personally greets the bride, one does not get a wife;
if one does not personally greet, one gets a wife.
Must one still personally greet?"
Wūlú Zǐ could not answer.
The next day, he went to Zōu
and informed Mencius of this.
Mencius said:
"What difficulty is there in answering this?
If you do not measure the base,
but only compare the tops,
a piece of wood an inch square can be made higher than a towering building.
Gold is heavier than feathers —
but is that to say that a hook of gold
and a cartload of feathers are the same?
When you take the gravity of food
and compare it with a minor point of ritual,
how is food alone weighty?
When you take the gravity of sex
and compare it with a minor point of ritual,
how is sex alone weighty?
Go and answer him, saying:
'If twisting your brother's arm and seizing his food
gets you food,
and not twisting
gets you no food,
then would you twist it?
If climbing over the eastern wall and embracing the maiden there
gets you a wife,
and not embracing
gets you no wife,
then would you embrace her?'"
12.2 Cáo Jiāo asked:
"Can everyone become a Yáo or a Shùn?
Is this so?"
Mencius said:
"Yes."
"I hear that King Wén was ten feet tall,
and Tāng was nine feet tall.
Now I am nine feet four inches tall,
yet I can only eat grain.
What should I do?"
Mencius said:
"What is there in that?
Simply do it, that is all.
Suppose there is a man here:
if his strength cannot lift a single chick,
then he is a weak man;
but if today he can lift a hundred jūn,
then he is a strong man.
Thus, if one lifts as much as Wū Huò could,
then that person is a Wū Huò.
Why should a man be troubled by inability?
It is merely a case of not doing it.
Walking slowly behind one's elders
is called respectfulness;
walking quickly ahead of one's elders
is called disrespectfulness.
But is walking slowly
something that a man cannot do?
It is something he does not do.
The way of Yáo and Shùn
is simply filial piety and brotherly respect.
If you wear the clothes of Yáo,
recite the words of Yáo,
and practice the deeds of Yáo,
then you are a Yáo.
If you wear the clothes of Jié,
recite the words of Jié,
and practice the deeds of Jié,
then you are a Jié."
Cáo Jiāo said:
"I have obtained an audience with the ruler of Zōu
and can borrow a lodging.
I wish to stay and receive instruction at your door."
Mencius said:
"The Way is like a great road.
How can it be hard to understand?
The trouble with men is that they do not seek it.
Go home and seek it,
and you will have teachers aplenty."
12.3 Gōngsūn Chǒu asked:
"Gāo Zǐ says:
'The "Xiǎo Pān"
is a poem of a petty man.'"
Mencius said:
"Why does he say so?"
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"Because of its resentment."
Mencius said:
"How rigid is
Master Gāo in his interpretation of poetry!
Suppose there is a man here:
if a man from Yuè draws his bow and shoots at him,
then he will speak of it with laughter and ease;
there is no other reason
than that they are distant from each other.
If his own elder brother draws his bow and shoots at him,
then he will speak of it with tears and sobs;
there is no other reason
than that they are close kin.
The resentment in the "Xiǎo Pān"
is due to loving one's parents.
Loving one's parents
is benevolence.
How rigid indeed
is Master Gāo in his interpretation of poetry!"
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"Why does the "Kǎi Fēng" not show resentment?"
Mencius said:
"In the "Kǎi Fēng",
the parent's fault is small;
in the "Xiǎo Pān",
the parent's fault is great.
If the parent's fault is great and one does not resent it,
that is to become more distant from them.
If the parent's fault is small and one resents it,
that is to be provoked by a trifle.
Becoming more distant
is unfilial;
being provoked by a trifle
is also unfilial.
Confucius said:
'Shùn was indeed the most filial;
at fifty he still yearned for his parents.'"
12.4 Sòng Kēng was about to go to Chǔ.
Mencius met him at Shí Qiū
and said:
"Master, where are you going?"
Sòng Kēng said:
"I have heard that Qín and Chǔ are at war.
I am going to see the King of Chǔ
and persuade him to cease hostilities.
If the King of Chǔ is displeased,
I will go to see the King of Qín
and persuade him to cease.
With these two kings, I hope to find common ground."
Mencius said:
"Allow me not to ask for the details,
but I wish to hear your general idea.
How will you persuade them?"
Sòng Kēng said:
"I will speak of the disadvantages."
Mencius said:
"Your aim is great,
but your approach is not acceptable.
If you persuade the kings of Qín and Chǔ with advantage,
and they, delighted by advantage,
withdraw their armies,
then the soldiers will be pleased to stop
and delight in advantage.
Ministers who
harbor advantage in serving their rulers,
sons who
harbor advantage in serving their fathers,
younger brothers who
harbor advantage in serving their elder brothers —
this means that rulers and ministers,
fathers and sons, and brothers will abandon benevolence and righteousness,
and interact with one another harboring advantage.
Yet such a state without perishing
has never existed.
If you persuade the kings of Qín and Chǔ with benevolence and righteousness,
and they, delighted by benevolence and righteousness,
withdraw their armies,
then the soldiers will be pleased to stop
and delight in benevolence and righteousness.
Ministers who
harbor benevolence and righteousness in serving their rulers,
sons who
harbor benevolence and righteousness in serving their fathers,
younger brothers who
harbor benevolence and righteousness in serving their elder brothers —
this means that rulers and ministers,
fathers and sons,
and brothers will abandon advantage,
and interact with one another harboring benevolence and righteousness.
Yet such a state without becoming a true king
has never existed.
Why must you speak of advantage?"
12.5 Mencius was residing in Zōu.
Jì Rèn was the guardian of Rèn,
and sent gifts of money to Mencius,
who accepted them without acknowledging.
While residing in Píng Lù,
Chǔ Zǐ was the chancellor of Qí,
and sent gifts of money,
which Mencius accepted without acknowledging.
Later, Mencius went from Zōu to Rèn
and visited Jì Zǐ;
but when he went from Píng Lù to Qí,
he did not visit Chǔ Zǐ.
Wū Lú Zǐ was delighted and said:
"I have found a point of doubt."
He asked:
"Master, when you went to Rèn, you visited Jì Zǐ;
but when you went to Qí, you did not visit Chǔ Zǐ.
Was it because he was only a chancellor?"
He replied:
"No.
The Book of History says:
'The offering of tribute is in the many ceremonies;
if the ceremonies are not equal to the goods offered,
it is called no offering,
showing that the attention was not set on the offering.'
This is because it cannot be considered a proper offering."
Wūlú Zǐ was pleased.
Someone asked him about it.
Wūlú Zǐ said:
"Jì Zǐ was unable to go to Zōu,
while Chǔ Zǐ was able to go to Pínglù."
12.6 Chúnyú Kūn said:
"Those who put fame and achievement first
are acting for others;
those who put fame and achievement later
are acting for themselves.
You, Master, were among the three high ministers,
but before your fame and achievements reached
either the ruler or the people, you left.
Would a benevolent man indeed do this?"
Mèng Zǐ said:
"One who, dwelling in a low position,
does not serve a worthy person with an unworthy person,
is Bó Yí;
one who went to Tāng five times
and to Jié five times,
is Yī Yǐn;
one who does not dislike a corrupt ruler
and does not refuse a small office,
is Liǔ Xià Huì.
The ways of these three men were not the same,
but their direction was one.
What was that one thing?
I say:
Benevolence.
The gentleman is simply concerned with benevolence.
Why must they be the same?"
The other said:
"At the time of Duke Mù of Lǔ,
Gōngyí Zǐ was in charge of government,
Zǐ Liǔ and Zǐ Sī were ministers,
yet the reduction of Lǔ's territory became even more severe.
Is this how it is—that the worthy are of no benefit to a state?"
Mèng Zǐ said:
"Yú did not use Bǎilǐ Xī and perished,
while Duke Mù of Qín used him and became hegemon.
If one does not use worthy men, one perishes—
how could one merely have territory reduced?"
The other said:
"In former times,
when Wáng Bào dwelt in Qí,
the people west of the river were good at singing;
when Mián Jū dwelt in Gāotáng,
the people east of Qí were good at singing;
the wives of Huá Zhōu and Qǐ Liáng
were good at weeping for their husbands
and changed the customs of the state.
What is within
must manifest without.
To engage in a matter
and achieve no result—
this I have never seen.
Therefore, there are no worthy men;
if there were, I would surely know them."
Mèng Zǐ said:
"Kǒng Zǐ served as Minister of Crime in Lǔ,
but was not employed;
then when he followed in a sacrifice,
the roasted meat was not sent to him,
so he left without even taking off his ceremonial cap.
Those who did not understand thought it was because of the meat,
while those who understood knew it was because of the lack of propriety.
Yet Kǒng Zǐ himself wanted to leave on account of a minor fault,
and did not wish to leave without cause.
The actions of the gentleman
are indeed not understood by the multitude."
12.7 Mèng Zǐ said:
"The Five Hegemons
were offenders against the Three Kings;
the present feudal lords
are offenders against the Five Hegemons;
the present high ministers
are offenders against the present feudal lords.
When the Son of Heaven visits the feudal lords, it is called a 'tour of inspection';
when the feudal lords appear at the court of the Son of Heaven, it is called 'reporting on duties.'
In spring, he inspects the plowing and aids the deficient;
in autumn, he inspects the harvest and assists the needy.
When entering a region,
if the lands are opened up,
the fields are well cultivated,
the aged are nourished and the worthy honored,
and men of excellence are in office,
then rewards are given;
rewards are given in land.
When entering a region,
if the lands are neglected,
the old are abandoned and the worthy are overlooked,
and cruel officials are in office,
then reprimands are given.
If a feudal lord fails to appear once,
his rank is reduced;
if he fails to appear twice,
his territory is reduced;
if he fails to appear three times,
the army is sent to remove him.
Thus the Son of Heaven executed punishment but did not attack,
while the feudal lords attacked but did not execute punishment.
The Five Hegemons—
they were those who dragged along the feudal lords to attack other feudal lords.
Therefore I say:
'The Five Hegemons
were offenders against the Three Kings.
Among the Five Hegemons,
Duke Huán was the most powerful.
At the assembly of Kuíqiū,
the feudal lords bound the sacrificial animals and placed the documents, but did not taste the blood.
The first command said:
'Execute the unfilial;
do not alter the designated heir;
do not make a concubine the wife.'
The second command said:
'Honor the worthy and foster talent,
to manifest virtue.'
The third command said:
'Respect the old and be kind to the young;
do not forget guests and travelers.'
The fourth command said:
'There should be no hereditary offices for officers;
there should be no concurrent holding of duties;
in selecting officers, get the right men;
do not arbitrarily execute high ministers.'
The fifth command said:
'Do not build crooked embankments;
do not obstruct the sale of grain;
do not make enfiefments without reporting them.'
It was said:
'All of us in this league,
after the covenant,
shall return to good relations.'
The present feudal lords
all violate these five prohibitions.
Therefore I say:
'The present feudal lords
are offenders against the Five Hegemons.'
To abet a ruler's faults
is a small offense;
to anticipate and encourage a ruler's faults
is a great offense.
The present high ministers all encourage their rulers' faults.
Therefore I say:
'The present high ministers
are offenders against the present feudal lords.'"
12.8 Lǔ wished to make Shèn Zǐ a general.
Mèng Zǐ said:
"To use the people without first teaching them
is called afflicting the people.
One who afflicts the people
would not be tolerated in the age of Yáo and Shùn.
If with one battle you defeat Qí
and thus acquire Nányáng,
even so it would not be permissible."
Shèn Zǐ, looking displeased, said:
"This is something that Huá Lí does not understand."
Mèng Zǐ said:
"I will clearly tell you.
The territory of the Son of Heaven is a thousand lǐ square;
without a thousand lǐ,
it is insufficient to receive the feudal lords.
The territory of the feudal lords is a hundred lǐ square;
without a hundred lǐ,
it is insufficient to preserve the records of the ancestral temple.
When the Duke of Zhōu was enfeoffed in Lǔ,
it was a hundred lǐ square;
the land was not insufficient,
yet he restricted himself to a hundred lǐ.
When Tài Gōng was enfeoffed in Qí,
it was also a hundred lǐ square;
the land was not insufficient,
yet he restricted himself to a hundred lǐ.
Now Lǔ has five times a hundred lǐ square.
If a true king were to arise,
do you think Lǔ would be reduced
or increased?
To take from one side and give to the other—
even a benevolent man would not do this,
how much less for one who kills people to obtain it!
The gentleman in serving his ruler
strives to lead his ruler on the proper path,
setting his mind on benevolence alone."
12.9 Mèng Zǐ said:
"Those who now serve rulers
all say,
'We can open up lands for our ruler
and fill his treasuries.'
Those who are called good ministers today
were called thieves of the people in antiquity."
If a ruler does not tend towards the Way,
does not set his mind on benevolence,
and yet one seeks to enrich him,
this is enriching a tyrant like Jié.
'I can bind allied states for you,
and in battle I will surely conquer.'
Those whom people today call good ministers
are what in ancient times were called enemies of the people.
If a ruler does not tend towards the Way,
does not set his mind on benevolence,
and yet one seeks to fight fiercely for him,
this is aiding a tyrant like Jié.
Following the present path,
without changing the present customs,
even if one were given the whole world,
he could not hold it for a single morning."
12.10 Bái Guī said:
"I wish to levy a tax of one part in twenty.
What do you think?"
Mencius said:
"Your way
is the way of the barbarians (Mò).
In a state of ten thousand households,
if only one person made pottery, would that be acceptable?"
He said:
"No,
the vessels would be insufficient for use."
Mencius said:
"In the land of the Mò,
the five grains do not grow,
only millet grows;
there are no city walls,
palaces,
ancestral temples,
or rites of sacrifice,
no feudal lords' gifts of silk and provisions,
and no array of officials with their duties.
Therefore, a tax of one part in twenty suffices.
But now to dwell in the Central States (Zhōngguó),
to cast aside human relations,
and to have no gentlemen (jūnzǐ),
how could that be acceptable?
If potters are too few,
a state cannot even be maintained,
how much less if there are no gentlemen?
Those who wish to make the tax lighter than the way of Yáo and Shùn
are great Mò and small Mò;
and those who wish to make it heavier than the way of Yáo and Shùn
are great Jié and small Jié."
12.11 Bái Guī said:
"My methods of controlling water surpass those of Yǔ."
Mencius said:
"You are mistaken.
When Yǔ controlled the water,
he followed the natural course of the water.
Therefore, Yǔ used the four seas as his drain,
but now you, sir, use neighboring states as your drain.
Water flowing backwards
is called floodwater (jiàng shuǐ).
Floodwater is
a deluge,
which is what benevolent people detest.
You, sir, are mistaken."
12.12 Mencius said:
"If a gentleman lacks good faith (liàng),
how can he hold fast to anything?"
12.13 The state of Lǔ wished to put Yuèzhèngzǐ in charge of government.
Mencius said:
"When I heard of this,
I was so delighted I could not sleep."
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"Is Yuèzhèngzǐ strong?"
He said:
"No."
"Does he have wisdom and foresight?"
He said:
"No."
"Is he widely informed and learned?"
He said:
"No."
"Then why were you delighted and unable to sleep?"
He said:
"In his conduct, he delights in what is good."
"Is delighting in the good sufficient?"
He said:
"Delighting in the good is more than enough for ruling the whole world,
how much more so for the state of Lǔ?
For if one truly delights in what is good,
then everyone within the four seas
will think nothing of a journey of a thousand lǐ
to come and tell him of what is good.
But if one does not delight in what is good,
then people will say with a self-satisfied air,
'I already know it.'
The tone and expression of that self-satisfied air
keeps people at a distance of a thousand lǐ.
If gentlemen are halted a thousand lǐ away,
then slanderous flatterers and face-pleasers will come.
Dwelling with slanderers and flatterers,
even if one wishes to govern the state well,
is it possible?"
12.14 Chén Zǐ said:
"Under what conditions did the gentlemen of antiquity
take office?"
Mencius said:
"There were three circumstances under which they would serve,
and three under which they would leave.
If one is welcomed with utmost respect and propriety,
and when one speaks, one's words are to be put into practice,
then one serves.
If the respect and courtesy have not yet declined
yet one's words are not put into practice,
then one leaves.
Next,
even if one's words are not yet put into practice,
if one is welcomed with utmost respect and propriety,
then one serves.
If the respect and courtesy decline,
then one leaves.
At the lowest level,
if one has no food in the morning,
no food in the evening,
and is so hungry one cannot leave the door,
and the ruler, hearing of it,
says:
'In great matters I cannot carry out his way,
nor can I follow his advice,
but to let him starve on my soil
is shameful for me,'
and provides relief,
then one may accept it,
but only to escape death."
12.15 Mencius said:
"Shùn rose from the midst of the fields,
Fù Yuè was lifted from the building frames,
Jiāo Gé was raised from the fish and salt trade,
Guǎn Yíwú was lifted from the hands of the jailer,
Sūn Shū'áo was raised from the coast,
and Bǎilǐ Xī was lifted from the marketplace.
Thus, when Heaven is about to assign a great responsibility to a person,
it first must embitter his heart and mind,
labor his sinews and bones,
starve his body and skin,
deprive his person of resources,
and frustrate his actions and undertakings,
thereby stirring his mind, hardening his nature,
and increasing his capacities.
People are always prone to error,
and only then can they reform;
they are distressed in mind,
and weighed down in thought,
and only then do they arise;
their countenance shows signs,
and their voice expresses feelings,
and only then are they understood.
Within the state, if there are no law-upholding ministers and remonstrating aides,
and abroad, if there are no hostile states or external troubles,
the state will invariably perish.
Only then does one understand that we live in worry and peril
and die in comfort and ease."
12.16 Mencius said:
"Teaching also has many methods.
For me to disdain teaching someone,
that itself is a form of teaching."
13.1 Mencius said:
"He who exhausts his heart
knows his nature.
Knowing his nature,
he then knows Heaven.
Preserving his heart,
nurturing his nature —
this is the way to serve Heaven.
Whether one dies young or lives long makes no difference;
one cultivates one's person and waits for it —
this is the way to establish one's destiny."
13.2 Mencius said:
"Nothing is not fate,
but accept what is proper;
therefore, one who knows fate
does not stand beneath a crumbling wall.
Dying after fulfilling the Way to the utmost
is proper fate;
dying in shackles and fetters
is not proper fate."
13.3 Mencius said:
"Seek and you will get it;
let go and you will lose it.
This is seeking that benefits the getting,
for what is sought lies within oneself.
Seeking has its proper Way,
and getting depends on fate.
This is seeking that does not benefit the getting,
for what is sought lies outside oneself."
13.4 Mencius said:
"All things are complete within me.
To reflect on oneself and be sincere —
there is no greater joy.
To forcefully practice altruistic conduct
— no path is closer to benevolence."
13.5 Mencius said:
"People act without understanding what they do,
they practice habits without examining them,
they follow these paths all their lives without knowing the Way—
such are the multitude."
13.6 Mencius said:
"A person cannot be without a sense of shame.
To feel shame at being shameless
is to be without shame."
13.7 Mencius said:
"The sense of shame is of great importance to a person.
Those who excel in cunning and deceit
have no use for shame.
If one is not ashamed of being inferior to others,
how can one ever equal them?"
13.8 Mencius said:
"The worthy kings of antiquity
loved goodness and forgot their power;
the worthy scholars of antiquity
were they any different?
They delighted in their Way
and forgot the power of others.
Therefore, if kings and dukes did not show utmost respect and complete courtesy,
they could not gain frequent audiences with them.
If even audiences could not be frequent,
how could they possibly get them as ministers?"
13.9 Mencius said to Sòng Gōujiàn:
"Do you delight in traveling?
I will tell you about traveling.
When others know you, be self-possessed;
when others do not know you, also be self-possessed."
The other said:
"How can one be self-possessed?"
Mencius said:
"Honor virtue and delight in righteousness,
then you can be self-possessed.
Therefore, when a scholar is in straitened circumstances, he does not lose righteousness;
when he is successful, he does not depart from the Way.
If he does not lose righteousness in straitened circumstances,
he thereby finds fulfillment in himself;
if he does not depart from the Way when successful,
the people do not lose hope in him.
The ancients,
when they achieved their ambitions,
bestowed benefits upon the people;
when they did not achieve their ambitions,
they cultivated their own character and became known in the world.
In straitened circumstances, they cultivated themselves alone;
when successful, they brought goodness to all under Heaven."
13.10 Mencius said:
"Those who rise only after King Wén appears
are ordinary people.
As for heroic scholars,
they rise even without King Wén."
13.11 Mencius said:
"If one were given the wealth of the Hán and Wèi families,
and yet regarded it as nothing,
then he would far surpass others."
13.12 Mencius said:
"When the people are employed in the way of ease,
though they labor, they do not complain.
When the people are put to death in the way of life,
though they die, they do not resent the one who kills them."
13.13 Mencius said:
"The people under a hegemon
are joyful and content;
the people under a true king
are broad and serene.
Though they are killed, they do not resent;
though benefited, they do not praise;
the people daily move toward goodness
without knowing who does it.
Where a noble person passes, transformation occurs;
where he abides, the effect is divine.
Above and below, he flows in unison with Heaven and Earth.
Can it be said that this is a small contribution?"
13.14 Mencius said:
"Kind words
do not enter people as deeply as kind sounds;
good government
does not win the people as well as good teaching.
Good government makes the people fear it;
good teaching makes the people love it.
Good government wins the people's wealth;
good teaching wins the people's hearts."
13.15 Mencius said:
"What a person can do without learning
is his innate ability;
what he knows without thinking
is his innate knowledge.
Young children
all know to love their parents;
when they grow up,
they all know to respect their elder brothers.
Loving one's parents
is benevolence;
respecting one's elders
is righteousness.
There is no other reason;
this applies to all under Heaven."
13.16 Mencius said:
"When Shùn lived deep in the mountains,
he dwelled among trees and stones,
and roamed with deer and pigs.
How he differed from the wild men of the mountains
was very slight.
But when he heard one good word
or saw one good deed,
it was like a river bursting its banks—
overwhelming and unstoppable."
13.17 Mencius said:
"Do not do what you would not do;
do not desire what you would not desire.
That is all there is to it."
13.18 Mencius said:
"Those who possess virtue, wisdom, skill, and knowledge
always have some affliction.
Only the lonely minister and the disfavored son
keep their hearts anxious,
and their thoughts about troubles deep,
so they become accomplished."
13.19 Mencius said:
"There are those who serve the ruler;
those who serve a ruler
merely to please him;
there are those who are ministers for the security of the state;
those who find joy in securing the state;
there are those who are people of Heaven;
those who practice the Way only when it can be carried out in all under Heaven;
and there are those who are great persons;
those who rectify themselves, and then all things are rectified."
13.20 Mencius said:
"The noble person has three delights,
and ruling all under Heaven is not among them.
That both parents are alive,
and brothers are without trouble—
this is one delight;
that looking up, one is not ashamed before Heaven,
and looking down, one is not ashamed before others—
this is a second delight;
that one gets the finest talents of all under Heaven
and educates them—
this is a third delight.
The noble person has three delights,
and ruling all under Heaven is not among them."
13.21 Mencius said:
"Broad territory and many people—
the noble person desires these,
but his delight does not lie in them;
standing in the center of all under Heaven,
and settling the people of the four seas—
the noble person delights in this,
but his nature does not lie in it.
What the noble person considers his nature
is not increased even if his Way prevails greatly,
nor diminished even if he lives in poverty—
this is because his portion is fixed.
What the noble person considers his nature
is benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, rooted in his heart.
The complexion it gives
is pure and serene, showing in the face,
filling the back,
and extending to the four limbs—
the four limbs speak of it without words."
13.22 Mencius said:
"Bó Yí fled from Zhòu
and lived by the shore of the North Sea.
Hearing that King Wén had arisen, he stirred and said:
'Why not go back?
I hear that the Western Lord is good at caring for the aged.'
Tàigōng fled from Zhòu
and lived by the shore of the East Sea.
Hearing that King Wén had arisen, he stirred and said:
'Why not go back?
I hear that the Western Lord is good at caring for the aged.'
When there is one in all under Heaven who is good at caring for the aged,
then all benevolent people turn to him as their home.
With a homestead of five mǔ,
plant mulberry trees around the walls,
and let women raise silkworms—
then the aged can be clothed in silk.
Five hens,
two sows,
raised at the proper times—
then the aged can lack no meat.
With a hundred mǔ of fields,
let men cultivate them—
then a family of eight mouths
can have enough without hunger.
What is meant by the Western Lord being good at caring for the aged is that
he regulated the fields and dwellings,
taught the people to plant trees and raise livestock,
and instructed their wives and children
so that they might care for their elders."
Without silk, a person of fifty cannot keep warm;
without meat, a person of seventy cannot be satisfied.
If they are not warm or satisfied,
this is called suffering from cold and hunger.
Among King Wén’s people,
there were no elderly suffering from cold and hunger—
this is what that refers to.”
13.23 Mèngzǐ said:
“Make the fields productive,
lighten the taxes and levies—
then the people can be made wealthy.
Consume resources according to the seasons,
use them according to ritual—
then wealth will be inexhaustible.
The people cannot live without water and fire;
if someone knocks at their door in the dusk
seeking water and fire,
there is no one who will not give them—
such is their abundance.
When a sage governs the world,
he makes grains as abundant as water and fire.
When grains are as abundant as water and fire,
how can the people fail to be benevolent?”
13.24 Mèngzǐ said:
“When Confucius climbed Mount Dōng,
he felt Lǔ was small;
when he climbed Mount Tài,
he felt the whole world was small.
Therefore, for one who has seen the ocean, rivers are hard to find impressive;
for one who has studied at the gate of a sage, words are hard to find adequate.
There is a method for observing water:
one must observe its ripples.
The sun and moon have brightness,
and every crevice that admits light is illuminated.
Flowing water, as a thing,
does not advance until it fills the hollows;
the gentleman, in devoting himself to the Way,
does not reach understanding until he has achieved a mature pattern.”
13.25 Mèngzǐ said:
“Rising at cockcrow,
and tirelessly doing good—
such a person belongs to Shùn’s kind.
Rising at cockcrow,
and tirelessly seeking profit—
such a person belongs to Zhí’s kind.
If you want to know the difference between Shùn and Zhí,
there is nothing else—
it is the gap between profit and goodness.”
13.26 Mèngzǐ said:
“Yáng Zǐ held to self-interest:
even pulling out one hair to benefit the whole world,
he would not do it.
Mò Zǐ held to universal love:
even wearing down his head and heels to benefit the world,
he would do it.
Zǐ Mò held to the middle.
Holding to the middle comes close.
But holding to the middle without balance
is like holding to one extreme.
What I dislike about holding to one extreme is
that it harms the Way—
it raises one thing and abandons a hundred.”
13.27 Mèngzǐ said:
“The hungry find any food sweet,
the thirsty find any drink sweet—
this is not the true taste of food and drink,
because hunger and thirst harm it.
Is it only the mouth and belly that suffer the harm of hunger and thirst?
The human mind also suffers harm.
If a person can avoid letting the harm of hunger and thirst harm the mind,
then not matching others will not cause him worry.”
13.28 Mèngzǐ said:
“Liǔxià Huì would not exchange his integrity
even for the Three Dukes.”
13.29 Mèngzǐ said:
“One who strives
is like one digging a well—
even if he digs to nine rèn
but does not reach the spring,
it is still an abandoned well.”
13.30 Mèngzǐ said:
“Yáo and Shùn
followed their nature;
Tāng and Wǔ
embodied it;
the Five Hégemon
borrowed it.
When something is borrowed for a long time without being returned,
how can one know it is not truly theirs?”
13.31 Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
“Yī Yǐn said:
‘I will not be intimate with those who are disobedient.’
He exiled Tài Jiǎ to Tóng,
and the people were greatly pleased.
When Tài Jiǎ became worthy,
he returned him,
and the people were greatly pleased.
For a worthy person serving as a minister,
if his ruler is not worthy,
can he indeed be exiled?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“If one has Yī Yǐn’s intention,
then it is permissible;
if one lacks Yī Yǐn’s intention,
it is usurpation.”
13.32 Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
“The Book of Odes says:
‘Do not eat without deserving it.’
The gentleman cultivates without farming, yet eats—
why is this?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“When a gentleman dwells in a state,
if the ruler employs him,
the ruler becomes secure, wealthy, honored, and dignified;
if the children and younger brothers follow him,
they become filial, fraternal, loyal, and trustworthy.
‘Do not eat without deserving it’—
what is greater than this?”
13.33 Prince Diàn asked:
“What is the business of a scholar?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“To elevate his aspirations.”
He said:
“What do you mean by elevating his aspirations?”
He said:
“It is simply rén and yì.
To kill one innocent person
is not rén;
to take what is not one’s own
is not yì.
Where does dwelling lie?
It lies in rén.
Where does the path lie?
It lies in yì.
Dwelling in rén and following yì—
the great man’s tasks are complete.”
13.34 Mèngzǐ said:
“Zhòng Zǐ, if offered the State of Qí through unrighteous means,
would not accept it—
everyone believes this.
But this is only the righteousness of refusing a basket of rice and a bowl of soup.
There is no greater fault than losing the bonds of kin,
ruler and minister,
superior and inferior.
To trust his great virtue
based on this small matter—
how can that be acceptable?”
13.35 Táo Yìng asked:
“If Shùn were the Son of Heaven,
and Gāo Yáo were the judge of criminals,
and Gǔ Sǒu killed someone—
what would be done?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“He would be arrested, nothing more.”
He said: “In that case, would Shùn not forbid it?”
He said:
“How could Shùn forbid it?
The authority was received from someone.”
He said: “Then what would Shùn do?”
He said:
“Shùn would regard abandoning the world
like abandoning a worn-out sandal.
He would steal his father away and flee,
settle by the seacoast,
and live joyfully all his life,
so happy that he would forget the world.”
13.36 Mèngzǐ went from Fàn to Qí,
and seeing the King of Qí’s son from afar,
he sighed and said:
“One’s dwelling changes one’s aura,
nourishment changes one’s body—
how great is dwelling!
Are not these all the sons of men?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“The prince’s palaces, carriages, horses, and clothing
are mostly the same as others’,
yet why is the prince like that?
His dwelling makes him so.
How much more is this true for one who dwells in the world’s broad dwelling?
When the ruler of Lǔ went to Sòng,
he called out at the Dié-zé gate.
The guard said:
‘This is not our ruler—
how is it his voice sounds like our ruler?’
This has no other reason—
their dwellings are similar.”
13.37 Mèngzǐ said:
“To feed without loving
is to treat like a pig;
to love without respect
is to keep like a beast.
Respect and reverence
are what exist before the gifts are presented.
If respect and reverence have no substance,
the gentleman cannot be detained by empty forms.”
13.38 Mèngzǐ said:
“Form and color
are one’s natural endowment;
only a sage can then realize his form fully.”
13.39 King Xuān of Qí wished to shorten the mourning period.
Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
"Would it not be better to observe a full year's mourning than to stop altogether?"
Mèngzǐ replied,
"This is like someone twisting his elder brother's arm,
and you telling him, [07-08]'Just do it gently and slowly.' You should simply teach him filial piety and brotherly respect."
There was a prince whose mother had died,
and his tutor requested permission for him to observe several months of mourning.
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked,
"What about such a case?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"This is someone who wishes to complete the full mourning period but cannot.
Even adding a single day
is better than stopping altogether.
I speak of those who are not prevented but simply do not do it."
13.40 Mèngzǐ said,
"There are five ways in which the superior man teaches:
some he transforms like timely rain;
some he helps to perfect their virtue;
some he helps to develop their talents;
some he answers their questions;
and some he influences by private cultivation.
These five are the ways the superior man teaches."
13.41 Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
"The Way is indeed lofty and beautiful,
like climbing to heaven,
seeming unattainable.
Why not make it something people can strive for
and work diligently toward daily?"
Mèngzǐ replied,
"A great craftsman does not discard the plumb line for a clumsy workman;
Yì did not alter his bow-drawing standard for a poor archer.
The superior man draws the bow but does not release the arrow,
showing it in full leap.
He stands in the middle of the Way,
and those with ability follow him."
13.42 Mèngzǐ said,
"When the Way prevails in the world, one follows it with his person;
when the Way does not prevail, one sacrifices his person for the Way.
I have never heard of sacrificing the Way for a person."
13.43 Gōngdū Zǐ said,
"When Téng Gēng was in your school,
he seemed to be treated with due courtesy,
yet you did not answer his questions. Why was that?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"If one asks relying on his noble rank,
or on his worth,
or on his seniority,
or on his meritorious service,
or on old acquaintance,
in all such cases I do not answer.
Téng Gēng had two of these."
13.44 Mèngzǐ said,
"If one stops what should not be stopped,
there is nothing he will not stop.
