If one treats lightly those who should be treated with weight,
there is nothing he will not treat lightly.
Those who advance too quickly
will retreat just as quickly."
13.45 Mèngzǐ said,
"The superior man loves things but does not treat them with benevolence;
he treats the people with benevolence but does not treat them with family affection.
He shows family affection to his kin, then benevolence to the people,
then love to all things."
13.46 Mèngzǐ said,
"The wise have no lack of knowledge, but they prioritize what is urgent;
the benevolent have no lack of love, but they prioritize being close to the worthy.
The wisdom of Yáo and Shùn did not extend to all things;
they attended to urgent matters first.
The benevolence of Yáo and Shùn
did not extend to loving everyone;
they prioritized being close to the worthy.
If one cannot observe three years of mourning,
yet scrutinizes the finer degrees of mourning;
if one wolfs down food and gulps soup,
yet fusses about not using teeth to tear dried meat,
this is called not knowing what is important."
14.1 Mèngzǐ said,
"How unkind was King Huì of Liáng!
The benevolent extend their love from what they love to what they do not love.
The unkind extend their lack of love from what they do not love to what they love."
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked,
"What does this mean?"
"King Huì of Liáng, for the sake of territory,
caused his people to be ruined and sent them to war.
Suffering a great defeat,
he was about to fight again,
fearing he could not win,
he drove the sons he loved to sacrifice themselves.
This is what I mean by
extending from what one does not love to what one loves."
14.2 Mèngzǐ said,
"In the Spring and Autumn period, there were no righteous wars.
One side might be better than another,
but that is all.
A punitive expedition is when a superior attacks an inferior;
states of equal standing do not punish each other."
14.3 Mèngzǐ said,
"If one believed everything in the Book of History,
it would be better to have no Book of History at all.
In the Wu Cheng chapter,
I accept only two or three bamboo strips.
The benevolent are invincible in the world.
When one of utmost benevolence attacks one of utmost unkindness,
how could blood flow so as to float pestles?"
14.4 Mèngzǐ said,
"If someone says,
'I am skilled in formations,
I am skilled in battle,'
that is a great crime.
If a ruler loves benevolence,
he will have no enemy in the world.
When he campaigns to the south, the northern barbarians complain;
when he campaigns to the east, the western barbarians complain,
saying, 'Why does he put us last?'
When King Wǔ attacked Yīn,
he had three hundred war chariots
and three thousand tiger-like warriors.
The king said,
'Do not fear!
I come to bring you peace,
not to be an enemy to the common people.'
Then the people bowed their heads like collapsing horns.
To 'punish' means to 'correct.'
Each desires to correct himself;
what need is there for war?"
14.5 Mèngzǐ said,
"Carpenters and wheelwrights
can give others the compass and square,
but cannot make them skillful."
14.6 Mèngzǐ said,
"When Shùn ate coarse rice and wild herbs,
he seemed as if he would do so for life.
When he became Son of Heaven,
wearing embroidered robes,
playing the lute,
and attended by the two daughters
as if they had always been his, he was as if it were his natural state."
14.7 Mèngzǐ said,
"Only now do I understand the gravity of killing a person's kin:
kill another's father,
and he will kill yours;
kill another's elder brother,
and he will kill yours.
Thus, though not killing them with one's own hand,
it is but one step away."
14.8 Mèngzǐ said,
"In ancient times, customs barriers were set up
to repel violence;
today, customs barriers are set up
to commit violence."
14.9 Mèngzǐ said,
"If one does not practice the Way himself,
he cannot make it practiced even by his wife and children.
If he employs others not according to the Way,
he cannot make even his wife and children follow him."
14.10 Mèngzǐ said,
"Those who are abundant in wealth
cannot be killed by a bad year;
those who are abundant in virtue
cannot be thrown into confusion by a wicked age."
14.11 Mèngzǐ said,
"A person who loves fame can yield a state of a thousand chariots;
but if he is not the right person,
he will show displeasure even over a basket of rice and a bowl of soup."
14.12 Mèngzǐ said,
"If one does not trust the benevolent and worthy,
the state will be empty;
without propriety and righteousness,
the upper and lower orders will be in disorder;
without proper government,
wealth and resources will be insufficient."
14.13 Mèngzǐ said,
"One may gain a state without benevolence,
but gaining all under heaven without benevolence
has never happened."
14.14 Mencius said,
"The people are the most important;
the altars of the soil and grain come next;
the ruler is the least important.
Therefore, winning the hearts of the common people makes one the Son of Heaven;
winning the favor of the Son of Heaven makes one a feudal lord;
winning the favor of a feudal lord makes one a high minister.
If a feudal lord endangers the altars of the soil and grain,
he is replaced.
When the sacrificial victims are ready,
the grain vessels are clean,
and the sacrifices are performed at the proper times,
yet droughts or floods occur,
then the altars of the soil and grain are replaced."
14.15 Mencius said,
"Sages are
teachers for a hundred generations.
Bó Yí and Liǔ Xià Huì are examples.
Thus, those who hear of Bó Yí's character:
the stubborn become honest,
and the weak-willed develop resolve;
those who hear of Liǔ Xià Huì's character:
the mean become generous,
and the petty become broad-minded.
They arose more than a hundred generations ago,
and those who hear of them even a hundred generations later are all inspired.
Could anyone but a sage achieve this?
How much more so for those who were personally influenced by them?"
14.16 Mencius said,
"Rén (humanity)
is what it means to be human.
When combined and spoken of together,
it is the Way."
14.17 Mencius said,
"When Confucius left Lǔ,
he said,
'I am taking my time in leaving;
this is the way to leave the state of one's parents.'
When leaving Qí,
he drained the water from the rice and left immediately;
this is the way to leave another state."
14.18 Mencius said,
"The reasons why the noble man was stranded between Chén and Cài
were because he had no connections with either their superiors or subordinates."
14.19 Mò Jī said,
"I am greatly reviled by many mouths."
Mencius said,
"It does no harm.
A scholar is often annoyed by such many mouths.
The Book of Songs says,
'My heart is anxious and troubled,
I am hated by the crowd of petty men.'
This refers to Confucius.
'Though he did not extinguish their anger,
he also did not diminish his own reputation.'
This refers to King Wén."
14.20 Mencius said,
"The worthy illuminate others with their own clarity;
today, people try to illuminate others with their own confusion."
14.21 Mencius said to Gāo Zǐ,
"A mountain path, once
regularly trodden upon, becomes a road;
if it is left unused for a while,
then weeds will block it.
Now, weeds have blocked your mind."
14.22 Gāo Zǐ said,
"The music of Yǔ
surpasses that of King Wén."
Mencius said,
"How can you say that?"
He replied,
"Because the bell stand is worn through."
Mencius said,
"Is that sufficient proof?
The ruts at the city gate—
are they made by just two horses?"
14.23 Qí was suffering a famine.
Chén Zhēn said,
"Everyone in the state thinks that you
will again open the granary of Táng.
Perhaps you should not do it again."
Mencius said,
"This would be like Féng Fù.
There was a man of Jìn named Féng Fù
who was skilled at wrestling tigers,
and later became a good man.
Then he went to the wilderness,
where a crowd was chasing a tiger.
The tiger backed into a corner,
and no one dared to confront it.
They saw Féng Fù
and ran to welcome him.
Féng Fù rolled up his sleeves and got out of his carriage.
Everyone was delighted,
but the scholars laughed at him."
14.24 Mencius said,
"The mouth's relation to flavors,
the eye's relation to colors,
the ear's relation to sounds,
the nose's relation to smells,
and the four limbs' relation to ease and comfort—
these are aspects of human nature,
yet they are also subject to destiny;
the noble man does not call them 'nature' simply.
The relation of rén (humanity) to father and son,
the relation of yì (righteousness) to ruler and minister,
the relation of lǐ (ritual) to guest and host,
the relation of zhì (wisdom) to the worthy,
and the relation of the sage to the Heavenly Way—
these are matters of destiny,
yet they also have an aspect of human nature;
the noble man does not call them 'destiny' simply."
14.25 Hào Shēng Bù Hài asked,
"What kind of person is
Yuè Zhèng Zǐ?"
Mencius said,
"He is a good person,
a trustworthy person."
"What is meant by 'good'?
What is meant by 'trustworthy'?"
Mencius said,
"Being desirable is called 'good';
having it within oneself is called 'trustworthy';
being fully realized in oneself is called 'beautiful';
being fully realized and shining forth is called 'great';
being great and transforming others is called 'sage';
being sage and unfathomable is called 'spirit.'
Yuè Zhèng Zǐ is
between the first two
and below the last four."
14.26 Mencius said,
"Those who flee from Mò Zǐ's school will inevitably turn to Yáng Zhū's school;
those who flee from Yáng Zhū's school will inevitably turn to the Confucian school.
When they come,
we simply accept them.
Now, those who debate with the followers of Yáng Zhū and Mò Zǐ
are like people chasing a stray pig:
once it has entered the pigsty,
they then tie it up as well."
14.27 Mencius said,
"There are taxes on cloth and silk,
taxes on grain,
and taxes on labor service.
The noble man uses only one of these
and defers the other two.
If two are used,
the people will die of starvation;
if three are used,
fathers and sons will be separated."
14.28 Mencius said,
"A feudal lord's treasures are three:
land, people, and governance.
Those who treasure pearls and jade
will surely bring disaster upon themselves."
14.29 Péng Chéng Kuò held office in Qí.
Mencius said,
"Péng Chéng Kuò will meet his death!"
Péng Chéng Kuò was killed,
and a disciple asked,
"How did you know he would be killed?"
Mencius said,
"His character
has minor talents,
but he has not learned the great Way of the noble man—
this is enough to bring about his own death."
14.30 Mencius went to Téng
and lodged in the upper palace.
A pair of unfinished sandals were on the window,
and the innkeeper searched for them but could not find them.
Someone asked him,
"Is it possible that your followers have hidden them?"
Mencius said,
"Do you think they came here to steal sandals?"
The other replied,
"Probably not."
Mencius said, "In establishing my school,
I do not pursue those who leave,
nor do I turn away those who come.
If they come with such an intention,
I simply accept them."
14.31 Mencius said,
"Everyone has things they cannot bear to do;
extending this to what they can bear
is rén (humanity).
Everyone has things they will not do;
extending this to what they do
is yì (righteousness).
If people can extend their mind that does not wish to harm others,
then their rén will be inexhaustible.
If people can extend their mind that does not engage in burglary or theft,
then their yì will be inexhaustible.
If people can extend their mind that refuses to be treated with contempt,
then nowhere they go will they fail to act with yì.
When a scholar speaks when he should not speak,
this is to entice with words;
when he does not speak when he should speak,
this is to entice with silence—
both are like burglary or theft."
Mencius said,
"Words that are near at hand but point to far-reaching principles
are good words.
To keep to what is simple while extending it broadly
is the good Way.
The words of a gentleman
do not go beyond what is right before him,
yet the Way is present in them.
What a gentleman guards
is the cultivation of his own person,
and thereby the whole world is brought to peace.
People's fault is that they neglect their own field
and weed the fields of others.
What they demand of others is heavy,
but what they take upon themselves is light."
Mencius said,
"Yáo and Shùn
acted through their innate nature;
Tāng and Wǔ
returned to it through effort.
To move, to change expression, and to behave in every gesture fully according to ritual
is the utmost of abundant virtue.
To weep in mourning for the dead with genuine grief
is not for the sake of the living.
To practice virtue without deviating
is not for the sake of seeking emolument.
Words must always be trustworthy
not to make one's conduct appear correct.
The gentleman acts according to the standard,
simply awaiting his destiny."
Mencius said,
"When persuading a great person,
one should look down upon them,
not regarding their awe-inspiring height.
Though their halls are several rèn high,
and their rafters project several chǐ,
if I were to attain my ambition, I would not do such things.
Though before them food is spread over a zhàng square,
and they have several hundred attendant concubines,
if I were to attain my ambition, I would not do such things.
Though they indulge in music and drink,
drive about in hunting,
with a thousand chariots following behind,
if I were to attain my ambition, I would not do such things.
What they do
is all that I would not do;
what I do
is all according to the ancient standards.
Why should I stand in awe of them?"
Mencius said,
"There is no better way to nourish the mind than to reduce desires.
If a person has few desires,
though there might be some loss of the mind,
it is slight.
If a person has many desires,
though there might be some preservation of the mind,
it is slight."
Zēng Xī was fond of the zao fruit,
and Zēng Zǐ could not bear to eat zao fruit.
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked,
"Which is more delicious, minced meat or the zao fruit?"
Mencius said,
"Minced meat, of course!"
Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
"Then why did Zēng Zǐ eat minced meat
but not the zao fruit?"
Mencius said,
"Minced meat is something that is shared in common,
while the zao fruit is something personal.
In tabooing names, one does not taboo the surname,
for the surname is shared,
while the personal name is unique."
Wàn Zhāng asked,
"When Confucius was in Chén,
he said,
'Why not return home!
The young men of my school are ambitious and impetuous,
striving to advance,
not forgetting their original intentions.'
When Confucius was in Chén,
why did he long for the wild-minded scholars of Lǔ?"
Mencius said,
"Confucius
'could not find those who followed the middle Way to associate with,
so he had to take the wild and the aloof!
The wild advance eagerly,
while the aloof refrain from doing certain things.'
Did Confucius not desire the middle Way?
Since he could not be sure of finding it,
he thought of the next best."
"May I ask what kind of person qualifies as wild?"
Mencius said,
"Men like Qín Zhāng, Zēng Xī, and Mù Pí
were what Confucius called wild."
"Why were they called wild?"
Mencius said,
"Their ambitions were lofty and clamorous,
saying,
'The ancients!
The ancients!'
Yet when one examined their conduct,
it fell short.
Since the wild could not be found,
he wanted to associate with those who looked down on the impure,
that is, the aloof,
who were the next in order.
Confucius said,
'Those who pass my door but do not enter my chamber—
I am not grieved by them—
they are only the village honest men!
The village honest man
is the thief of virtue.'"
[Wàn Zhāng] said,
"What kind of person qualifies as a village honest man?"
Mencius said,
"Why are they so clamorous?
Their words do not match their conduct,
nor their conduct their words,
and yet they say,
'The ancients! The ancients!'
Why do they walk so alone and aloof?
Born in this age,
they act for this age,
and whatever is good enough is fine.
Those who fawningly flatter the world
are the village honest men."
Wàn Zǐ said,
"Everyone in the village calls them honest men,
and wherever they go, they are seen as honest men.
Yet Confucius regarded them as thieves of virtue—
why?"
Mencius said,
"If you criticize them, nothing can be singled out;
if you attack them, nothing can be attacked.
They go along with the vulgar ways,
fit in with the corrupt world.
In their dwelling, they seem loyal and trustworthy;
in their conduct, they seem incorruptible and pure.
All are pleased with them,
and they consider themselves right,
yet they cannot be admitted into the Way of Yáo and Shùn.
Therefore they are called
'the thieves of virtue.' Confucius said,
'I hate what is similar but not genuine:
I hate the darnel weed,
for fear it will confuse the grain;
I hate flattery,
for fear it will confuse righteousness;
I hate glib talk,
for fear it will confuse good faith;
I hate the music of Zhèng,
for fear it will confuse true music;
I hate the color purple,
for fear it will confuse vermilion;
I hate the village honest man,
for fear he will confuse virtue.'
The gentleman simply returns to the constant standard.
When the constant standard is correct,
then the common people will be roused;
when the common people are roused,
there will be no wickedness."
Mencius said,
"From Yáo and Shùn down to Tāng,
there were over five hundred years.
Men like Yǔ and Gāo Yáo
saw and knew the Way;
men like Tāng
heard and knew it.
From Tāng down to King Wén,
there were over five hundred years.
Men like Yī Yǐn and Lái Zhū
saw and knew it;
men like King Wén
heard and knew it.
From King Wén down to Confucius,
there were over five hundred years.
Men like Tài Gōng Wàng and Sàn Yīshēng
saw and knew it;
men like Confucius
heard and knew it.
From Confucius down to the present,
there have been over a hundred years.
The age of the sages is not far from us—
indeed, it is very near;
